meta.title: Digital health care job roles reference
meta.disclaimer: This is an illustrative reference profile for a generic digital health care organisation. It is not an official job description for any employer, and its job evaluation scores are not a formal evaluation.

bands.title: Band 1
bands.knowledge: Basic literacy and numeracy; learns simple routine tasks on the job.
bands.autonomy: Follows clear instructions; work is checked often.

bands.title: Band 2
bands.knowledge: Knows the routines and procedures of the work area; may hold an entry qualification.
bands.autonomy: Works to set procedures, with supervision available.
bands.leadership: May show new starters routine tasks.
bands.accountability: Quality and timeliness of own routine work.

bands.title: Band 3
bands.knowledge: Knowledge of a range of procedures, some non-routine; typically a level 3 qualification or equivalent experience.
bands.autonomy: Works within procedures; decides how to organise own work; refers problems upward.
bands.scope: Own work and some tasks for the wider team.
bands.leadership: May allocate routine work or train others in procedures.
bands.accountability: Accuracy of own work and of records kept.

bands.title: Band 4
bands.knowledge: Detailed knowledge of the work area, typically from a foundation degree, apprenticeship, or equivalent experience.
bands.autonomy: Works within guidelines; resolves most day-to-day problems; manager available for advice.
bands.scope: Own work and a defined service or process.
bands.leadership: May supervise a small team or coordinate others' work.
bands.accountability: Delivery of a defined service or process.

bands.title: Band 5
bands.knowledge: Professional or technical knowledge, typically from a degree or equivalent experience.
bands.autonomy: Works to broad objectives within professional standards; plans own work.
bands.scope: Own professional work within a team or product.
bands.leadership: May guide and check the work of support staff and apprentices.

bands.title: Band 6
bands.knowledge: Specialist knowledge across a range of procedures, built through further training or experience.
bands.autonomy: Works independently; interprets policy for own area; seeks advice on complex issues.
bands.leadership: May lead a small team or mentor colleagues.
bands.accountability: Outcomes of own workstream and quality of advice given.

bands.title: Band 7
bands.knowledge: Highly developed specialist knowledge, typically to master's level or equivalent experience.
bands.autonomy: Works to organisational policy; decides how results are achieved; is the expert others consult.
bands.scope: Several products or services, or a specialist function.
bands.leadership: Leads a team or a professional practice area.
bands.accountability: Delivery of a service or specialist function, and its budget if held.

bands.title: Band 8a
bands.knowledge: Expert knowledge of a discipline and its management.
bands.autonomy: Interprets organisational policy for a service; sets the team's direction.
bands.scope: A service area or a discipline across the organisation.
bands.leadership: Manages a team, or leads a discipline without line management.
bands.accountability: A service area, its staff, and its budget.

bands.title: Band 8b
bands.knowledge: Expert knowledge across several disciplines or a large service.
bands.autonomy: Shapes policy and strategy for a large area.
bands.scope: Several services or teams, or a principal-level discipline.
bands.leadership: Manages managers, or is the principal authority in a discipline.
bands.accountability: Several services, their staff, and their budgets.

bands.title: Band 8c
bands.knowledge: Expert knowledge, and wide organisational and sector understanding.
bands.autonomy: Sets strategy for a function; accountable to a director.
bands.leadership: Leads a function through several management layers.
bands.accountability: A function's performance, workforce, and budget.

bands.title: Band 8d
bands.knowledge: Strategic knowledge across functions and the wider health and care system.
bands.autonomy: Shapes organisation-wide strategy; deputises for a director.
bands.scope: A major function or several functions.
bands.leadership: Leads several functions or a large department.
bands.accountability: Major functions, large budgets, and organisation-wide risks.

bands.title: Band 9
bands.autonomy: Sets organisation strategy with the executive team.
bands.scope: The organisation, and its partners across the system.

factors.name: Communication and relationship skills
factors.description: Skills needed to communicate with, and build relationships with, colleagues, patients, the public, and partners. Considers how complex, sensitive, or contentious the information is, and any barriers to understanding or acceptance.

levels.1: Gives and receives routine information orally, mainly with colleagues.
levels.2: Gives and receives routine information orally, in writing, or electronically, with colleagues and others.
levels.3: Gives routine information needing tact or persuasion, or complex or sensitive information, or straightforward training to groups.
levels.4: Gives complex, sensitive, or contentious information needing persuasion, negotiation, or training skills, or highly complex information.
levels.5: Gives highly complex or contentious information needing developed persuasion and negotiation, presents to large groups, or communicates where there are significant barriers to acceptance.
levels.6: Gives highly complex, highly contentious information where there are significant barriers to acceptance, using the highest level of communication skills.

factors.name: Knowledge, training, and experience
factors.description: The knowledge and experience needed to do the job, from any source, including formal training, qualifications, and experience.

levels.1: A few routine procedures, learned on the job in a short induction.
levels.2: A range of routine procedures, learned through on-the-job training and induction.
levels.3: A range of procedures, some non-routine, needing base-level theory (for example a level 3 qualification or equivalent experience).
levels.4: A range of procedures, mostly non-routine, needing intermediate theory (for example a foundation degree or equivalent experience).
levels.5: Expertise in a specialism, underpinned by theory or practical experience (degree level or equivalent).
levels.6: Specialist knowledge across the range of the specialism (postgraduate diploma level or equivalent).
levels.7: Highly developed specialist knowledge across the range of the specialism (master's level or equivalent).
levels.8: Advanced knowledge (doctorate plus further training or equivalent), or specialist knowledge across more than one discipline built over a long period.

factors.name: Analytical and judgemental skills
factors.description: The analysis and judgement needed to process information, solve problems, and make decisions.

levels.1: Judgements on straightforward facts or situations.
levels.2: Judgements on facts or situations, some needing analysis.
levels.3: Judgements on a range of facts or situations needing analysis or comparison of options.
levels.4: Judgements on complex facts or situations needing analysis, interpretation, and comparison of options.
levels.5: Judgements on highly complex facts or situations needing analysis, interpretation, and comparison of options.

factors.name: Planning and organisational skills
factors.description: The planning and organising needed to run activities, programmes, services, or strategies.

levels.2: Plans straightforward tasks or activities, some ongoing.
levels.3: Plans several complex activities, adjusting plans as needed.
levels.4: Plans a broad range of complex activities or strategies, adjusting them as needed.
levels.5: Forms long-term strategic plans, with uncertainty and effects across the organisation.

factors.name: Physical skills
factors.description: The physical skills needed, such as dexterity, coordination, keyboard skills, and driving.

levels.2: Skills gained through practice, such as standard keyboard use or driving.
levels.3: Developed skills needing speed or accuracy, such as advanced keyboard use.
levels.4: Highly developed skills needing precision or speed and high hand–eye coordination.
levels.5: The highest level of precision, speed, and coordination.

factors.name: Responsibility for patient and client care
factors.description: Responsibility for assessing, treating, caring for, or advising patients and clients. For most digital and corporate roles this is incidental contact only.

levels.1: Helps patients, clients, or relatives during incidental contact.
levels.2: Gives general non-clinical advice, information, or services directly to patients or the public.
levels.3: Gives personal care, basic clinical technical services, or basic clinical advice.
levels.4: Carries out clinical care, provides clinical technical services, or advises on the care of patients.
levels.5: Develops programmes of care, provides specialist clinical technical services, or gives specialised advice on patient care.
levels.6: Develops specialised care, gives highly specialised advice, or is accountable for part of a clinical service.
levels.7: Accountable for delivering a clinical or care service.
levels.8: Corporate responsibility for clinical or care services.

factors.name: Responsibility for policy and service development
factors.description: Responsibility for developing and implementing policies and services, and how far the effects reach.

levels.1: Follows policies set by others; may comment on changes.
levels.2: Implements policies for own area and proposes changes to its practices.
levels.3: Implements policies for own area and proposes changes that affect other areas.
levels.4: Implements policy and develops policy or services for a service or several areas.
levels.5: Implements and develops a range of policies or services for a directorate.
levels.6: Corporate responsibility for major policy or service development across or beyond the organisation.

factors.name: Responsibility for financial and physical resources
factors.description: Responsibility for money, budgets, equipment, stock, buildings, and other assets.

levels.1: Takes personal care of equipment and resources used in own work.
levels.2: Handles cash or valuables, looks after equipment used by others, controls stock, or authorises small payments.
levels.3: Authorises payments, buys some assets or supplies, monitors or holds a delegated budget, or maintains assets.
levels.4: Holds or sets the budget for a department or service, or buys or maintains its assets.
levels.5: Holds or sets budgets, or manages assets, for several services.
levels.6: Corporate responsibility for the organisation's finances or assets.

factors.name: Responsibility for people
factors.description: Responsibility for managing, supervising, training, or developing staff, or for providing people (HR) services.

levels.1: Shows own work routines to new or less experienced colleagues.
levels.2: Supervises or coordinates staff day to day, trains others regularly, or gives basic HR advice.
levels.3: Manages a group of staff day to day, teaches core or specialist training, or gives core HR advice.
levels.4: Line manages a function or department, designs training programmes as a main duty, or delivers a full range of HR services.
levels.5: Line manages several departments, or manages training or a large part of HR across the organisation.
levels.6: Corporate responsibility for the organisation's people or HR function.

factors.name: Responsibility for information resources
factors.description: Responsibility for information and information systems, paper or digital, including records, data, and the systems that hold them.

levels.1: Records information that the job holder produces.
levels.2: Enters or stores data compiled by others, or occasionally writes reports or queries.
levels.3: Takes formal minutes, regularly writes reports or queries, or maintains information systems as a significant duty.
levels.4: Adapts or designs information systems to others' specifications, or runs information systems for a department as the main duty.
levels.5: Designs and develops major information systems, or runs information systems for several services as the main duty.
levels.6: Manages and develops information systems across the organisation as the main duty.
levels.7: Corporate responsibility for the organisation's information systems.

factors.name: Responsibility for research and development
factors.description: Responsibility for formal research, development, evaluation, audits, testing, and trials.

levels.1: Carries out surveys or audits for own work; occasionally takes part in research or testing.
levels.2: Regularly does research, development, trials, or equipment and system testing as part of the job.
levels.3: Carries out research or development within formal programmes as a main duty.
levels.4: Coordinates and carries out research and development programmes.
levels.5: Initiates and develops research and development programmes that support the organisation's objectives.
levels.6: Initiates and develops research and development programmes with effects beyond the organisation.

factors.name: Freedom to act
factors.description: How far the job holder decides what to do and how, and how closely their work is supervised.

levels.1: Works within set procedures, with supervision close by.
levels.2: Follows standard procedures and precedent; someone is usually available to ask; work may be checked.
levels.3: Follows defined policies and procedures; work is managed rather than supervised.
levels.4: Results are defined, but the job holder decides how to achieve them, within broad policy.
levels.5: Works within general policies, and in most cases decides how to interpret them.
levels.6: Interprets overall policy and strategy to set goals and standards.

factors.name: Physical effort
factors.description: The physical effort needed, considering its frequency, duration, and intensity.

levels.1: Sitting, standing, and walking, with little physical effort.
levels.2: Frequent sitting or standing in a restricted position, or occasional light to moderate effort.
levels.3: Frequent light effort for long periods, or frequent moderate effort for short periods.
levels.4: Ongoing light effort, frequent moderate effort for long periods, or occasional intense effort.
levels.5: Ongoing moderate effort, or frequent intense effort.

factors.name: Mental effort
factors.description: The concentration needed, considering its frequency, duration, and how predictable the work is.

levels.1: General attention; occasional concentration on predictable work.
levels.2: Frequent concentration on predictable work, or occasional concentration on unpredictable work.
levels.3: Frequent concentration on unpredictable work, or occasional prolonged concentration.
levels.4: Frequent prolonged concentration, or occasional intense concentration.

factors.name: Emotional effort
factors.description: The emotional demands of the job, from direct or indirect exposure to distressing circumstances, such as reading distressing case records or handling serious incidents.

levels.1: Rare exposure, or occasional indirect exposure, to distressing circumstances.
levels.2: Occasional exposure, or frequent indirect exposure, to distressing circumstances.
levels.3: Frequent exposure to distressing circumstances, or occasional exposure to highly distressing ones.
levels.4: Occasional exposure to traumatic circumstances, or frequent exposure to highly distressing ones.

factors.name: Working conditions
factors.description: Exposure to unpleasant conditions or hazards. Near-continuous screen use on most days counts at level 2.

levels.2: Occasional unpleasant conditions, frequent travel or outdoor work, or near-continuous screen use on most days.
levels.3: Frequent unpleasant conditions, or occasional highly unpleasant ones.
levels.4: Some exposure to hazards, or frequent highly unpleasant conditions.

skills.name: Accessibility
skills.description: Accessibility involves ensuring your service can be used by as many people as possible, including those with impaired vision, motor difficulties, cognitive impairments, learning disabilities and deafness.

levels.awareness:
You can:
- understand accessibility and that users have different accessibility needs
- help fix accessibility issues under the direction of others
levels.working:
You can:
- understand users have different accessibility needs
- build user interfaces that meet accessibility standards and fix accessibility issues under the direction of others
levels.practitioner:
You can:
- build user interfaces that meet a predefined set of standards
- champion accessibility to internal stakeholders
- offer design feedback to mitigate the risk of failing accessibility testing
- offer recommendations on the best tools and methods to use when accessibility testing
levels.expert:
You can:
- show a strong understanding of accessibility and be an advocate for users with accessibility needs
- build user interfaces that meet a predefined set of standards
- champion accessibility to internal and external stakeholders
- offer design solutions to mitigate the risk of failing accessibility testing
- recommend the best tools and methods to use when accessibility testing

esco.label: test system accessibility for users with special needs

skills.name: Adapting to delivery methodologies
skills.description: Adapting to delivery methodologies involves contributing to discussions on the appropriate delivery methodology to use, and adapting your approach based on the delivery methodology of the team.

levels.awareness:
You can:
- explain the differences between delivery methodologies, such as scrum or kanban
- explain how your approach would change based on the delivery methodology
- explain why iteration is important
- explain how roles in a multidisciplinary team work together to support delivery
levels.working:
You can:
- explain how products and services are delivered through different methodologies
- follow an appropriate approach to complete your work within the delivery methodology used by your team
- adapt how you work and the work you produce based on your team's delivery methodology to ensure you deliver value
- adapt how you work with other roles in a multidisciplinary team in line with the delivery methodology
levels.practitioner:
You can:
- determine the approach for your role within the team's delivery methodology
- define and agree the scope of delivery for your role within a multidisciplinary team
- negotiate and agree delivery priorities with the team and relevant stakeholders
- clearly communicate the value of iterative delivery and realising benefits early
levels.expert:
You can:
- set and iterate standards for working within different delivery methodologies
- actively promote collaboration and agreement to ensure the team delivers value at the right time
- experiment with new and innovative ways of working to enhance delivery outcomes
- research new and evolving delivery methodologies and identify how your role would work within them

skills.name: Agile and Lean practices
skills.description: Agile and Lean practices involves encouraging teams to build incrementally, test and iterate their work based on regular feedback and other useful data.

levels.awareness:
You can:
- explain the basic principles of Agile and Lean methodology
- discuss ways to apply Agile and Lean principles in a multi-disciplinary team
- explain why iteration is important
levels.working:
You can:
- demonstrate experience in applying Agile principles in practice
- provide a clear, open and transparent framework in which teams can deliver
- show an awareness of Agile tools and are starting to use them intelligently
- visualise and make visible the work of the team
levels.practitioner:
You can:
- compare and select the most appropriate delivery methods and processes
- recognise, reflect and adapt when something does not work, encouraging experimentation
- use a blended approach depending on the context
- help teams to measure, evaluate and visualise outcomes
- encourage reflective practice to improve ways of working
levels.expert:
You can:
- coach and lead teams in Agile and Lean good practices
- create and tailor the right approach for a team, challenging, evaluating and iterating the approach through the life cycle
- experiment with new and innovative ways of working to improve delivery across the organisation
- act as a recognised expert and advocate for Agile and Lean approaches

skills.name: Agile research practices
skills.description: Agile delivery involves encouraging teams to build incrementally, test and iterate their work based on regular feedback and other useful data.

levels.awareness:
You can:
- describe agile working and the roles in a multidisciplinary digital team
levels.working:
You can:
- understand and explain the benefits and limitations of agile working
- design and conduct your research so the findings can be embedded into an agile workflow
- understand and work with the different roles in a multidisciplinary digital team to plan and do user research
levels.practitioner:
You can:
- advocate for agile working
- adapt how you design and conduct research to respond to the complexity of the product environment
- understand the strategic decisions the team needs to make so you can design appropriate research
- influence decisions about priorities and agile processes in the team
levels.expert:
You can:
- advocate for agile working at the organisational level and with senior stakeholders
- help organisations adopt agile research practices
- set standards and expectations of how research insights should be delivered to support delivery by agile teams
- coach and guide other user researchers to adopt agile ways of working

skills.name: Agile working
skills.description: Agile delivery involves encouraging teams to build incrementally, test and iterate their work based on regular feedback and other useful data.

levels.awareness:
You can:
- show an awareness of Agile methodology and the ways to apply the principles in practice
- take an open-minded approach
- explain why iteration is important
- iterate quickly
levels.working:
You can:
- demonstrate experience working in Agile, and an awareness of Agile tools and how to use them
- advise colleagues on how and why Agile methods are used and provide a clear, open and transparent framework in which teams can deliver
- adapt and reflect and be resilient
- see outside of the process
levels.practitioner:
You can:
- identify and compare the best processes or delivery methods to use, including measuring and evaluating outcomes
- help the team to decide the best approach
- help teams to manage and visualise outcomes, prioritise work and adhere to agreed minimum viable product (MVP), priorities and scope
levels.expert:
You can:
- coach and lead teams in Agile and Lean practices, determining the right approach for the team to take and evaluating this through the life of a project
- think of new and innovative ways of working to achieve the right outcomes
- act as a recognised expert and advocate for the approaches, continuously reflecting and challenging the team

skills.name: Analysis
skills.description: Analysis involves examining, interpreting and analysing data to help make informed decisions.

levels.awareness: This skill level is currently not defined.
levels.working:
You can:
- apply the approach to real problems and consider all relevant information
- apply appropriate rigour to ensure a full solution is designed and achieves the business outcome
levels.practitioner:
You can:
- monitor the analysis of a technical solution and ensure analysis is reused for similar problem sets
- review solutions and identify areas for change
- drive the collection of information that is used and analysed
- feed back on policy and requirements
levels.expert:
You can:
- provide direction and lead on change regarding factors that feed into analysis
- monitor changes in the technical environment and assess whether risks are still at acceptable levels or whether previous decisions need to be revisited
- direct and influence others on best practice and policy

skills.name: Analysis and insight
skills.description: Analysis and insight involves examining, interpreting and analysing data to help make informed decisions.

levels.awareness: This skill level is currently not defined.
levels.working:
You can:
- understand and work with colleagues to apply core techniques for analysis and insight
- present clear insights that colleagues can understand and use
levels.practitioner:
You can:
- understand and help teams to apply a range of techniques to analyse data and provide insight
- be proactive and present compelling findings that inform wider decisions
- apply innovative approaches to resolve problems
levels.expert:
You can:
- understand, teach and supervise a wide range of analysis techniques
- help organisations create and learn from strategic insights
- apply innovative approaches to resolve problems

levels.awareness:
You can:
- show an awareness of the need for careful analysis of research data to produce clear findings
levels.working:
You can:
- understand how to apply basic techniques for the analysis of research data and synthesis of findings
- effectively involve your team in analysis and synthesis
- present clear findings that colleagues can understand and use
levels.practitioner:
You can:
- understand and help teams to apply a range of methods to analyse research data and synthesise findings
- effectively engage sceptical colleagues in analysis and synthesis
- advise on the choice and application of techniques, and can critique colleagues’ findings to assure best practice
levels.expert:
You can:
- help an organisation to adopt a wide range of analysis and synthesis techniques, and to continually assure, improve and innovate their practices to generate clear and valuable findings

skills.name: Applied maths, statistics and scientific practices
skills.description: Applied mathematics and statistics involves applying analytical methods including exploratory data analysis, visualisation and statistical testing to help make accurate recommendations.

levels.awareness:
You can:
- show an understanding of the benefits of applied mathematics and statistics, and can use this knowledge to carry out data science tasks
- carry out general analysis techniques for data inspection, exploration and visualisation
- interpret statistical output effectively and accurately
- show an awareness of different performance and accuracy metrics for statistical assessment and validation
levels.working:
You can:
- apply analytical methods including exploratory data analysis and statistical testing to a specific data set, to reach accurate and reliable conclusions
- understand and use different performance and accuracy metrics for model validation in data science projects, hypothesis testing and information retrieval
- compare selected applied mathematics and statistical methods and identify their differences
- access and use the statistical and scientific tools available within the organisation
levels.practitioner:
You can:
- apply designated quantitative techniques such as time series analysis, optimisation and simulation to create and embed appropriate models for analysis and prediction
- provide guidance on matching data sources with relevant applied mathematics and statistical techniques to meet analysis goals
- apply appropriate statistical techniques to available data to discover new relations and offer insight into research problems, helping to improve organisational processes and support decision making
- access and use the statistical tools available within the organisation
levels.expert:
You can:
- identify opportunities to develop statistical insight, reports and models to support organisational objectives, while collaborating across the organisation effectively
- critique statistical analyses
- use a variety of data analytics techniques (such as data mining and prescriptive and predictive analytics) for complex data analysis through the whole data life cycle
- use model outputs to produce evidence and help design services and policies
- understand a broad range of statistical tools, particularly those deployed within the organisation, and can use these appropriately and help others to use them

skills.name: Applying statistical and analytical tools and techniques
skills.description: Applying statistical and analytical techniques involves using and evaluating methods to answer research questions and make data-informed recommendations.

levels.awareness:
You can:
- support the development of statistical and analytical insights and reports under supervision
- explain the benefits of basic statistical and analytical techniques
- explain the value of quality assurance and best practices in developing statistical and analytical outputs
levels.working:
You can:
- contribute to the development of statistical and analytical insights and reports
- apply appropriate statistical and analytical techniques under supervision to answer research questions and organisational needs
- follow and apply quality assurance standards
- respond to stakeholder questions about analytical and statistical techniques
levels.practitioner:
You can:
- lead the development of valuable statistical insights and reports
- identify and apply a range of statistical and analytical techniques and tools, and support others in applying them
- quality assure statistical techniques and analytical outputs across a team
- engage with stakeholders and share statistical and analytical techniques to increase understanding and trust
levels.expert:
You can:
- identify opportunities to develop statistical insights and reports that support organisational objectives
- develop and guide others in a range of statistical and analytical techniques and tools
- oversee the quality assurance of statistical techniques and analytical outputs, continually improving and innovating practices
- use statistical and analytical outputs to influence stakeholders across the organisation and beyond

skills.name: Applying user-centred insights
skills.description: Applying user-centred insights involves understanding all user needs and the problems that need to be solved, and applying insights to make decisions that meet these needs.

levels.awareness:
You can:
- explain the difference between user needs and what a user wants
- explain the purpose of user stories
- explain why applying user-centred insights is important
- explain how you approach understanding user needs
levels.working:
You can:
- identify and engage users and stakeholders to identify user needs and trends
- decide when you need more user insights and when you have enough to make a decision
- work with others to define the problem and research goals
- use quantitative and qualitative user insights to improve product or service outcomes
levels.practitioner:
You can:
- use user insights to represent users in internal discussions
- advocate for research to be completed with all types of users of the product or service
- use user needs to agree the work that needs to be done and determine priorities with the team
- work with others to understand and recommend tools to get the appropriate user insight
levels.expert:
You can:
- advocate for a range of effective research approaches across the organisation
- coach others in making decisions that meet user needs across a range of channels
- advocate for continuous use of user insights in teams
- use user insights to make strategic decisions to provide the best user experience

levels.awareness:
You can:
- identify relevant information that can inform your architectural work, such as strategies, roadmaps, policies and technical trends
- understand how your work supports the team in enabling change​
levels.working:
You can:
- align your work with the work being done by other architects and technical professionals
- track emerging issues, strategies, roadmaps, patterns and technologies over time to assess opportunities and risks to your work
- identify how other teams contribute to delivering outcomes through change
levels.practitioner:
You can:
- work to support wider organisational objectives beyond your immediate goals​
- track emerging internal and external issues over time that could affect the work of teams across the organisation
- take action to solve or mitigate problems by influencing colleagues across the organisation
levels.expert:
You can:
- assess how trends in society and industry practices might impact the organisation
- work with people outside of your organisation to inform policies, strategies and standards
- anticipate changes to policy and build resilience through your architectural work
- coach others in identifying important trends

skills.name: Architecture communication
skills.description: Communication involves conveying information using the most effective medium and language for the audience.

levels.awareness:
You can:
- show an awareness of different ways of creating architecture representations for a limited audience, including technical and non-technical stakeholders
- gather and explain information to be used in architecture representations
levels.working:
You can:
- listen to the needs of technical and business stakeholders
- create and use different architecture representations to communicate effectively, achieving agreement with technical and non-technical stakeholders
- provide support in discussions about architectural topics within a multidisciplinary team
levels.practitioner:
You can:
- lead the communication of complicated, complex or risky architecture topics with technical and non-technical stakeholders
- communicate with senior stakeholders across your organisation
- adapt your message and communication techniques to your audience
- advocate on behalf of a team to other stakeholders
- manage stakeholder expectations effectively
levels.expert:
You can:
- communicate with technical and non-technical stakeholders at all levels, and across organisations, using architecture communication techniques​
- mediate between people in difficult architectural discussions
- gain support from business and technical stakeholders for architectural initiatives with high levels of risk, impact and complexity
- coach and support others in architecture communication

skills.name: Asset and configuration management
skills.description: Asset and configuration management involves managing the life cycle of IT assets, such as hardware, software, intellectual property, licences and warranties, the configuration of components, and the relationships between them. Consideration is given to the usage, disposal, compliance, inventory, sustainability, cost optimisation and protection of the IT asset portfolio.

levels.awareness:
You can:
- track, log and correct information to protect assets and components
levels.working:
You can:
- maintain secure configuration and accurate information
- control IT assets in one or more areas
- verify the location and state of IT assets
levels.practitioner:
You can:
- manage configuration items and related information
- manage service compliance and risk
levels.expert:
You can:
- manage configuration management for the organisation, ensuring value for the business and adherence to company policies
- ensure that changes to assets are recorded and controlled appropriately
- advocate organisational commitment to asset control

skills.name: Assurance and audit liaison
skills.description: Gathering assurance that controls work, supporting internal and external audits, and tracking audit recommendations to completion.

levels.awareness:
You can:
- explain how audits and assurance work in the organisation
- provide evidence when asked
levels.working:
You can:
- coordinate evidence for audits and inspections
- track audit recommendations and chase overdue actions
levels.practitioner:
You can:
- plan assurance mapping across the organisation's main risks
- work with internal and external auditors to agree scope and findings
- report on assurance gaps to committees
levels.expert:
You can:
- design the organisation's assurance framework
- advise the audit committee and board on the strength of assurance

esco.label: attend to detail in preparation for audits

skills.name: Availability and capacity management
skills.description: Availability and capacity management involves ensuring services are available with as little downtime or disruption as possible, and that we have sufficient resources to support emerging business needs.

levels.awareness:
You can:
- explain availability and capacity management processes
levels.working:
You can:
- manage service components to ensure they meet business needs and key performance indicators (KPIs)
levels.practitioner:
You can:
- ensure the correct implementation of availability and capacity management standards and procedures

roles.title: Software developer
roles.summary: Software developers build, test, and maintain the software behind the organisation's digital health services, such as patient-facing apps, clinical systems, integration services, and data platforms. They work in multidisciplinary product teams, write code that is safe, secure, accessible, and maintainable, and support their services in live operation.
healthContext: Software can affect patient care, so developers follow the clinical risk management process and contribute evidence to safety cases.
Code often handles confidential health information, so developers apply information governance and secure coding practices by default.
Many services exchange data with other health and care systems, using open interoperability standards such as HL7 FHIR.
Some software may be regulated as a medical device, so developers need to know when to ask for regulatory advice.

pcfRole.name: Software developer
pcfRole.description:
A software developer designs, runs and improves software that meets user needs.

In this role, you will:
- be responsible for writing clean, secure code following a test-driven approach
- create code that is open by default and easy for others to reuse

levels.title: Apprentice software developer
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
An apprentice developer attends certified training and develops skills on the job.

At this role level, you will:
- spend a substantial portion of time shadowing others
- work with other developers to write code and tests
- build your knowledge
- follow a test-driven approach
- write code that is automatically tested
responsibilities: Learn the team's languages, tools, and ways of working through structured training and pairing.
Write and test small, well-defined pieces of code under close supervision.
Follow secure coding, information governance, and clinical safety procedures.
Take part in team ceremonies such as stand-ups, planning, and retrospectives.
Work towards an apprenticeship or equivalent qualification.
qualifications: Enrolled on, or working towards, a software development apprenticeship or equivalent.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Knowledge is scored at the level the job needs once training is complete enough to do the work; information resources reflects work on systems designed by others.

levels.title: Junior software developer
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A junior developer learns on the job by delivering software components.

At this role level, you will:
- develop skills while working under supervision to deliver stories in a multidisciplinary team
- understand and be proficient in different types of testing
- be aware of but not responsible for security
- coach and mentor more junior colleagues
responsibilities: Build and test features for the team's products, working from user stories with guidance.
Write automated tests and fix defects, including in services that support patient care.
Contribute evidence to clinical safety cases, such as test results and change records.
Handle health data securely, following information governance rules.
Support live services, under guidance, as part of the team's support arrangements.
qualifications: A degree in computing or a related subject, a completed apprenticeship, or equivalent experience.

levels.title: Software developer
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A developer delivers software components that form part of a product.

At this role level, you will:
- develop software to meet user needs
- follow best practice guidelines and help to improve those guidelines
- write clean, secure and well-tested code
- coach and mentor more junior colleagues
- operate the services you build and identify issues in production
responsibilities: Design, build, and test features and services independently, choosing suitable approaches.
Review code and help maintain the team's engineering standards.
Build integrations with other health and care systems using open standards such as HL7 FHIR.
Take part in hazard identification and help put clinical safety controls into code and tests.
Investigate and fix problems in live services, including out-of-hours support where the service needs it.
Mentor junior and apprentice developers.
qualifications: A degree in computing or a related subject, or equivalent experience.
Experience of building and supporting production software.

levels.title: Senior software developer
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A senior developer delivers and integrates software to form a complete service.

At this role level, you will:
- plan and lead development on sets of related stories
- have an understanding of the whole system and take responsibility for teaching this to others
- work with other disciplines to understand what needs to be built
- coach and mentor more junior colleagues
- operate the production services you build
- find ways to improve system robustness, resilience and stability
There are 2 different roles at this level - a technical role and a management role.
responsibilities: Lead the technical design and delivery of significant features and services.
Set and maintain engineering standards for the team, including testing, security, and accessibility.
Make technical decisions that balance user needs, clinical safety, security, and cost.
Lead incident investigation for the team's services and drive the fixes.
Work with clinical safety officers to make sure safety controls are designed in and tested.
Coach and develop developers in the team.
qualifications: Substantial experience of designing, building, and supporting production software, at a level equivalent to a master's degree.

levels.title: Lead software developer
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A lead developer leads development on one or a small number of related project teams.

At this role level, you will:
- guide the ways in which the team works
- be proficient in a wide range of technical systems
- be involved in identifying appropriate technology and approaches, deciding when software should be written
- contribute to the developer community
- provide technical leadership, coaching and mentoring your team
- promote knowledge sharing and adoption of good practice
There are 2 different roles at this level - a technical role and a management role.
responsibilities: Lead the engineering for a product or group of teams, setting technical direction.
Make sure the software is designed for safety, security, resilience, and interoperability.
Work with architects, product managers, and clinical leads to shape the product roadmap.
Lead the development community of practice and set standards across teams.
Line manage or lead developers, supporting their development and performance.
qualifications: Extensive experience of leading software engineering for complex services.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: The UK GDaD PCF lists both lead and principal developer as most often at G7 or G6; this reference places lead at Band 8a and principal at Band 8b.

levels.title: Principal software developer
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A principal developer leads and plans development across large or multiple teams.

At this role level, you will:
- be an expert in many technical areas or a specialist with very deep knowledge in a particular technical area
- use this knowledge, and work with related disciplines, to keep multiple teams working effectively
- develop capability by facilitating internal mobility, shaping career paths and recruiting talent, ensuring they collaborate
- identify, test and champion the adoption of emerging technologies
There are 2 different roles at this level - a technical role and a management role.
responsibilities: Set the engineering strategy, standards, and practices for the organisation's software development.
Advise senior leaders on technology choices, risks, and investment.
Lead the resolution of the most complex technical problems across services.
Represent the organisation in cross-organisation and open source engineering communities.
Lead and develop lead developers and grow the organisation's engineering capability.
qualifications: Extensive experience of leading engineering across multiple teams or organisations.

roles.title: Frontend developer
roles.summary: Frontend developers build the user interfaces of the organisation's digital health services, such as patient-facing websites and apps, online forms, and screens that clinicians and care staff use during care. They write accessible, fast, and secure code that works for everyone, including people who are unwell, anxious, or using older devices, and they work in multidisciplinary product teams with designers, researchers, and clinicians.
healthContext: Many users are unwell, in pain, older, or disabled, so accessibility and plain, calm interfaces are essential rather than optional.
A confusing or wrong display of clinical information, such as a medication dose, a result, or an appointment time, can harm patients, so frontend work follows the clinical risk management process.
Interfaces often show confidential health information, so developers design for privacy, for example on shared devices and in busy clinical areas.
Clinicians use interfaces under time pressure and with frequent interruptions, so screens must be quick, predictable, and hard to misread.
Patients reach services on a wide range of devices and connections, so services use progressive enhancement and work on slow networks.

pcfRole.name: Frontend developer
pcfRole.description:
A frontend developer designs, builds and improves website software that meets user needs.

In this role, you will:
- be responsible for writing clean, accessible code following a progressive enhancement approach
- create code that is open by default and easy for others to reuse
- design software which meets user needs and creates meaningful interactions and relationships with users
- have an understanding of the three fundamental frontend technologies (HTML, CSS and JavaScript)

levels.title: Apprentice frontend developer
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
An apprentice frontend developer attends certified training and develops skills on the job.

At this role level, you will:
- spend a substantial portion of time shadowing others
- work with other developers to write code and tests
- write code that follows web standards
- build your understanding of accessibility
- build your knowledge
- develop software which meets user needs
responsibilities: Learn the team's design system, languages, and tools through structured training and pairing.
Build small interface components under close supervision, following the organisation's design system.
Test components with assistive technologies, such as screen readers, with support from colleagues.
Follow information governance and clinical safety procedures when working with test and live data.
Work towards an apprenticeship or equivalent qualification.
qualifications: Enrolled on, or working towards, a software development apprenticeship or equivalent.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Knowledge is scored at the level the job needs once training is complete enough to do the work.

levels.title: Junior frontend developer
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A junior frontend developer learns on the job by delivering software components.

At this role level, you will:
- work independently, with guidance from more senior developers, to identify user issues and needs
- write clean code that follows web standards
- build your understanding of accessibility
- build your knowledge
- develop software which meets user needs
responsibilities: Build and test interface features for patient-facing and staff-facing services, working from user stories with guidance.
Use the organisation's design system and patterns so that services look and behave consistently.
Fix accessibility defects and check pages against accessibility standards such as WCAG.
Make sure clinical information, such as dates, doses, and results, is displayed exactly as specified.
Contribute evidence to clinical safety cases, such as test results and screenshots of changes.
qualifications: A degree in computing or a related subject, a completed apprenticeship, or equivalent experience.

levels.title: Frontend developer
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A frontend developer builds software components, primarily in the form of user interfaces.

At this role level, you will:
- collaborate and work closely with other disciplines to develop designs and working prototypes based on user needs and in support of organisational aims
- develop software components that form part of a product to meet user needs
- write clean, well-tested code that follows web standards
- coach and mentor more junior colleagues
responsibilities: Design and build accessible, responsive interfaces for health services independently, choosing suitable approaches.
Work with designers and user researchers to test prototypes with patients, clinicians, and care staff.
Build interfaces that call health data APIs, such as HL7 FHIR services, and handle errors and missing data safely.
Take part in hazard workshops and build safety controls into the interface, such as confirmation steps and clear warnings.
Protect confidential information in the browser, for example by managing sessions and caching carefully on shared devices.
Review code and mentor junior and apprentice frontend developers.
qualifications: A degree in computing or a related subject, or equivalent experience.
Experience of building and supporting accessible production web services.

levels.title: Senior frontend developer
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A senior frontend developer is an experienced developer who works with minimal support and can influence and mentor others.

At this role level, you will:
- help set direction and embed good practice within teams
- make decisions based on research
- plan and lead development on sets of related stories, working with other disciplines to understand what needs to be built
- have an understanding of the whole system
- teach and mentor others
responsibilities: Lead the frontend design and delivery of significant features, such as booking, results, or clinical workflow screens.
Set and maintain frontend standards for the team, including accessibility, performance, security, and testing.
Contribute components and patterns to the organisation's design system and make sure they are safe and accessible.
Work with clinical safety officers to make sure interface hazards are identified, controlled, and tested.
Make sure services work well on slow connections, older devices, and assistive technologies.
Coach and develop frontend developers in the team.
qualifications: Substantial experience of designing, building, and supporting accessible production web services, at a level equivalent to a master's degree.

levels.title: Lead frontend developer
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A lead frontend developer is an expert practitioner who influences and mentors others.

At this role level, you will:
- set direction and assure the quality of development across teams
- lead multiple or highly complex services
- contribute to the community, providing technical leadership, coaching and mentoring
- promote knowledge sharing and adoption of good practice
- be proficient in a wide range of technical systems and able to identify appropriate technology and approaches
responsibilities: Lead frontend engineering across a group of teams or a major patient-facing service.
Own the technical direction of the organisation's design system and frontend libraries.
Make sure interfaces across services meet accessibility standards and are assured for clinical safety.
Work with architects, designers, and clinical leads to shape product roadmaps and frontend technology choices.
Lead the frontend community of practice and line manage or lead frontend developers.
qualifications: Extensive experience of leading frontend engineering for complex, accessible services.

levels.title: Head of frontend development
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A head of frontend development is an expert practitioner with broad industry experience. They are an expert in many technical areas, or specialists with very deep knowledge in a particular technical area.

At this role level, you will:
- define and assure best practice while influencing, leading and mentoring others
- influence and develop organisational strategy and priorities, collaborating with counterpart colleagues across government
- ensure the right conditions and environment for frontend developers to work effectively
- develop departmental capability by facilitating internal mobility, shaping career paths and recruiting talent
responsibilities: Set the frontend strategy, standards, and practices for all of the organisation's digital services.
Be accountable for the accessibility and usability of the organisation's interfaces for patients and staff.
Advise senior leaders on frontend technology, design system investment, and the risks of poor interfaces to care.
Represent the organisation in cross-organisation design system and accessibility communities.
Lead and develop frontend developers across the organisation, including recruitment and career paths.
qualifications: Extensive experience of leading frontend development across multiple teams or organisations.

roles.title: DevOps engineer
roles.summary: DevOps engineers build and run the tools, pipelines, environments, and platforms that let the organisation's teams deliver digital health services safely and often. They automate build, test, release, and infrastructure, make services observable and resilient, and help teams keep clinical systems available when patients and clinicians need them.
healthContext: Many services support care around the clock, so deployments, monitoring, and recovery must keep downtime to a minimum, including out of hours.
Release pipelines produce evidence for clinical safety cases, such as test results, change records, and the exact version deployed.
Environments may hold confidential health information, so engineers control access, protect secrets, and keep live data out of test environments.
Health services are common targets for cyber attacks, so pipelines and platforms build in security scanning, patching, and tested backups.
Some services must meet strict standards for availability and disaster recovery, agreed with clinical and operational leads.

pcfRole.name: Development operations (DevOps) engineer
pcfRole.description:
Commonly referred to as ‘DevOps engineers’, development operations engineers support the development and operation of software through tools, environments and practices.

In this role, you will be responsible for underpinning good development processes including managing tools and testing environments, central code control, maintaining development standards and writing software that automates systems.

levels.title: Apprentice DevOps engineer
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
An apprentice DevOps engineer attends certified training and develops skills on the job.

At this role level, you will:
- spend a significant proportion of your time shadowing others
- be involved in implementation but not planning
- build on your knowledge
responsibilities: Learn the team's pipelines, cloud platforms, and tools through structured training and shadowing.
Make small, well-defined changes to scripts, pipelines, and configuration under close supervision.
Follow change, security, and information governance procedures for every environment.
Help monitor services and report alerts to experienced colleagues.
Work towards an apprenticeship or equivalent qualification.
qualifications: Enrolled on, or working towards, a DevOps, software, or infrastructure apprenticeship or equivalent.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Knowledge is scored at the level the job needs once training is complete enough to do the work.

levels.title: Junior DevOps engineer
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A junior DevOps engineer learns on the job by building software components.

At this role level, you will:
- assist in the building of a complex story
- work under supervision
- be involved in implementation but not planning
responsibilities: Build and maintain parts of build, test, and deployment pipelines with guidance.
Write infrastructure as code and automation scripts, and test them before use.
Keep test environments free of live patient data and manage secrets safely.
Respond to monitoring alerts and support incident response under guidance.
Record deployments and changes so they can support clinical safety and audit evidence.
qualifications: A degree in computing or a related subject, a completed apprenticeship, or equivalent experience.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: The UK GDaD PCF suggests Band 4 for both apprentice and junior levels; this reference places the junior level at Band 5 to avoid two levels in one band, because the job builds pipeline components with less supervision.

levels.title: DevOps engineer
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A DevOps engineer delivers automated software components that form part of a development operations toolchain.

At this role level, you will:
- transform technical requirements into DevOps processes
- build complex stories without additional support
- manage live test environments
- identify and resolve issues that are preventing delivery
responsibilities: Design and build pipelines, environments, and platform components independently.
Automate security checks, such as dependency and container scanning, and act on the results.
Build monitoring, logging, and alerting so teams can see problems before they affect patients and staff.
Plan and test backups, failover, and recovery for services that support care.
Investigate and fix problems in live services, including out-of-hours support where the service needs it.
Mentor junior and apprentice DevOps engineers.
qualifications: A degree in computing or a related subject, or equivalent experience.
Experience of building and running automated delivery pipelines and cloud infrastructure.

levels.title: Senior DevOps engineer
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A senior DevOps engineer delivers and integrates software to form a complete DevOps toolchain. They are responsible for planning and designing large groups of stories.

At this role level, you will:
- transform technical requirements into an effective DevOps toolchain to enable product delivery
- provide coaching and mentoring to more junior colleagues
- ensure that deployment strategies for products are repeatable, scalable and highly available
- have deep technical knowledge, providing support to delivery teams and solving complex problems
There are 2 different roles at this level - a technical role and a management role.
responsibilities: Lead the design of the delivery toolchain and platform for a product or group of services.
Set standards for releases, so that deployments to clinical services are repeatable, reversible, and well evidenced.
Agree availability, recovery time, and recovery point targets with service owners and clinical leads, and design to meet them.
Lead technical incident response and post-incident reviews for the platforms the team runs.
Make sure platforms meet security and information governance requirements, including access control and audit logging.
Coach and develop DevOps engineers in the team.
qualifications: Substantial experience of designing and running delivery toolchains and platforms, at a level equivalent to a master's degree.

levels.title: Lead DevOps engineer
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A lead DevOps engineer leads one or a small number of related project teams and contributes to the development of the strategic direction.

At this role level, you will:
- act as a technical product owner, developing medium to long term strategies for product lines
- provide technical leadership and guidance through coaching and mentoring
- lead the sharing of knowledge and good practice
There are 2 different roles at this level - a technical role and a management role.
responsibilities: Lead DevOps and platform engineering for a group of teams, acting as technical owner of the shared platform.
Set the medium-term roadmap for the organisation's delivery tooling, hosting, and observability.
Make sure shared platforms are resilient, secure, and able to meet the availability needs of clinical services.
Manage platform costs and capacity with finance and service owners.
Lead the DevOps community of practice and line manage or lead DevOps engineers.
qualifications: Extensive experience of leading DevOps or platform engineering for complex services.

levels.title: Principal DevOps engineer
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A principal DevOps engineer leads and plans development across large or multiple teams, defining the strategic vision for delivery.

At this role level, you will:
- identify, test and champion the adoption of emerging technologies
- ensure that security, stability and capacity are embedded in the development and deployment of services
- develop a team’s capability by rewarding high performers
- shape career paths and recruit the right talent
- identify skills gaps and important dependencies within technical teams
There are 2 different roles at this level - a technical role and a management role.
responsibilities: Set the strategy for how the organisation builds, releases, hosts, and runs its digital health services.
Advise senior leaders on hosting, resilience, cyber security, and platform investment.
Make sure business continuity and disaster recovery plans for critical clinical services are realistic and tested.
Evaluate and champion new technologies and practices, balancing innovation against safety and stability.
Grow the organisation's DevOps capability, including recruitment, career paths, and skills plans.
qualifications: Extensive experience of leading DevOps and platform engineering across multiple teams or organisations.

roles.title: Integration engineer (health interoperability)
roles.summary: Integration engineers connect the organisation's clinical and business systems so that health and care information flows safely to where it is needed. They design, build, test, and support interfaces, APIs, and message flows using standards such as HL7 FHIR and HL7 version 2, map data and clinical codes between systems, and keep integrations running in live service.
healthContext: A lost, delayed, duplicated, or wrongly matched message, such as a test result or referral, can lead directly to harm, so integration work follows the clinical risk management process.
Integrations carry large volumes of confidential health information between organisations, so every flow needs a lawful basis, secure transport, and audit.
Health systems use many standards and versions, from HL7 version 2 messages to HL7 FHIR APIs and IHE profiles, often with local variations.
Clinical meaning must survive the journey, so engineers map clinical terminologies such as SNOMED CT correctly and match patients reliably.
Many integrations support care around the clock, so they need monitoring, alerting, and clear routes for resolving failed messages.

levels.title: Junior integration engineer
levels.summary: A junior integration engineer builds, tests, and supports integrations between health and care systems, working from specifications and with guidance from more experienced engineers.
responsibilities: Build and change message mappings, transformations, and API calls from agreed specifications.
Test integrations against specifications and sample messages, including error and edge cases.
Monitor message flows, investigate failed or rejected messages, and resolve or escalate them.
Handle health data securely, following information governance rules for live and test data.
Record changes and test results so they can be used as clinical safety evidence.
qualifications: A degree in computing or a related subject, a completed apprenticeship, or equivalent experience.

levels.title: Integration engineer
levels.summary: An integration engineer designs, builds, and supports integrations between health and care systems independently, and helps define how systems should exchange data.
responsibilities: Design and build integrations, APIs, and message flows using HL7 FHIR, HL7 version 2, and messaging patterns.
Analyse source and target systems and write interface specifications and data mappings, including clinical codes.
Build patient matching, validation, and error handling so that information reaches the right record.
Take part in hazard workshops and build safety controls into integrations, such as alerts for failed or delayed messages.
Work with suppliers and partner organisations to test and go live with new connections.
Investigate and fix problems in live integrations, and mentor junior integration engineers.
qualifications: A degree in computing or a related subject, or equivalent experience.
Experience of building and supporting integrations between production systems.

levels.title: Senior integration engineer
levels.summary: A senior integration engineer leads the design and delivery of complex integrations across many systems and organisations, and sets integration standards for their area.
responsibilities: Lead the technical design of complex integrations, such as shared care records, results, and referrals across organisations.
Write and maintain FHIR profiles, implementation guides, and interface standards for the organisation.
Design integrations to be secure, resilient, and observable, with clear routes for resolving failures.
Work with clinical safety officers to identify integration hazards and make sure controls are designed in and tested.
Make sure each data flow has an agreed lawful basis and data sharing arrangements, working with information governance colleagues.
Coach and develop integration engineers in the team.
qualifications: Substantial experience of designing and supporting health or other complex integrations, at a level equivalent to a master's degree.

levels.title: Lead integration engineer
levels.summary: A lead integration engineer leads the organisation's integration engineering, sets its technical direction and standards, and assures critical integrations across many systems.
responsibilities: Lead integration engineering across the organisation, setting direction, patterns, and standards.
Assure the design of critical integrations, such as those that carry results, medicines, or alerts.
Shape the integration platform roadmap with architects, product managers, and suppliers.
Represent the organisation in cross-organisation interoperability and standards work.
Line manage or lead integration engineers and grow the integration community of practice.
qualifications: Extensive experience of leading integration engineering for complex health or care systems.

roles.title: Enterprise architect
roles.summary: Enterprise architects give the organisation a joined-up view of its services, information, applications, and technology, and use it to turn health and care strategy into a coherent plan for change. They set architecture principles, standards, and roadmaps, guide investment decisions, and make sure digital change supports safe, joined-up care for patients across organisations.
healthContext: Care pathways cross many organisations and systems, so the architecture must support sharing of records, results, and referrals across boundaries.
The estate often includes long-lived clinical systems, medical devices, and supplier contracts that are hard to change, so roadmaps must plan transitions carefully.
Architecture decisions affect patient safety, privacy, and the resilience of services that run around the clock.
Open standards such as HL7 FHIR, SNOMED CT, and IHE profiles are key to avoiding lock-in and enabling interoperability.
Funding is constrained and closely scrutinised, so architects must show value for money and reuse of shared platforms where they exist.

pcfRole.name: Enterprise architect
pcfRole.description:
Enterprise architects are leaders working across different levels within an organisation to translate the business strategy into business change and technical delivery.

In this role, you will:
- identify priorities for change to enable delivery at pace
- lead and influence the delivery of cross-cutting capabilities that enable change
- own the enterprise architecture vision, strategy and roadmaps from a business, technology and data perspective, including ‘as is’, ‘to be’ and transitional states
- consult and support collaboration across the business
- understand the organisation’s ecosystem and its interdependencies, including reference architectures
- take a strategic view across all architectural domains, portfolios and programmes
- guide the organisation to make appropriate business, technology and data decisions by recommending reuse, sustainability and scalability, to achieve value for money and reduce risk
- establish architectural principles, policies and standards
- collaborate and consult with stakeholders to assure business, technology and data decisions are aligned with enterprise architecture strategy
- develop the architecture community
- carry out horizon scanning across industry, identifying emerging trends and their potential impact and opportunity for the organisation

levels.title: Enterprise architect
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
An enterprise architect supports other architects in developing the strategy.

At this role level, you will:
- network and communicate with stakeholders across domains or enterprises, and identify opportunities for improvement
- use best practice
- use emerging technologies and approaches
- learn to identify influences or risks
- play a part in successful delivery of the team’s objectives
responsibilities: Model the organisation's current services, information, applications, and technology for a domain, such as diagnostics or community care.
Keep the architecture repository up to date, including application and data flow catalogues.
Review proposals against architecture principles and standards, and record the findings for design authorities.
Identify where systems duplicate capability or depend on unsupported technology, and raise the risks.
Work with solution architects and clinical leads to understand how care pathways use systems.
qualifications: A degree in computing, business, or a related subject, or equivalent experience.
Experience of architecture, analysis, or technical design in a complex organisation.

levels.title: Senior enterprise architect
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A senior enterprise architect supports lead architects in ensuring the strategy is developed, agreed and followed.

At this role level, you will:
- network and communicate with stakeholders across domains or enterprises
- identify opportunities for improvement
- support a community or team
- use best practice
- use emerging technologies and approaches
- play an active part in the team and understand how to deliver the team’s objectives to meet organisational goals
- identify influences or risks
- play a part in successful delivery of the long-term strategy
responsibilities: Develop target architectures and transition roadmaps for one or more domains of the organisation.
Shape business cases so that investments fit the target architecture and reuse shared platforms.
Lead architecture reviews at design authorities and make recommendations on significant proposals.
Plan the replacement or retirement of legacy clinical and corporate systems, including data migration and safety risks.
Make sure interoperability, security, and information governance needs are built into roadmaps.
qualifications: Substantial experience of enterprise or solution architecture, at a level equivalent to a master's degree.
Knowledge of an enterprise architecture framework, such as TOGAF, or equivalent experience.

levels.title: Lead enterprise architect
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A lead enterprise architect plays a high level role in ensuring the strategy is developed, agreed and followed.

At this role level, you will:
- network and communicate with senior stakeholders across enterprises, and seek opportunities for improvement
- support at least one community or team, or a combination of both
- find and use best practice and emerging technologies and approaches
- lead teams including enterprise architects and help them understand how to deliver the team’s objectives to meet organisational goals
- horizon scan for influences or risks
- support successful delivery of the long-term strategy
- take a leading role in the overall direction of business and digital capabilities
responsibilities: Own the enterprise architecture for a major part of the organisation, such as clinical systems or shared infrastructure.
Chair or lead the architecture design authority and set the standards that projects must meet.
Advise directors on investment priorities, supplier strategy, and technology risks.
Work with partner organisations to align architectures across care pathways and shared records.
Lead and develop enterprise architects and grow the architecture community of practice.
qualifications: Extensive experience of enterprise architecture in a complex organisation.

levels.title: Principal enterprise architect
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A principal enterprise architect leads at the highest level and is responsible for ensuring the strategy is developed, agreed and followed.

At this role level, you will:
- network and communicate with senior stakeholders across enterprises, and actively seek opportunities for improvement
- support multiple communities and teams
- find and use best practice
- find and use emerging technologies and approaches
- inspire other enterprise architects and help them understand how to meet organisational goals
- horizon scan for external influences or risks
- support successful delivery of the long-term strategy
- be responsible for the overall direction of business and digital capabilities
- be responsible for the creation, maintenance and consumption of a Digital Twin
responsibilities: Set the organisation's enterprise architecture vision, principles, and strategy, aligned with its health and care strategy.
Advise the executive team and board on the architecture, risks, and value of major digital investments.
Lead the organisation's architecture practice, governance, and standards.
Represent the organisation in cross-organisation architecture and interoperability forums.
Build architecture capability across the organisation, including recruitment and career paths.
qualifications: Extensive experience of leading enterprise architecture across organisations.

roles.title: Solution architect
roles.summary: Solution architects design how a new or changed service will work end to end, from user needs and clinical workflows to applications, data, integrations, hosting, and security. They make sure each solution fits the organisation's architecture, meets its safety, privacy, and interoperability needs, and can be built, run, and supported affordably.
healthContext: Solutions often combine bought clinical systems, in-house services, and shared platforms, so architects must design across supplier boundaries.
Design choices can introduce clinical hazards, such as lost results or wrong patient matching, so solution designs feed into the clinical safety case.
Every new data flow of patient information needs a lawful basis and a data protection impact assessment, so architects work closely with information governance.
Interoperability with other health and care organisations, using standards such as HL7 FHIR, is usually a core requirement.
Some solutions include software that is a medical device, which changes the design, assurance, and supplier requirements.

pcfRole.name: Solution architect
pcfRole.description:
A solution architect designs solutions for problems that affect the organisation.

In this role, you will:
- ensure a problem and the desired outcomes are properly defined
- ensure the scope of a solution meets the organisation's requirements
- stay up to date on technology trends and approaches
- understand organisational objectives and external drivers, for example, legislation or financial constraints
- work with others to develop business and technical strategies
- work within business and technical constraints
- design and document solutions so they can be implemented by the organisation
- comply with standards and governance
- communicate and work effectively with stakeholders
- manage risks and decisions in a transparent way

levels.title: Associate solution architect
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
An associate solution architect supports other solution architects to design solutions. You will usually work under supervision.

At this role level, you will:
- support the design of solutions by working with stakeholders
- help your team achieve its objectives
responsibilities: Gather requirements from product teams, clinicians, and suppliers to inform solution designs.
Draw current and target state diagrams, such as context, data flow, and integration views.
Draft sections of solution designs and decision records under supervision.
Check designs against architecture standards, security, and information governance requirements.
Help prepare designs for review at design authorities.
qualifications: A degree in computing or a related subject, or equivalent experience.
Experience of analysis, development, or technical design.

levels.title: Solution architect
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A solution architect is responsible for a single solution. They usually work independently on solutions where risk is low. They also often support or contribute to work led by more senior solution architects.

At this role level, you will:
- build relationships with stakeholders across different business or technical areas in the organisation
- be proactive in identifying opportunities to improve the organisation
- follow best practice for solution design
- use emerging technologies and approaches
- help your team achieve its objective
responsibilities: Design end-to-end solutions for lower-risk services, such as staff tools or simple patient-facing services.
Compare options, including buying, building, and reusing shared platforms, and recommend one with clear reasons.
Design integrations, data flows, and identity and access for the solution, using open standards where they exist.
Contribute to hazard identification and data protection impact assessments for the solution.
Present designs to design authorities and support delivery teams through build and go-live.
