A data governance manager plans, monitors and enforces the management of data assets.

In this role, you will:
- catalogue, monitor and identify data assets that are essential to the organisation’s operations or services
- assign ownership of data, ensuring there is a clear RACI (responsible, accountable, consulted and informed) matrix in the organisation
- incorporate governance of data into routine processes
- support or manage risk processes around data
- advocate for better use and management of data within the organisation
- encourage better data literacy within the organisation

levels.title: Data governance manager
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A data governance manager defines, implements and manages data governance frameworks, policies and standards.

At this role level, you will:
- work on the design and implementation of practical data governance solutions to support organisational needs
- identify opportunities and make recommendations to improve the quality and trustworthiness of data throughout the organisation
- implement and establish wider data management competencies within the organisation (such as data quality, metadata management, master data management, data modelling, and development of data standards and data strategy)
- apply data governance to optimise the safety and value of data throughout the data life cycle
- work within the organisation to minimise data risks and increase data literacy
responsibilities: Run the organisation's data governance framework, including data ownership, stewardship, and decision-making groups.
Maintain the data catalogue, business glossary, and data standards, including agreed clinical and operational definitions.
Monitor data quality for key data sets and work with data owners to fix root causes.
Work with information governance colleagues on data sharing agreements and data protection impact assessments for new data uses.
Record and manage data risks and issues, and escalate them to the right owner.
Improve data literacy among staff who create and use health data.
qualifications: A degree or professional qualification in data, information management, or a related subject, or equivalent experience.
Experience of data governance or data management in a complex organisation.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: The UK GDaD PCF suggests HEO to G7 for this level, which maps to Band 6. This reference places it at Band 7 because, in a health care organisation, the role usually governs confidential patient data across the whole organisation and develops data policy that affects several services.

levels.title: Lead data governance manager
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A lead data governance manager undertakes complex work related to the principles and practices of data governance, and co-ordinates with data owners to lead wider data management competencies.

At this role level, you will:
- lead the formation, implementation and management of data governance frameworks, policies and standards
- implement and establish wider data management competencies within the organisation (such as data quality assurance, metadata management, master data management, data modelling, and development of data standards and data strategy)
- be responsible for understanding and managing the organisational data risks and issues, and co-ordinating with data owners to accept or resolve them
responsibilities: Lead the design and running of data governance frameworks, policies, and standards across the organisation.
Coordinate data owners and stewards to manage data risks, accept or resolve them, and report them to senior committees.
Lead wider data management work, such as master data for patients, staff, and sites, and reference data.
Agree data governance arrangements for data shared with health and care partners and researchers.
Advise programmes on how new systems and data uses meet data standards and governance rules.
Line manage data governance staff.
qualifications: Extensive experience of leading data governance or data management.

levels.title: Head of data governance
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
The head of data governance works with the chief data officer across the organisation and government, providing strategic oversight and leadership in all aspects of data governance and use. They ensure high standards are maintained in-line with regulations and ethical requirements.

At this role level, you will:
- work with the chief data officer to provide strategic oversight of data governance throughout the organisation
- set and monitor the adherence to data governance policies, frameworks and standards
- be accountable for understanding and managing the organisational data risks and issues, and co-ordinating with data owners to accept or resolve them
- act as a senior advisor across government on the best practice of data security development, in accordance with the data enterprise architecture
- maintain effective long-term relationships at a senior level with important decision-makers and influencers
- advocate improved data risk management and practices within the organisation
- encourage better data literacy and understanding of data governance within the organisation
responsibilities: Work with the chief data officer and the executive owner of information risk to set the strategy for data governance and use.
Set data governance policies and standards and monitor how well the organisation follows them.
Be accountable for managing the organisation's data risks, and report on them to the board.
Represent the organisation on data governance with health and care partners, regulators, and patient groups.
Promote openness with patients and the public about how their data is used.
Lead and develop the data governance function.
qualifications: Extensive experience of leading data governance across an organisation.

roles.title: Clinical coder
roles.summary: Clinical coders read patients' health records and translate diagnoses, procedures, and other clinical information into standard classification codes, such as ICD for diagnoses and a procedure classification for interventions. Coded data is used for payment, service planning, clinical audit, research, and public health statistics, so its accuracy matters well beyond the coding team. Coders work closely with clinicians to clarify records, and increasingly use clinical terminologies such as SNOMED CT and computer-assisted coding tools.
healthContext: Coders read complete case notes, which often describe serious illness, injury, abuse, self-harm, and death, so the work is emotionally demanding and teams need good support and supervision.
Coded data drives payment for activity, mortality and outcome indicators, and service planning, so errors can affect funding, published performance, and decisions about care.
Coding depends on the quality of clinical documentation, so coders query unclear records with clinicians and help improve how care is recorded.
Coders handle full identifiable health records every day, so confidentiality and correct access are essential.
Automated and computer-assisted coding, and mapping from SNOMED CT to classifications, are changing the work, and coders check that automated codes are correct.

levels.title: Trainee clinical coder
levels.summary: A trainee clinical coder learns to code straightforward hospital episodes under close supervision, working towards a clinical coding qualification.
responsibilities: Code straightforward episodes, such as day cases, from health records using classification rules, with all work checked by a senior coder.
Learn medical terms, anatomy, and the national and international coding standards through structured training.
Find, track, and return health records correctly, and keep them secure.
Record coded data in the patient administration or coding system accurately and on time.
Raise unclear or missing information with a senior coder.
qualifications: Good literacy and keyboard skills, and enrolment on a clinical coding training programme, or equivalent.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Mental effort is level 4 because coders concentrate for long periods reading and interpreting detailed case notes. Emotional effort is level 2 because coders frequently read records describing distressing events.

levels.title: Clinical coder
levels.summary: A clinical coder codes a full range of routine episodes independently and accurately, meeting agreed deadlines and quality standards.
responsibilities: Code inpatient, day case, and outpatient episodes accurately across common specialties, using classification rules and local policies.
Query unclear, missing, or conflicting clinical information with clinicians and record the outcome.
Check codes suggested by computer-assisted coding or terminology maps, and correct them where needed.
Meet deadlines for coding completeness, so data is ready for payment and reporting.
Take part in coding audits and act on their findings.
qualifications: A recognised clinical coding qualification, or working towards one with equivalent experience.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Mental and emotional effort reflect long periods of concentration on case notes that often describe serious illness, injury, and death.

levels.title: Senior clinical coder
levels.summary: A senior clinical coder codes complex episodes across specialties, acts as a source of expert advice for other coders, and checks and trains less experienced coders.
responsibilities: Code complex episodes, such as critical care, cancer, multiple procedures, and deaths, across specialties.
Resolve difficult coding questions with consultants and other senior clinicians, explaining coding rules clearly.
Check the work of trainee coders and give them feedback and on-the-job training.
Validate coded data before it is submitted and fix errors with the right team.
Work with clinical teams to improve the quality of clinical documentation.
qualifications: A recognised clinical coding qualification, or equivalent experience.
Experience of coding complex episodes across a range of specialties.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Emotional effort stays at level 2, as complex episodes such as deaths and cancer care are a regular part of the work.

levels.title: Clinical coding auditor and trainer
levels.summary: A clinical coding auditor and trainer audits the accuracy of coded data, designs and delivers coding training, and advises the organisation on coding standards. In some organisations this level also leads a coding team day to day.
responsibilities: Plan and carry out coding audits across specialties, measuring accuracy against national and international standards.
Report audit findings to coding, clinical, finance, and information teams, and agree improvement actions.
Design and deliver coding training, from foundation courses for new coders to refresher training on standard changes.
Advise clinicians and managers on how coding affects payment, mortality indicators, and performance data.
Lead the introduction of changes in classification versions, coding standards, and coding tools.
Lead a coding team day to day where the organisation combines this with audit and training.
qualifications: A recognised clinical coding qualification and a recognised clinical coding audit or training qualification, or equivalent experience.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: People is level 3 because designing and teaching specialist coding training is a main duty. Research is level 2 because coding audit is a regular part of the job.

levels.title: Clinical coding manager
levels.summary: A clinical coding manager leads the organisation's clinical coding service, including its coding teams, quality programme, and links with clinical, finance, and information teams.
responsibilities: Lead the clinical coding service and its team leaders, making sure coding is complete, accurate, and on time.
Set coding policies and the coding quality programme, in line with national and international standards.
Hold the coding budget and plan the workforce, including recruitment, training, and accreditation.
Advise senior leaders on how coding affects funding, mortality and outcome indicators, and published data.
Lead the adoption of new coding technology, such as computer-assisted coding and terminology mapping, with clinical safety and information governance colleagues.
Support the wellbeing of coders who regularly read distressing records.
qualifications: A recognised clinical coding qualification and extensive experience of coding, audit, and leading coders, or equivalent experience.

roles.title: Business analyst
roles.summary: Business analysts help the organisation understand problems in health and care services and find the right changes to solve them. They analyse how clinical, administrative, and patient-facing processes work today, define user and business needs and requirements, and help teams make sure new digital services fit real care pathways and deliver measurable benefits.
healthContext: Processes cross organisational and professional boundaries, so analysts map whole care pathways, including handoffs between clinicians, care staff, patients, and other organisations.
Requirements often carry clinical risk, so analysts work with clinical safety officers to make sure safety-related requirements are captured, traced, and tested.
Many requirements concern sharing health data between systems, so analysts need a working grasp of interoperability standards such as HL7 FHIR and clinical terminologies such as SNOMED CT.
Benefits in care are often about safety, quality, staff time, and patient experience, not only cost, so analysts help define measures that clinicians recognise.

pcfRole.name: Business analyst
pcfRole.description:
Business analysts help teams to:
- analyse and understand a business problem or opportunity
- undertake research and analysis to understand how a business or business area works, considering the people, organisation, processes, information, data and technology
- identify areas for improvement, explore feasible options, analyse the effects of change and define success measures
- identify and elaborate user and business needs to enable effective design, development and testing of services and business change
- make decisions related to prioritisation and minimum viable product by using analysis led insights
- ensure new products and services meet business and user needs, and are aligned with organisational goals
- understand any business and policy constraints that need to be considered, and assess the implications

levels.title: Trainee business analyst
levels.pcfLevelDescription: A trainee business analyst receives direction from more senior business analysts. At this level, you will work with others or under supervision to build and develop your skills.
responsibilities: Learn business analysis techniques through structured training, shadowing, and supervised work.
Record notes and draft process maps from workshops with clinical and administrative staff.
Maintain requirements logs, user stories, and traceability records under direction.
Help prepare test scenarios for user acceptance testing.
Follow information governance rules when handling documents that include patient information.
qualifications: Working towards a business analysis apprenticeship or qualification, or equivalent experience.

levels.title: Junior business analyst
levels.pcfLevelDescription: A junior business analyst receives direction from more senior business analysts but is responsible for the output of specific tasks. At this level, you will have limited skills and will work with others or under supervision. You will support stakeholder relationship management.
responsibilities: Map current and future processes for clinical and administrative workflows, such as referrals, appointments, or results handling.
Elicit and write requirements and user stories for well-defined pieces of work.
Gather data on process performance, such as waiting times or manual workarounds, to support analysis.
Prepare and run user acceptance test scenarios with clinical and operational users.
Flag requirements that could affect patient safety to the team and the clinical safety officer.
qualifications: A degree, a business analysis qualification or apprenticeship, or equivalent experience.

levels.title: Business analyst
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A business analyst leads small to medium size projects and supports larger and more complex projects.

At this role level, you will:
- manage stakeholder relationships
- work independently
- have a good understanding of your work area
- develop the business analysis community by sharing best practice and mentoring others
responsibilities: Lead the analysis for small and medium projects, from problem definition to benefits measurement.
Run workshops with clinicians, care staff, and managers to understand pain points and agree options.
Model care pathways and information flows, including data exchanged with other health and care systems.
Define safety-related and data requirements, and trace them through design, build, and test.
Build benefits cases with measures such as staff time released, errors avoided, or patient experience.
Mentor junior and trainee business analysts.
qualifications: A degree or a recognised business analysis qualification, or equivalent experience.
Experience of business analysis on digital change projects.

levels.title: Senior business analyst
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A senior business analyst has a good understanding of strategic arenas and leads large or complex projects.

At this role level, you will:
- have functional or people management responsibilities, or a combination of both
- mentor others
- develop best practice
- own stakeholder relationships
- manage community of practice activities within a business area
responsibilities: Lead business analysis on large or complex programmes, such as replacing a clinical system or redesigning a care pathway.
Analyse options and their effect on care, safety, staff workload, and cost, and present recommendations to boards.
Make sure clinical risk, information governance, and equality impacts are analysed and addressed in requirements.
Define and track the benefits of change, and set up how they will be measured after go-live.
Line manage or lead business analysts and run community of practice activities.
qualifications: Substantial experience of business analysis on complex change, at a level equivalent to a master's degree.

levels.title: Lead business analyst
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A lead business analyst has a good understanding of the enterprise arena and works in highly complex problem spaces, typically spanning multiple products or services.

At this role level, you will:
- be a leader in the business analysis community (across government and externally)
- have functional management or people management accountabilities, or a combination of both
- actively share knowledge and be seen as a go-to person in the field
- mentor others
- own the main stakeholder relationships
responsibilities: Lead analysis for highly complex problems that span several products, services, or organisations in a care system.
Shape the business case and benefits realisation plan for major investments.
Set business analysis standards, such as requirements traceability for safety-related and regulated software.
Work with clinical leads, architects, and product managers to align analysis with organisational strategy.
Line manage business analysts and lead their professional development.
qualifications: Extensive experience of leading business analysis across complex, multi-team change.

levels.title: Head of business analysis
levels.pcfLevelDescription: The head of business analysis leads the business analysis function across the enterprise area and builds business analysis capability for the organisation.
responsibilities: Lead the business analysis function and set its strategy, standards, and ways of working.
Build business analysis capability, including recruitment, career paths, and training.
Advise executive and clinical leaders on the analysis needed for major health and care transformation.
Make sure benefits realisation is planned, measured, and reported across the portfolio.
Manage the function's budget and workforce plan.
qualifications: Extensive experience of leading a business analysis function or practice.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Information resources is scored at level 6 because the head of business analysis owns the organisation-wide standards for how requirements, process models, and benefits records are kept across all change work.

roles.title: Delivery manager
roles.summary: Delivery managers help multidisciplinary teams deliver digital health services that work for patients, clinicians, and care staff. They create the conditions for teams to work well, remove blockers, manage risks and dependencies, and keep delivery moving at a sustainable pace, using agile and lean ways of working.
healthContext: Releases to services that support patient care must pass clinical safety and information governance checks, so delivery managers build these into the team's plans and definition of done.
Delivery often depends on clinicians and care staff who have limited time away from patients, so delivery managers plan research, testing, and training around clinical rotas.
Changes to live clinical services need careful timing, so delivery managers plan go-lives with operational teams to avoid peak clinical periods and to have support in place.
Teams often depend on suppliers of clinical systems and on other health and care organisations, so delivery managers manage external dependencies and contracts.

pcfRole.name: Delivery manager
pcfRole.description: A delivery manager is accountable for the delivery of products and services.

levels.title: Associate delivery manager
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
At this role level, you will:
- work on a small or mature Agile team
- learn on the job
- potentially work alongside a delivery manager on a larger team, shadowing and providing support, or working to deliver an element under guidance and mentorship
responsibilities: Facilitate team ceremonies such as stand-ups, planning, show and tells, and retrospectives.
Keep the team's board, risk and issue log, and dependency records up to date.
Track the clinical safety, information governance, and accessibility tasks needed before each release.
Arrange sessions with clinicians, care staff, and patients for research and testing, working around clinical rotas.
Shadow and support a delivery manager on a larger team, delivering parts of the work under guidance.
qualifications: Some experience of working in or with a delivery team, or equivalent experience.

levels.title: Delivery manager
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A delivery manager is accountable for the performance of the team.

At this role level, you will:
- build and maintain teams, ensuring they are motivated, collaborating and working well
- identify obstacles and help the team to overcome them
- focus the team on what is most important to the delivery of products and services
- encourage and facilitate continuous improvement of the delivery team
- coach and mentor both team members and others to apply the most appropriate Agile and Lean tools and techniques
The complexity or breadth of products or teams will vary in this role, depending on the context.
responsibilities: Lead the delivery of a digital health product or service through discovery, alpha, beta, and live.
Plan releases with operational and clinical teams, including go-live support, training, and rollback plans.
Make sure clinical safety, information governance, and accessibility assurance happens in step with delivery, not at the end.
Manage the team's budget, supplier contracts, and resourcing.
Report progress, risks, and benefits to governance boards in plain terms.
Build a healthy team culture and coach team members in agile ways of working.
qualifications: Substantial experience of delivering digital products or services using agile methods.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: There is no Band 6 level because the UK GDaD PCF has no delivery manager level between associate (EO/HEO) and delivery manager (SEO/G7).

levels.title: Senior delivery manager
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A senior delivery manager is accountable for the effective delivery of complex, high risk products and services. The role is similar to a delivery manager role, but senior delivery managers have more experience across a range of products and services, throughout the entire product life cycle, and have greater responsibility and accountability as the main point of escalation.

At this role level, you will:
- have strong communication skills and engage senior stakeholders
- coach and mentor delivery managers
responsibilities: Lead the delivery of complex or high-risk services, such as those used in urgent care or that replace a core clinical system.
Act as the main point of escalation for delivery risks, issues, and dependencies across several teams.
Plan large-scale rollouts across sites and organisations, with clinical safety officers and operational leads.
Manage budgets, commercial arrangements, and supplier performance for the service.
Line manage and develop delivery managers.
qualifications: Extensive experience of delivering complex digital services across their whole life cycle.

levels.title: Head of delivery management
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A head of (Agile) delivery management is an experienced practitioner who exemplifies what good looks like across the delivery roles.

At this role level, you will:
- represent and champion the role within your department, across government and in industry
- lead the community of practice for this role and build capability and excellence (in an Agile, Lean practice)
- be responsible for the recruitment of the right people to the right teams
- support professional development and continuous improvement of your community
- work with other heads of roles to promote effective cross-functional delivery
- be a skilled team leader who can confidently communicate the value of the role to digital and non-digital stakeholders
- be credible and influential across departments
responsibilities: Lead the delivery management profession and set the organisation's standards for agile delivery.
Recruit, develop, and deploy delivery managers across the portfolio.
Make sure delivery approaches meet clinical safety, information governance, and assurance requirements without slowing teams needlessly.
Advise executive and clinical leaders on delivery risks, capacity, and priorities.
Manage the profession's budget and workforce plan.
qualifications: Extensive experience of leading delivery across multiple teams and of leading a delivery practice.

roles.title: Product manager
roles.summary: Product managers make sure the organisation's digital health products meet the needs of patients, clinicians, and care staff and deliver value for the health and care system. They set the product vision and roadmap, prioritise the work of multidisciplinary teams using evidence, and are accountable for the outcomes their products achieve, including their effect on care.
healthContext: Product decisions can affect patient safety, so product managers own the clinical risk of their product with the clinical safety officer and make sure hazards are managed before release.
Products serve many user groups with different needs, such as patients, carers, clinicians, and administrative staff, and product managers must balance them fairly.
Some products may be regulated as medical devices, so product managers need to know when regulation applies and plan for it.
Outcomes in care include safety, quality, access, equity, and staff time, so product managers define success measures that clinical and operational leaders recognise.
Products often depend on national and regional health data standards and shared platforms, so product managers work across organisational boundaries.

pcfRole.name: Product manager
pcfRole.description:
A product manager makes sure that their products provide value and achieve the right outcomes by balancing user and business needs.

In this role, you will:
- work with multidisciplinary teams, bringing together their views, user needs and business needs, to frame the problem
- work with multidisciplinary teams to provide the right outcomes for users and the organisation
- make decisions on priorities for your teams
- ensure teams comply with appropriate standards

levels.title: Associate product manager
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
An associate product manager is responsible for features, components or part of a product, contributing to the delivery of value.

This can be an entry-level role for civil servants who are looking to move into a digital role or those on emerging talent schemes.

At this role level, you will:
- work with product managers to advocate for user needs throughout the organisation, prioritising delivery of greatest value
- manage a smaller product with support, or a subset of features of a larger product
- learn product management approaches and methods
responsibilities: Own the backlog for a feature or part of a product, working with a product manager.
Turn evidence from user research with patients, clinicians, and care staff into prioritised user stories.
Work with clinical safety officers to record and review hazards for the features you own.
Track product measures, such as uptake, completion rates, and support calls, and report what they show.
Represent the product at show and tells and with operational stakeholders.
qualifications: Experience in a digital, clinical, or operational role, or equivalent experience.

levels.title: Product manager
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A product manager is responsible for product quality and value, working with the team to identify, implement and improve strategies and tactics for their products. They might recruit and manage people in the product profession, ensuring people with the right skills are hired, supported and developed.

This can be an entry-level role for new product managers who have been working in other digital roles.

At this role level, you will:
- lead a product through different phases of the product life cycle, from discovery, through development, delivery and continuous improvement, to retirement
- support lead and senior product managers
- prioritise work for your teams and be able to measure outcomes
responsibilities: Set the vision, roadmap, and success measures for a digital health product.
Prioritise the team's work, balancing user needs, clinical safety, policy, technical constraints, and cost.
Accept clinical risk for product changes with the clinical safety officer, and stop releases that are not safe.
Work with clinical and operational leaders to make sure the product fits care pathways and is adopted.
Make sure the product meets accessibility, information governance, and service standards.
Measure the product's outcomes, including its benefits for patients and staff.
qualifications: Substantial experience of product management or of a related digital role.

levels.title: Senior product manager
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A senior product manager can work on a group of products that share a value proposition, or a single product that is complex, high risk or sensitive. They are responsible for product quality and value, working with teams to identify, implement and improve strategies and tactics for their products. They might also be involved in parts of programme management activity.

At this role level, you will:
- lead products through different phases of the product life cycle, from discovery, through development, delivery and continuous improvement, to retirement
- make decisions based on the overall quality and value of your products
- manage associate product managers and product managers
- be involved in recruiting associate product managers, product managers and contractors
responsibilities: Lead a group of related products, or a single product that is complex, high risk, or sensitive, such as one used in emergency care.
Build product strategy from evidence about patient needs, clinical practice, and health and care policy.
Make sure the product meets medical device regulation where it applies.
Manage the product's budget and make the case for investment with benefits for care.
Coach and line manage product managers.
qualifications: Extensive experience of managing digital products through their whole life cycle.

levels.title: Lead product manager
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A lead product manager is responsible for a product portfolio or end-to-end service, and the delivery of product quality and value. They work with teams to identify, implement and improve strategies and tactics for their products. They are a member of the management team for their product area and provide product leadership and direction across multiple teams.

At this role level, you will:
- manage people and manage products
- maintain the high level roadmap
- be involved in a range of programme management activities relevant to the product portfolio
- be involved in recruiting product managers at all levels and contractors
- provide leadership in your programmes and across the local community, working closely with the head of product, where they exist
responsibilities: Lead a product portfolio or end-to-end service, such as all products that support one care pathway.
Set product direction across several teams and make sure products work together for patients and staff.
Work with clinical leads and the clinical safety officer to manage clinical risk across the portfolio.
Hold the portfolio budget and report benefits to senior governance boards.
Lead and develop product managers in the product area.
qualifications: Extensive experience of leading products across multiple teams.

levels.title: Head of product
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A head of product provides support to all product managers in the organisation and to the product community across government. They lead on product strategy, working closely with lead product managers and their business units. They are responsible for setting and raising standards for product management in their organisation.

At this role level, you will:
- coach others in product management
- work with organisation management and other communities to represent product community interests
- oversee every member of the community, including their role, assignments, development, pay and performance
- manage recruitment, development, moves and exits from the community, covering civil servants and contractors
- line manage senior and lead product managers
responsibilities: Set the organisation's product strategy, working with executive, clinical, and operational leaders.
Set and raise standards for product management, including how products manage clinical risk and measure outcomes.
Lead the product profession, including recruitment, career paths, and capability building.
Decide investment priorities across products, using evidence of need, value, and equity.
Represent the organisation's products with partners across the health and care system.
qualifications: Extensive experience of leading product management across an organisation.

roles.title: Project manager
roles.summary: Project managers plan and deliver projects that change how the organisation supports health and care, such as deploying a clinical system to new sites, moving services to new infrastructure, or introducing new digital tools for care staff. They control scope, time, cost, quality, and risk, using recognised project methods, and make sure projects deliver the benefits they promised for patients and staff.
healthContext: Projects that change clinical systems or workflows need clinical safety assurance before go-live, so project managers plan hazard workshops, safety case sign-off, and clinical safety officer input into the schedule.
Go-lives must not disrupt patient care, so project managers plan cutovers, business continuity arrangements, and floor-walking support with clinical and operational teams.
Projects often need data protection impact assessments and information sharing agreements, so project managers plan these early with information governance colleagues.
Benefits in care, such as staff time released or fewer errors, take time to appear, so project managers set up baselines and hand over benefits tracking to the service.

levels.title: Assistant project manager
levels.summary: An assistant project manager supports the delivery of projects, or manages small, well-defined projects with guidance from a more senior project manager.
responsibilities: Maintain project plans, risk and issue logs, action logs, and dependency records.
Organise and minute project meetings and boards, and follow up actions.
Manage small, well-defined pieces of work, such as a site rollout or a training schedule, with guidance.
Track readiness tasks for go-live, such as clinical safety sign-off, data protection checks, and staff training.
Prepare highlight reports and track project spending against budget.
qualifications: A foundation project management qualification, or equivalent experience.

levels.title: Project manager
levels.summary: A project manager runs projects of moderate size and complexity from start to close, such as rolling out a digital service to several care settings.
responsibilities: Plan and manage projects from start-up to closure, controlling scope, time, cost, quality, and risk.
Plan go-lives with clinical and operational teams, including cutover, business continuity, and support arrangements.
Make sure clinical safety, information governance, and accessibility assurance is planned and completed before go-live.
Manage the project budget and supplier deliverables.
Report to the project board and escalate risks and issues outside tolerance.
Set baselines for benefits and hand over benefits tracking to the service.
qualifications: A recognised project management qualification, such as a practitioner-level certificate, or equivalent experience.
Experience of managing projects that change services or systems.

levels.title: Senior project manager
levels.summary: A senior project manager leads large, complex, or high-risk projects, such as replacing a clinical system across an organisation, and may manage other project staff.
responsibilities: Lead large or high-risk projects, such as clinical system replacements or multi-site deployments.
Manage complex dependencies with suppliers, other projects, and partner health and care organisations.
Lead go-live decisions with the clinical safety officer, operational leads, and the senior responsible owner.
Manage the project budget and commercial arrangements, including change control with suppliers.
Make sure benefits for patients and staff are defined, owned, and measured.
Manage and develop project managers and project support staff.
qualifications: A recognised project management qualification, or equivalent experience.
Substantial experience of managing complex projects in a regulated or safety-critical setting.

levels.title: Lead project manager
levels.summary: A lead project manager leads the most complex projects or a group of related projects, and sets project management practice for their area.
responsibilities: Lead the most complex projects, or a group of related projects, across several services or organisations.
Set project management standards, templates, and assurance for the area, and coach project managers.
Advise senior responsible owners and boards on delivery options, risks, and recovery of struggling projects.
Manage significant budgets and contracts, and make sure projects give value for money.
Make sure clinical safety and information governance requirements are met across the group of projects.
Line manage project managers.
qualifications: Extensive experience of leading complex projects, with a recognised project management qualification or equivalent experience.

levels.title: Head of project management
levels.summary: A head of project management leads the organisation's project management practice and the project managers who deliver its digital change.
responsibilities: Lead the project management practice, including its methods, standards, tools, and assurance.
Allocate project managers to the organisation's projects and manage the practice's capacity.
Build project management capability, including recruitment, training, and career paths.
Advise executive leaders on project health, delivery risks, and lessons learned.
Manage the practice's budget.
qualifications: Extensive experience of leading projects and project managers, with a recognised project management qualification or equivalent experience.

roles.title: Programme delivery manager
roles.summary: Programme delivery managers are accountable for delivering complex digital health services that need several teams, suppliers, or organisations to work together, or that carry high technical, clinical, or public risk. They manage dependencies, budgets, commercial arrangements, and people across the programme, and make sure it delivers its intended benefits for patients, clinicians, and care staff.
healthContext: Programmes often change how care is delivered across several organisations, so programme delivery managers coordinate clinical, operational, and digital leaders who have different priorities and governance.
Clinical risk must be managed across the whole programme, not only within each team, so they work with clinical safety officers to keep a programme-level view of hazards and safety cases.
Programmes frequently involve large contracts with suppliers of clinical systems, so commercial and contract management is a major part of the role.
Benefits in care, such as shorter waits, safer prescribing, or staff time released, must be defined, owned by the service, and tracked long after the programme closes.

pcfRole.name: Programme delivery manager
pcfRole.description: A programme delivery manager is accountable for the delivery of complex products and services that are being delivered by multiple teams or have high technical or political risk.

levels.title: Programme delivery manager
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A programme delivery manager is accountable for the delivery of complex products and services that are delivered by multiple teams or have high technical or political risk.

At this role level, you will:
- manage dependencies of varying complexity, potentially planning and feeding into larger programmes and portfolios
- remove blockers and manage risks, commercials, budgets and people
- balance objectives and redeploy people and resources as priorities change
- have an in-depth knowledge of Agile and other methodologies
- be responsible for understanding, managing and communicating to complex stakeholder groups, balancing priorities
- be the initial escalation point for the programme
- have an awareness of the bigger picture
- support the programme director by overseeing the delivery of their vision for the programme
- support and coach delivery managers
responsibilities: Lead the delivery of a programme of several teams, such as introducing a new digital service across a care pathway.
Plan and manage dependencies between teams, suppliers, and partner health and care organisations.
Keep a programme-level view of clinical risk with the clinical safety officer, and make sure each release has the assurance it needs.
Manage the programme budget, contracts, and supplier performance.
Report progress, risks, and benefits to the programme board and senior responsible owner.
Line manage delivery managers and build a healthy delivery culture across the programme.
qualifications: Extensive experience of delivering complex, multi-team digital services or programmes.

levels.title: Senior programme delivery manager
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A programme delivery manager is accountable for the delivery of complex products and services that are delivered by multiple teams or have high technical or political risk.

At this role level, you will:
- manage dependencies of varying complexity, potentially planning and feeding into larger programmes and portfolios
- remove blockers and manage risks, commercials, budgets and people
- balance objectives and redeploy people and resources as priorities change
- have an in-depth knowledge of Agile and other methodologies
- be responsible for understanding, managing and communicating to complex stakeholder groups, balancing priorities
- be the initial escalation point for the programme
- have an awareness of the bigger picture
- support the programme director by overseeing the delivery of their vision for the programme
- support and coach delivery managers
responsibilities: Lead the delivery of the organisation's largest or highest-risk programmes, such as replacing the core electronic patient record or a system-wide shared care record.
Coordinate delivery across several organisations in a care system, aligning their plans, governance, and go-live decisions.
Lead commercial strategy and negotiation with major suppliers, and manage programme budgets across several years.
Make sure clinical safety, information governance, and business continuity are assured at programme level before major go-lives.
Lead and develop programme and delivery managers, and set delivery standards across the portfolio.
Advise executive leaders on programme risk, options, and recovery.
qualifications: Extensive experience of leading large, high-risk programmes across organisations.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: The UK GDaD PCF has one programme delivery manager level, at G7 or G6. This reference adds a senior level at Band 8c for the largest, multi-organisation programmes, with larger budgets (financial resources level 5) and more contentious communication (level 6).

roles.title: Digital portfolio manager
roles.summary: Digital portfolio managers help the organisation choose, track, and govern its portfolio of digital projects, programmes, and products so that it invests in the work that does most for patients, clinicians, and care staff. They run portfolio governance and reporting, help leaders prioritise with good evidence, and make sure the portfolio delivers the benefits it promised.
healthContext: Digital work competes for funding with front-line care, so portfolio managers help leaders show the benefits of digital investment for patients and staff.
Portfolio governance must include clinical safety, information governance, and cyber security assurance, so portfolio managers track these alongside time, cost, and scope.
Many digital projects depend on capacity in clinical and operational teams, such as clinicians to test or staff to train, so portfolio managers watch for clashes in demand on services.
Funding often comes from several sources with their own reporting rules and deadlines, so portfolio managers keep reporting accurate and on time.

pcfRole.name: Digital portfolio manager
pcfRole.description: A digital portfolio manager co-ordinates and manages a group , or ‘portfolio’, of digital projects. In this role, you will use an iterative and flexible approach to help define governance processes for this portfolio.

levels.title: Digital portfolio analyst
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A digital portfolio analyst supports the tracking, analysis and delivery of outcomes across a portfolio of digital projects. This role level may be called ‘associate digital portfolio manager’ in your organisation.

As you will be learning basic portfolio management skills, you will report to a more senior portfolio manager.
responsibilities: Collect and check status, risk, finance, and benefits data from projects across the portfolio.
Maintain the portfolio register and dashboards, and spot gaps or inconsistencies in reporting.
Prepare papers and reports for portfolio governance boards.
Track assurance milestones, such as clinical safety sign-off and data protection impact assessments, across projects.
Support portfolio managers with prioritisation and planning analysis.
qualifications: A degree or relevant qualification, or equivalent experience of analysis or reporting.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: The UK GDaD PCF places both the analyst and manager levels at HEO or SEO. This reference places the analyst at Band 5, because it is a learning level that reports to a portfolio manager, and the manager at Band 6, so the two levels are not in the same band.

levels.title: Digital portfolio manager
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A digital portfolio manager helps to co-ordinate and manage a portfolio of digital projects.

At this role level, you will:
- help to create environments that enable teams to deliver
- support the prioritisation of a group of projects and programmes
- help teams to follow governance and delivery processes
- help stakeholders understand the performance of work and any related risks
- support more senior portfolio managers and leadership in making improvements
responsibilities: Coordinate a portfolio of digital projects and programmes, such as all digital work for one directorate.
Help teams follow governance, assurance, and delivery processes, and make them proportionate.
Support leaders to prioritise work using evidence of need, benefit, risk, and capacity.
Report portfolio performance, risks, and benefits clearly to boards and stakeholders.
Spot clashes in demand on clinical and operational teams across projects and help resolve them.
qualifications: Experience of portfolio, programme, or project management, or equivalent experience.

levels.title: Senior digital portfolio manager
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A senior digital portfolio manager is responsible for co-ordinating and managing a portfolio of digital projects.

At this role level, you will:
- track, analyse and help deliver outcomes in your portfolio
- give guidance and deal with issues to help teams to deliver faster
- manage governance and assurance processes, and ensure standards are met
- provide information to stakeholders on work performance and related risks
responsibilities: Manage the organisation's digital portfolio, or a large part of it, and its governance and assurance processes.
Track and analyse outcomes and benefits across the portfolio, and act on issues to help teams deliver.
Make sure the portfolio meets standards, including clinical safety, information governance, and cyber security assurance.
Advise senior leaders on prioritisation, investment, and trade-offs, using clear evidence.
Manage portfolio reporting to funders and external bodies.
Line manage portfolio analysts and managers.
qualifications: Extensive experience of portfolio or programme management, at a level equivalent to a master's degree.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: There is no Band 7 level because the UK GDaD PCF moves from digital portfolio manager (HEO/SEO) to senior digital portfolio manager (G7).

levels.title: Head of digital portfolio
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A head of portfolio leads a team of digital portfolio managers. You will ensure the portfolio of digital projects delivers the best possible outcomes.

At this role level, you will:
- lead the tracking and governing of digital projects
- ensure the right controls are used
- address risks and deal with, or escalate, issues
- provide leaders with insights into the portfolio's future so they can make informed decisions
- build and lead a diverse, skilled and motivated team of digital portfolio managers
- ensure the portfolio team is meeting the needs of the organisation
- support the professional development of the portfolio community, including line management and coaching
responsibilities: Lead the digital portfolio function and the team of portfolio managers.
Set the portfolio strategy, controls, and governance, and make sure they are used.
Give executive leaders insight into the portfolio's future, so they can make investment decisions.
Make sure the portfolio's benefits for patients, staff, and the organisation are realised and reported.
Address portfolio-level risks and escalate issues to the executive team.
Manage the function's budget and capability.
qualifications: Extensive experience of leading portfolio management in a complex organisation.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Financial resources is scored at level 5 because the head of digital portfolio oversees investment across the whole digital portfolio, covering several services; information resources is level 6 because the portfolio register and reporting cover the whole organisation.

roles.title: Service owner
roles.summary: Service owners are accountable leaders for a digital health service from end to end, across its digital, operational, and clinical parts. They bring together multidisciplinary teams and service partners, set the service's strategy and priorities, own its budget and performance, and make sure it delivers safe, high-quality outcomes and benefits for patients, clinicians, and care staff.
healthContext: A digital health service is part of a wider care service, so service owners work as equals with clinical and operational leaders and share accountability for the patient's whole experience.
The service owner is accountable for the service's clinical risk being managed, working with the clinical safety officer and accepting residual risk at the right level.
Services handle confidential health information, so service owners make sure information governance, data protection, and cyber security are in place and reviewed.
Live services that support care must be resilient, so service owners make sure business continuity, incident response, and supplier support meet clinical needs.
Benefits in care must be measured and reported, so service owners keep performance indicators that cover safety, quality, access, equity, and cost.

pcfRole.name: Service owner
pcfRole.description:
A service owner is accountable for the quality, performance, benefits and outcomes of a service. They provide clear end-to-end direction, prioritisation, risk management and decision making for teams in line with department, policy and user outcomes.

In this role, you will:
- define success and quality measures for a service, driving continuous improvement towards these measures
- inform and influence stakeholders, getting consensus that enables work to progress
- ensure the delivery of change that realises the outcomes and benefits of your service

levels.title: Service owner
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A service owner is an accountable leader that brings together a multidisciplinary team to ensure delivery of a quality service. They advocate for their service and teams, and develop an open and trust-based culture.

At this role level, you will:
- ensure a strategy is in place that delivers the intended vision, outcomes and benefits
- prioritise areas of development, balancing user needs, business requirements and policy
- ensure appropriate governance and assurance is in place
- ensure appropriate funding is in place
- create the culture and environment for the team to do their best work
responsibilities: Be accountable for an end-to-end digital health service, such as online access to records or digital referrals, across its whole life cycle.
Set the service strategy and priorities with clinical and operational leaders, balancing user needs, safety, policy, and cost.
Own the service budget and make the case for investment based on benefits for patients and staff.
Make sure clinical risk, information governance, accessibility, and cyber security are managed and assured.
Monitor service performance and benefits, and lead improvement when the service falls short.
Represent the service at governance boards and with partners across the health and care system.
qualifications: Extensive experience of leading digital, operational, or clinical services.

levels.title: Senior service owner
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A service owner is an accountable leader that brings together a multidisciplinary team to ensure delivery of a quality service. They advocate for their service and teams, and develop an open and trust-based culture.

At this role level, you will:
- ensure a strategy is in place that delivers the intended vision, outcomes and benefits
- prioritise areas of development, balancing user needs, business requirements and policy
- ensure appropriate governance and assurance is in place
- ensure appropriate funding is in place
- create the culture and environment for the team to do their best work
responsibilities: Be accountable for a group of related digital health services, or for a critical service used across the care system, such as the electronic patient record.
Set a multi-year strategy for the services with executive, clinical, and operational leaders.
Own budgets and major supplier relationships across the services.
Accept and escalate clinical, information, and operational risk at a senior level, working with the clinical safety officer and the executive owner of information risk.
Lead service owners and multidisciplinary teams, and build a culture of openness and continuous improvement.
Lead the response to major service incidents that affect patient care, and the learning that follows.
qualifications: Extensive experience of leading large or critical services, including their budgets and suppliers.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: The UK GDaD PCF has one service owner level, at G7 or G6. This reference adds a senior level at Band 8c for services that are critical to care across the organisation, with budgets across several services (financial resources level 5) and regular involvement in serious incidents that affect patients (emotional effort level 2).

roles.title: User researcher
roles.summary: User researchers help teams understand the people who use and deliver health and care services, including patients, carers, clinicians, and care staff. They plan and carry out research safely and ethically, turn what they learn into clear insight, and make sure decisions about digital health services are based on evidence of real needs, including the needs of people who find services hardest to use.
healthContext: Research participants are often unwell, anxious, or in vulnerable circumstances, so researchers plan carefully for informed consent, safeguarding, and participants' wellbeing.
Research may hear about distressing experiences of illness, loss, or poor care, so researchers need support to manage the emotional effect on themselves and their team.
Clinicians and care staff have little time away from patients, so researchers plan research in clinical settings without disrupting care, often through observation and short sessions.
Some research counts as formal health research or uses patient data, so researchers need to know when ethics or research governance approval and data protection checks apply.
Health inequalities are real, so researchers make deliberate efforts to include people with low digital skills, disabilities, or limited English, and people who use services least.

pcfRole.name: User researcher
pcfRole.description: User researchers plan, design and carry out research activities with users that help teams get a deep understanding of the people that use government services. This research informs policy, proposition, service, content and interaction design so that services work well for users and achieve policy intent.

levels.title: Associate user researcher
levels.pcfLevelDescription: As a trainee in an entry-level role, working with more experienced user researchers, you will need to have an understanding of the role and show potential, although you will need guidance and training to produce good work and develop your skills.
responsibilities: Learn user research methods through training and by working alongside experienced researchers.
Take notes, help run sessions, and help recruit participants, following consent and safeguarding procedures.
Store research data securely and in line with information governance rules.
Help analyse research data and share findings with the team.
qualifications: Working towards a qualification or apprenticeship in a relevant field, or equivalent experience.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Emotional effort is level 2 at every user researcher level, because research with patients and carers often involves hearing about illness, loss, or poor care. Research is scored from level 2 here, rising to level 3 once research is the main duty.

levels.title: Junior user researcher
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A junior user researcher is embedded in a multidisciplinary team to carry out user research activities.

At this role level, you will:
- have some practical experience but need regular guidance and training to produce your best work and develop your skills
- work in combination with a more senior user researcher
responsibilities: Plan and run research sessions with patients, carers, and staff, with guidance from a more senior researcher.
Use methods such as interviews, usability testing, and contextual observation in care settings.
Get informed consent, adapt sessions for participants' needs, and raise any safeguarding concerns.
Analyse findings and present them to the team as clear, actionable insight.
Recruit diverse participants, including people who find services hard to use.
qualifications: A degree in a relevant subject, such as social science or psychology, or equivalent experience.

levels.title: User researcher
levels.pcfLevelDescription: A user researcher is usually embedded in a multidisciplinary team and responsible for planning and carrying out user research activities. At this level, you will be expected to work independently on a team.
responsibilities: Plan and carry out user research for a multidisciplinary team, choosing methods that fit the questions and the participants.
Research with clinicians and care staff in their work settings to understand clinical workflows and safety-critical tasks.
Plan research with people in vulnerable circumstances safely, and judge when ethics or research governance approval is needed.
Share insight that helps the team prioritise, including evidence about safety and accessibility.
Bring the team into research so they understand users first-hand.
qualifications: A degree in a relevant subject, or equivalent experience.
Experience of planning and carrying out user research.

levels.title: Senior user researcher
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A senior user researcher is an experienced practitioner who can plan and lead user research activities in larger teams and on more complex services.

At this role level, you will:
- build user-centred practices in new teams
- align user research activities with wider plans to inform a service proposition
- supervise and develop other user researchers to assure and improve research practice
responsibilities: Plan and lead research for complex services, such as those that span several care settings or serve people in crisis.
Align research with the service's wider plans and with other teams' research.
Plan safe research with people in vulnerable circumstances, and prepare ethics and research governance submissions.
Supervise and develop user researchers, and assure the quality and ethics of their work.
Build user-centred practice in new teams and with clinical stakeholders.
qualifications: Substantial experience of user research, at a level equivalent to a master's degree.

levels.title: Lead user researcher
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A lead user researcher is an expert practitioner, leading and aligning user research activities across several teams.

At this role level, you will:
- ensure that teams take a user-centred, evidence-based approach to service design and delivery
- develop and assure good user research practice
responsibilities: Lead and align user research across several teams or a whole programme.
Make sure teams take a user-centred, evidence-based approach, and that research reaches people most affected by health inequalities.
Set and assure research practice, including consent, safeguarding, data handling, and participant wellbeing.
Build shared research assets, such as research repositories and participant panels, that teams can reuse safely.
Line manage and develop user researchers.
qualifications: Extensive experience of leading user research across teams.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: There is no Band 8a level, because the UK GDaD PCF places lead user researcher at G7 or G6 and this reference follows the suggested Band 8b. Financial resources is level 3 for the research budget, such as participant recruitment and incentives.

levels.title: Head of user research
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A head of user research leads user researchers in an organisation and attracts and builds talent.

At this role level, you will:
- be an expert practitioner who can define and assure best practice
- influence organisational strategy and priorities
- collaborate with colleagues across government
responsibilities: Lead the user research profession and set its strategy, standards, and ethics.
Influence organisational strategy and priorities with evidence about patients, carers, and care staff.
Attract, build, and develop research talent, including career paths and recruitment.
Assure research practice across the organisation and act as the escalation point for high-risk research.
Represent research practice with ethics, safeguarding, and research governance bodies.
qualifications: Extensive experience of leading user research and a research practice.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: The UK GDaD PCF places both lead user researcher and head of user research at G7 or G6, with a suggested Band 8b. This reference places the head at Band 8c, in line with the heads of other user-centred design professions, because the head leads the profession across the organisation and initiates its research programmes.

roles.title: Service designer
roles.summary: Service designers design health and care services end to end, from the moment someone first needs help to the end of their care, across digital, phone, paper, and face-to-face channels. They work with patients, carers, clinicians, and care staff to map how services really work, find where they fail people, and design services that are safe, simple, and fair, and that work across organisational boundaries.
healthContext: Care pathways cross many organisations and professions, so service designers map whole journeys, including handoffs, waits, and the work patients and carers do to hold care together.
Changes to how a service works can create new clinical risks, so service designers work with clinical safety officers to identify hazards in new service models before they go live.
Digital services must not shut out people who cannot or will not use them, so service designers design assisted and non-digital routes alongside digital ones.
Clinical and operational staff are part of the service, so designs must fit their workflows, workload, and professional responsibilities, not only the patient's journey.

pcfRole.name: Service designer
pcfRole.description: Service designers design the end-to-end journey of a service. This helps a user complete their goal and government deliver a policy intent. In this role, your work may involve the creation of, or change to, transactions, products and content across both digital and offline channels provided by different parts of government.

levels.title: Associate service designer
levels.pcfLevelDescription: As a trainee in an entry-level position, working under supervision, you will need design aptitude, potential and an understanding of the role.
responsibilities: Learn service design methods through training and by working alongside experienced designers.
Help map user journeys and service blueprints from research with patients and staff.
Help prepare and run co-design workshops, following consent and information governance procedures.
Document design decisions and keep design artefacts up to date.
qualifications: Working towards a qualification or apprenticeship in design or a related field, or equivalent experience.

levels.title: Junior service designer
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
Junior designers are graduates with a degree in a relevant subject or relevant work experience.

At this role level, you will:
- explain design decisions, work collaboratively and have responsibility for a service
- work independently after being given direction by more senior designers
- independently identify user issues and important needs
responsibilities: Map current journeys and service blueprints for parts of a care pathway, such as booking or follow-up.
Design and test improvements to parts of a service, with direction from a more senior designer.
Run co-design sessions with patients, carers, and staff, adapting them so everyone can take part.
Identify where a service creates extra work or risk for patients or staff, and raise it with the team.
qualifications: A degree in design or a related subject, or equivalent experience.

levels.title: Service designer
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A service designer is a confident and competent designer who can develop designs based on evidence of user needs and organisational outcomes.

At this role level, you will:
- be trusted to make good decisions
- recognise when to ask for further guidance and support
- contribute to the development of design concepts
- interpret evidence-based research and incorporate this into your work
responsibilities: Design end-to-end services across channels, including assisted and non-digital routes for people who need them.
Map care pathways across organisations and design better handoffs between teams and services.
Design how the service works for staff, including roles, workload, and workflows, with operational leads.
Work with clinical safety officers to identify hazards in new service models and design controls.
Prototype and test service changes with patients, carers, and staff.
qualifications: A degree in design or a related subject, or equivalent experience.
Experience of designing services with users.

levels.title: Senior service designer
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A senior service designer is an experienced designer who works with minimal support and can influence and mentor others.

At this role level, you will:
- work with service managers and programme directors to develop design concepts
- potentially have responsibility across complex services
- help set direction and embed good practice within teams
- make important decisions based on research and understand how this research impacts others
responsibilities: Lead the design of complex services that span several care settings or organisations.
Shape the service vision with clinical, operational, and digital leaders.
Design new service models that improve safety, access, and equity, and test them with real users.
Make sure service changes are assessed for clinical risk, equality, and information governance effects.
Mentor designers and embed service design practice in teams.
qualifications: Substantial experience of service design, at a level equivalent to a master's degree.

levels.title: Lead service designer
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A lead service designer is an expert practitioner who influences and mentors others.

At this role level, you will:
- work with service managers and programme directors to develop design concepts
- set direction and assure the quality of design delivery across teams
- lead multiple or highly complex services
responsibilities: Set the design direction for multiple services or a whole care pathway, and assure the quality of design across teams.
Work with senior clinical and operational leaders to redesign how care is organised and delivered.
Make sure designs work for people most affected by health inequalities and for staff under pressure.
Set standards for how teams design for clinical safety and for assisted routes.
Line manage and develop service designers.
qualifications: Extensive experience of leading service design across teams.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: There is no Band 8a level, because the UK GDaD PCF places lead service designer at G7 or G6 and this reference follows the suggested Band 8b. Policy is level 5 because the lead designer shapes how a range of services across a directorate work.

levels.title: Head of service design
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A head of service design is an expert practitioner with broad industry experience, who can define and assure best practice while influencing, leading and mentoring others.

At this role level, you will:
- influence both design and organisational strategy and priorities
- collaborate with counterpart colleagues across government
- focus on ensuring the right conditions and environment for designers to work effectively
responsibilities: Lead the service design profession and set its strategy, standards, and ways of working.
Influence organisational strategy so that services are designed around the needs of patients, carers, and staff.
Build service design capability, including recruitment, career paths, and training.
Make the conditions for good design, such as access to users, time to research, and design in governance.
Work with peers across the health and care system to design joined-up services.
qualifications: Extensive experience of leading design and a design practice.

roles.title: Interaction designer
roles.summary: Interaction designers design how patients, carers, clinicians, and care staff use the organisation's digital health services, from patient-facing apps and forms to the screens clinicians use at the bedside. They design simple, accessible, and safe interactions, test them with real users, and use shared design systems so that services feel consistent and familiar.
healthContext: Clinicians often use systems under time pressure, with interruptions and on shared devices, so designs must support fast, accurate work and make the safe action the easy one.
Poor design can cause clinical harm, such as selecting the wrong patient or misreading a dose, so designers apply human factors principles and work with clinical safety officers.
Many users are unwell, anxious, older, or disabled, so designs must meet accessibility standards and work for people with low digital skills or health literacy.
Alerts and warnings are only useful if people notice and trust them, so designers help reduce alert fatigue and keep safety-critical information visible.

pcfRole.name: Interaction designer
pcfRole.description: An interaction designer works out the best way to let users interact with services, in terms of both overall flow and at the level of individual design elements.

levels.title: Associate interaction designer
levels.pcfLevelDescription: As a trainee in an entry-level position, working under supervision, you need aptitude, potential and an understanding of the role.
responsibilities: Learn interaction design methods and the team's design system through training and pairing.
Create sketches, wireframes, and simple prototypes under supervision.
Help test designs with users and record what works and what does not.
Follow accessibility standards and the design system's patterns, including those for patient identity and safety warnings.
qualifications: Working towards a qualification or apprenticeship in design or a related field, or equivalent experience.

levels.title: Junior interaction designer
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A junior interaction designer is a graduate with a degree in a relevant subject or an individual with some relevant work experience, or both.

At this role level, you will:
- explain design decisions
- work collaboratively
- have a responsibility as part of a service
- work independently after being given direction by more senior designers
- independently identify user issues and important needs
responsibilities: Design and prototype parts of a service, such as forms, flows, and screens, with direction from a more senior designer.
Test designs with patients, carers, and staff, and change them based on what you learn.
Design accessible interactions that work with assistive technologies.
Explain design decisions to the team, including how they reduce the chance of error.
qualifications: A degree in design or a related subject, or equivalent experience.

levels.title: Interaction designer
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
An interaction designer is a confident and competent designer who can develop designs based on evidence of user needs and organisational outcomes.

At this role level, you will:
- be trusted to make good decisions
- recognise when to ask for further guidance and support
- contribute to the development of design concepts
- interpret evidence-based research and incorporate this into your work
responsibilities: Design interactions for a digital health product, from early concepts to detailed, tested designs.
Design for clinical workflows, testing with clinicians and care staff in realistic scenarios, including interruptions.
Raise design-related hazards with the clinical safety officer and record how designs control them.
Use and contribute to the design system, including patterns for safety-critical information.
Work closely with developers to make sure designs are built as intended and remain accessible.
qualifications: A degree in design or a related subject, or equivalent experience.
Experience of designing digital services with users.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: The UK GDaD PCF places interaction designer at SEO or G7, with a suggested Band 7, the same as senior interaction designer. This reference places it at Band 6, the same as the service designer level with identical PCF skill levels, so the two interaction designer levels are not in the same band.

levels.title: Senior interaction designer
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A senior interaction designer is an experienced designer who works with minimal support and can influence and mentor others.

At this role level, you will:
- work with service managers and programme directors to develop design concepts
- potentially have responsibility across complex services
- help set direction and embed good practice within teams
- make important decisions based on research and understand how this research impacts others
responsibilities: Lead interaction design for complex services, such as clinical systems used across many care settings.
Apply human factors methods, such as task analysis, to safety-critical clinical workflows.
Provide design evidence for clinical safety cases and, where software is regulated, for usability files.
Help set direction and good practice for design in teams, and mentor other designers.
Make design decisions from research and data, and explain them to clinical and product leaders.
qualifications: Substantial experience of interaction design, at a level equivalent to a master's degree.

levels.title: Lead interaction designer
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A lead interaction designer is an expert practitioner who influences and mentors others.

At this role level, you will:
- work with service managers and programme directors to develop design concepts
- set direction and assure the quality of design delivery across teams
- lead multiple or highly complex services
responsibilities: Set design direction and assure the quality of interaction design across several teams or services.
Lead the design system, including accessible and safety-critical patterns that teams across the organisation reuse.
Lead human factors work on the highest-risk clinical services, with clinical safety officers.
Work with senior product and clinical leaders to develop design concepts for major services.
