Line manage and develop interaction designers.
qualifications: Extensive experience of leading interaction design across teams.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: There is no Band 8a level, because the UK GDaD PCF places lead interaction designer at G7 or G6 and this reference follows the suggested Band 8b. Policy is level 5 because the lead designer sets design standards for a range of services.

levels.title: Head of interaction design
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A head of interaction design is an expert practitioner with broad industry experience, who can define and assure best practice while influencing, leading and mentoring others.

At this role level, you will:
- influence both design and organisational strategy and priorities
- collaborate with counterpart colleagues across government
- focus on ensuring the right conditions and environment for designers to work effectively
responsibilities: Lead the interaction design profession and set its strategy, standards, and ways of working.
Influence design and organisational strategy so that services are usable, accessible, and safe.
Own the organisation's design system and make sure it meets accessibility and clinical safety needs.
Build design capability, including recruitment, career paths, and training.
Work with peers across the health and care system on shared design patterns.
qualifications: Extensive experience of leading design and a design practice.

roles.title: Content designer
roles.summary: Content designers make health and care information and services clear, so that patients, carers, clinicians, and care staff can understand what they need to know and do. They design content from evidence of user needs, write in plain English, work with clinical experts to keep it accurate, and look after content across its whole life, from creation to review and retirement.
healthContext: People often read health content when they are worried, unwell, or in a hurry, so content must be easy to understand and act on for people with low health literacy.
Wrong or out-of-date health information can cause harm, so content designers follow a clinical assurance process with review dates and named clinical reviewers.

Some topics are sensitive or high risk, such as urgent symptoms, mental health, medicines, and end of life care, so content designers work closely with clinicians and user researchers on tone and accuracy.
Clinical systems also need clear content, such as labels, instructions, and alerts, so content designers help reduce errors in clinical workflows.
Health content must be accessible and inclusive, including for people who use assistive technology, read in another language, or need easy read formats.

pcfRole.name: Content designer
pcfRole.description:
Content designers make things easier for people to understand and use. This can involve working on a single piece of content or on the end-to-end journey of a service to help users complete their goal and government deliver a policy intent. In this role your work may involve the creation of, or change to, a transaction, product or single piece of content that stretches across digital and offline channels.

In this role, you will:
- make sure appropriate content is shown to a user in the right place and in the best format
- start from discovery and work closely with user researchers, service designers and interaction designers

levels.title: Associate content designer
levels.pcfLevelDescription: As a trainee in an entry-level position, working under supervision, you need aptitude, potential and an understanding of the role. You will perform basic standard checks and copy edits.
responsibilities: Learn content design methods, the style guide, and the clinical review process through training and supervised work.
Carry out standard checks, copy edits, and updates to existing content.
Publish content using the content management system, following assurance steps.
Check content for accessibility, such as headings, link text, and alternative text.
qualifications: Working towards a qualification or apprenticeship in a relevant field, or equivalent experience.

levels.title: Junior content designer
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A junior content designer has some relevant work experience in content creation.

At this role level, you will:
- explain content decisions
- work collaboratively
- work independently after being given direction by more senior content designers
- independently identify user issues and needs
- support content team administration and publishing processes
- engage with and contribute to the cross-government content community
responsibilities: Write and update health content and service content, with direction from more senior content designers.
Use research and data to identify what users need to know and the words they use.
Work with clinical reviewers to check accuracy, and explain medical terms in plain English.
Support content publishing, review dates, and content team administration.
qualifications: A degree or relevant qualification, or equivalent experience of writing for the web.

levels.title: Content designer
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A content designer is responsible for creating, evaluating, updating and reviewing content at all stages of the end-to-end user journey.

At this role level, you will:
- be comfortable using evidence, data and research to make content decisions
- build relationships across government to focus on the needs of the user and to influence stakeholders
- contribute to and use the style guides and content patterns
- engage with and contribute to the cross-government content community
responsibilities: Design content across whole user journeys, such as finding a service, preparing for an appointment, and aftercare.
Design content for clinical systems, such as labels, instructions, and alerts, to reduce the chance of error.
Agree accuracy with clinical experts while keeping content clear and usable.
Test content with users, including people with low health literacy and people who use assistive technology.
Contribute to the style guide and content patterns.
qualifications: A degree or relevant qualification, or equivalent experience.
Experience of designing content for digital services.

levels.title: Senior content designer
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A senior content designer is an expert practitioner who develops content strategy and solutions for large-scale problems and high-profile events.

At this role level, you will:
- take responsibility for content quality, manage small teams and mentor content colleagues
- write and map user stories
- review the work of others to assure quality
- lead on cross-government content projects
- engage with and contribute to the cross-government content community
responsibilities: Develop content strategy for large or high-profile areas, such as a major condition area or a public health campaign.
Design content for sensitive and high-risk topics, such as urgent symptoms, mental health, and end of life care.
Set up clinical assurance, evidence sources, and review cycles for a body of health content.
Review others' work to assure quality, and manage or mentor content designers.
Write and map user stories with the team.
qualifications: Substantial experience of content design, at a level equivalent to a master's degree.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Emotional effort is level 2 because senior content designers regularly work on distressing topics, such as serious illness, self-harm, and bereavement.

levels.title: Lead content designer
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A lead content designer is an expert practitioner and leader who directs a team of content designers. They assure the content quality across whole teams and make sure content aligns to strategy and objectives while meeting the needs of users.

At this role level, you will:
- work closely with service managers, programme directors and senior stakeholders to resource teams, resolve problems and develop future projects
- promote the content design discipline, engage with the cross-government community and keep up to date with industry changes
responsibilities: Direct a team of content designers and assure content quality across several teams.
Make sure health content meets clinical assurance, accessibility, and style standards.
Work with senior clinical, communications, and product leaders to resource teams and resolve content problems.
Lead content for the organisation's most sensitive or high-risk information.
Line manage and develop content designers.
qualifications: Extensive experience of leading content design across teams.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: There is no Band 8a level, because the UK GDaD PCF places lead content designer at G7 or G6 and this reference follows the suggested Band 8b. Policy is level 5 because the lead sets content standards for a range of services; emotional effort is level 2, as for senior content designers.

levels.title: Head of content design
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A head of content design is an expert practitioner with broad industry experience who can define and assure best practice while influencing, leading and mentoring others.

At this role level, you will:
- develop a strategy for content that meets the organisation’s objectives
- lead a team capable of executing that strategy
- work with senior stakeholders to influence organisational strategy
- prioritise and collaborate with counterpart colleagues across government
- champion good content design practice within government and industry
responsibilities: Develop a content strategy that meets the organisation's objectives and the needs of patients and staff.
Set the organisation's standards for health information content and its clinical assurance.
Lead a content design team able to carry out the strategy, including recruitment and development.
Work with senior clinical and communications leaders to manage health information risks.
Prioritise content work across the organisation.
qualifications: Extensive experience of leading content design and a content practice.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: The UK GDaD PCF places both lead content designer and head of content design at G7 or G6, with a suggested Band 8b. This reference places the head at Band 8c, in line with the heads of other user-centred design professions, because the head sets content strategy and standards for the whole organisation.

roles.title: Accessibility specialist
roles.summary: Accessibility specialists help the organisation make its digital health services usable by as many people as possible, including disabled people and people with long-term conditions. They test services against accessibility standards and with assistive technologies, advise and train teams, and help embed accessibility into how services, clinical systems, and health information are designed, bought, and built.
healthContext: Many people who need health and care services most are disabled, older, or living with long-term conditions, so inaccessible services can stop people getting care.
Clinicians and care staff also have access needs, so internal clinical systems, including those bought from suppliers, must be accessible too.

Health information is often complex and published in many formats, such as documents, letters, and video, so specialists help teams make all of it accessible, including easy read and alternative formats.

Accessibility problems in clinical workflows can become safety problems, for example when a warning is not announced by a screen reader, so specialists work with clinical safety officers on these risks.

pcfRole.name: Accessibility specialist
pcfRole.description:
An accessibility specialist provides support, advice and guidance to other roles in the Government Digital and Data profession about how to create accessible digital services.

You will use knowledge of accessibility guidelines, provide technical expertise and bring the voice of disabled users to ensure that product teams make digital services that can be used by everyone.

levels.title: Junior accessibility specialist
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A junior accessibility specialist learns on the job by assisting with accessibility testing.

At this role level, you will:
- develop skills while working under supervision to provide accessibility testing
- understand and use different types of testing
- be aware of but not responsible for assistive technology testing
- engage with and contribute to the cross-government accessibility community
responsibilities: Test web pages, apps, and documents against accessibility standards, under supervision.
Record and explain accessibility issues clearly so teams can fix them.
Help with testing using assistive technologies, such as screen readers and magnifiers.
Help keep accessibility statements and issue logs up to date.
qualifications: Some experience of digital testing, design, or development, or equivalent experience.

levels.title: Accessibility specialist
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
An accessibility specialist can support teams in creating accessible services.

At this role level, you will:
- coach and mentor more junior colleagues
- support in providing training materials and learning content
- perform accessibility audits
- engage with and contribute to the cross-government accessibility community
responsibilities: Carry out accessibility audits of patient-facing services, clinical systems, and health information.
Test with a range of assistive technologies and support research with disabled users.
Advise teams on fixes and on accessible patterns for forms, alerts, and safety-critical information.
Review supplier products for accessibility during procurement and acceptance.
Create training and guidance, and coach more junior colleagues.
qualifications: Experience of accessibility testing and of current accessibility standards, or equivalent experience.

levels.title: Senior accessibility specialist
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A senior accessibility specialist works with people at a range of role levels to embed accessibility into the output of teams.

At this role level, you will:
- coach and mentor more junior colleagues
- input into accessibility strategy with business areas or teams
- create and deliver accessibility training
- engage with teams across different levels and capabilities
- potentially manage or lead individuals or sub-teams
- engage with and contribute to the cross-government accessibility community
responsibilities: Embed accessibility into teams' ways of working, from discovery to live service.
Contribute to accessibility strategy, including how accessibility is assured in procurement and service assessments.
Work with clinical safety officers where accessibility issues could affect patient safety.
Create and deliver accessibility training for designers, developers, content designers, and suppliers.
Lead or manage other accessibility specialists.
qualifications: Substantial experience of accessibility, at a level equivalent to a master's degree.

levels.title: Head of accessibility
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A head of accessibility is an expert practitioner who can create an accessibility vision or strategy for an organisation.

At this role level, you will:
- define and assure best practice while influencing, leading and mentoring others
- influence and develop organisational strategy and priorities, working with counterpart colleagues across government
- ensure the right conditions and environment for accessibility specialists to work effectively
- develop departmental capability by supporting internal movement of staff between roles, shaping career paths and recruiting talent
- understand and own the overall approach to accessibility risk (including how accessibility risk is communicated and how corporate legal compliance risk is managed within the organisation)
- engage with and contribute to the cross-government accessibility community
responsibilities: Set the organisation's accessibility vision, strategy, and standards, for patient-facing and internal services.
Assure compliance with accessibility law and standards across services, and report on it to senior leaders.
Make sure accessibility requirements are part of procurement and supplier contracts for clinical systems.
Influence organisational priorities so that disabled patients and staff are not excluded.
Lead and develop the accessibility team and community of practice.
qualifications: Extensive experience of leading accessibility in a complex organisation.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: There is no Band 8a level, because the UK GDaD PCF places head of accessibility at G7 or G6 and this reference follows the suggested Band 8b.

roles.title: Service desk analyst
roles.summary: Service desk analysts are the first point of contact for staff who need help with the organisation's digital services, from login and smartcard problems to faults in clinical systems and devices. They log, triage, resolve, or escalate incidents and requests, keep users informed, and spot patterns that point to wider problems. In many health care organisations the service desk runs around the clock, because clinical services do.
healthContext: Callers are often clinicians and care staff in the middle of patient care, so the desk prioritises by the effect on patients, not only by order of arrival.
Many clinical services run 24 hours a day, every day, so the service desk often works shifts and out-of-hours rotas.
Access to clinical systems uses role-based access and strong authentication, so the desk handles account, smartcard, and multi-factor authentication problems while checking identity carefully.
Callers may share confidential patient information while describing a fault, so analysts follow information governance rules for what they record in tickets.
The desk is often the first to see signs of a major incident or a cyber attack, such as many calls about the same system or a wave of suspicious emails, and must escalate them quickly.

pcfRole.name: Service desk manager
pcfRole.description:
A service desk manager is responsible for managing the first- and second-line technical support for all departmental IT applications and services across sites, including end-user computing. This includes multi-function devices and specialised IT equipment.

In this role, you will also be responsible for ensuring support for existing and emerging information and communications technology (ICT) services, including providing technical advice to project teams.

levels.title: Service desk analyst
levels.summary: A service desk analyst answers calls and tickets from staff, resolves common issues at first contact using scripts and knowledge articles, and passes other issues to the right team.
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A service desk analyst interacts with customers.

At this role level, you will:
- perform tasks such as taking calls from customers and trying to resolve their queries
- know when to escalate issues to your manager
responsibilities: Answer calls, chats, and self-service tickets from staff, and log each one accurately in the service management tool.
Resolve common issues at first contact using scripts and knowledge articles, such as password resets, account unlocks, and printer faults.
Check the caller's identity before changing accounts or access, following the organisation's procedures.
Ask how the issue affects patient care, set the priority, and pass the incident to the right resolver team.
Keep users updated on their tickets and confirm that the fix works before closing them.
Record only the information needed in tickets, without unnecessary patient details.
qualifications: A level 3 qualification in IT, an IT support apprenticeship, or equivalent experience.
Good customer service and keyboard skills, gained through work or study.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: The UK GDaD PCF suggests Band 4 for this level. This reference starts scripted first-line service desk work at Band 3, and places analysts who resolve more complex faults at Band 4. Mental effort reflects frequent concentration on unpredictable calls; emotional effort reflects frequent calls from staff under pressure in clinical areas.

levels.title: Technical service desk analyst
levels.summary: A technical service desk analyst resolves more complex faults at first contact, including remote fixes to devices and access to clinical systems, and handles urgent calls from clinical areas.
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A service desk analyst interacts with customers.

At this role level, you will:
- perform tasks such as taking calls from customers and trying to resolve their queries
- know when to escalate issues to your manager
responsibilities: Resolve more complex incidents and requests remotely, including device, software, and clinical system access faults.
Handle urgent calls from clinical areas, such as emergency departments, wards, and theatres, and start the major incident process when needed.
Process access requests for clinical systems, checking them against role-based access rules.
Write and improve knowledge articles so that more issues can be resolved at first contact.
Spot repeated calls about the same fault and raise them with incident and problem management.
Report suspected phishing emails and other security events to the security team.
Show new analysts how to use the desk's tools and procedures.
qualifications: Experience of IT support on a service desk or in a similar setting.
An IT service management foundation qualification, or equivalent experience.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Uses the same UK GDaD PCF level as the Band 3 analyst, for analysts who resolve more complex issues and handle urgent clinical calls. Communication is higher than the band profile because analysts often have to explain technical issues to busy clinical staff.

levels.title: Senior service desk analyst
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A senior service desk analyst monitors inbound calls, supports operators in service resolution and intervenes in difficult calls.

At this role level, you will:
- own and update the script for service desk analysts
- coach and develop one or more service desk analysts, and manage availability
responsibilities: Lead a shift on the service desk, balancing call queues against the clinical urgency of open incidents.
Take over difficult or escalated calls, including calls from senior clinicians during urgent care.
Keep scripts and knowledge articles accurate as clinical systems and devices change.
Act as the out-of-hours escalation point for the desk, and start the major incident process when many users are affected.
Check the quality of tickets, including identity checks and what is recorded about patients.
Plan rota cover so the desk is staffed at all times.
qualifications: Substantial service desk experience, including handling escalations.
An IT service management qualification, or equivalent experience.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Planning reflects shift and rota planning for a 24-hour desk. Emotional effort reflects frequent difficult calls from staff dealing with urgent patient care.

levels.title: Service desk manager
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A service desk manager identifies emerging issues and is a knowledge expert.

They are responsible for the resourcing and development of the team, including the preparation and co-ordination of service transition activities.
responsibilities: Run the service desk day to day, making sure it is staffed and responsive 24 hours a day, every day.
Set priorities and response targets that reflect clinical risk, agreed with clinical and operational leads.
Prepare the desk for new and changed clinical systems, including training, scripts, and extra cover at go-live.
Analyse ticket trends to find emerging issues, and work with problem management to remove their causes.
Make sure the desk follows identity checking, information governance, and security procedures, and acts on audit findings.
Line manage senior analysts and analysts, including recruitment, performance, and wellbeing for staff working shifts.
qualifications: Experience of leading a service desk team, including shift or out-of-hours cover.
An intermediate IT service management qualification, or equivalent experience.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Knowledge is one level below the band profile, as is usual for service desk roles; responsibility for people is higher because the manager runs a shift-based team.

levels.title: Head of service desk
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A head of service desk is responsible for managing a team who provides first- and second-line technical support.

At this role level, you will:
- ensure support of existing and emerging information and communications technology (ICT) services, and provide technical advice to project teams
- ensure that the support team undertakes development so that they can advise on future projects and current issues
- manage and monitor service desk service level agreements (SLAs) and performance
responsibilities: Set the direction for the service desk, including contact channels, self-service, and support for staff working across sites and in the community.
Agree service levels with clinical and corporate services, and report performance to senior leaders.
Make sure the desk can keep working during major incidents, cyber attacks, and system downtime, with clear business continuity procedures.
Advise project teams on how new clinical and corporate systems will be supported before they go live.
Manage the service desk budget, tools, and any outsourced or out-of-hours support contracts.
Lead and develop service desk managers, and build a supportive culture for staff working shifts.
qualifications: Extensive experience of managing IT support services, including 24-hour services.
An advanced IT service management qualification, or equivalent experience.

roles.title: End user computing engineer
roles.summary: End user computing engineers provide, support, and maintain the devices and software that staff use every day, such as laptops, desktops, tablets, mobile phones, printers, and the shared workstations on wards and in clinics. They fix faults on site and remotely, roll out and update devices, and keep them secure and compliant. Their work keeps clinicians and care staff able to see and record patient information at the point of care.
healthContext: Many devices are shared by clinical staff on wards, in clinics, and in emergency departments, often with fast user switching and smartcard or tap-in login.
A broken device in a clinical area can delay care, so engineers prioritise those faults and keep spare devices ready to swap.
Engineers work in clinical areas, so they follow infection prevention and control rules, respect patient privacy and dignity, and fit their work around clinical activity.
Devices hold or display confidential patient information, so they must be encrypted, patched, managed, and securely wiped or destroyed at the end of their life.
Some peripherals support clinical processes or connect to clinical equipment, such as wristband and label printers, barcode scanners, and dictation devices, so changes to them need care and testing.

pcfRole.name: End user computing engineer
pcfRole.description: An end user computing engineer is responsible for managing the product life cycle of all service-raised incidents (incident control) and all service requests (request control), requiring the use of knowledge management. In this role, you will also be responsible for informing customers on progress and advising on workarounds where necessary, as well as the support and maintenance of end user services.

levels.title: Associate end user computing engineer
levels.pcfLevelDescription: As a trainee, you will work in an established team and support end user computing engineers in their daily work, under their direction.
responsibilities: Set up, replace, and repair devices and peripherals under the direction of experienced engineers.
Fix common faults in clinical and office areas, such as printer, scanner, and login problems.
Follow infection prevention and control rules, and respect patient privacy, when working on wards and in clinics.
Record work, assets, and parts accurately in the service management tool.
Work towards an IT support apprenticeship or equivalent qualification.
qualifications: Enrolled on, or working towards, an IT support apprenticeship or equivalent.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Physical effort reflects frequent light effort, such as carrying devices and working under desks and in confined spaces. Knowledge is scored at the level the job needs once training is complete enough to do the work.

levels.title: End user computing engineer
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
An end user computing engineer works on-site, maintaining hardware and fixing technical problems as quickly as possible.

At this role level, you will:
- provide first-time resolution by troubleshooting and diagnosing or escalating faults (or both) to service desk managers, incident managers and problem managers to investigate and resolve
- coach associates and share knowledge with team colleagues
responsibilities: Diagnose and fix hardware and software faults on site and remotely, aiming to resolve them at the first visit.
Respond quickly to faults in clinical areas, and provide a replacement device when a repair would delay care.
Build, deploy, and update devices using the organisation's standard images and device management tools.
Keep devices patched, encrypted, and compliant, and securely wipe or dispose of them at the end of their life.
Configure and test clinical peripherals, such as wristband printers, label printers, and barcode scanners.
Coach associate engineers and share fixes through knowledge articles.
qualifications: A level 3 or higher qualification in IT, a completed apprenticeship, or equivalent experience.
Experience of supporting end user devices.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Physical effort reflects frequent light effort when moving and installing devices across sites.

levels.title: Senior end user computing engineer
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A senior end user computing engineer is responsible for managing the team but also gets involved in solving technical problems.

At this role level, you will:
- manage, co-ordinate and prioritise tasks to resolve technical incidents as quickly as possible
- work closely with infrastructure, capacity managers and availability managers to fix technical problems and identify and escalate repeat issues to the lead end user computing engineer, the incident or problem manager and software developers
responsibilities: Lead a team of engineers day to day, prioritising work by its effect on patient care and staff.
Plan and run device rollouts and refreshes for wards, clinics, and community teams, with as little disruption to care as possible.
Test device builds and updates with clinical applications and peripherals before they are rolled out.
Make sure devices meet security standards, including patch levels, encryption, and endpoint protection.
Support go-lives of clinical systems with floor walking and rapid device fixes.
Work with infrastructure, application, and security teams to fix complex and repeated faults.
qualifications: Substantial experience of supporting and managing end user devices, at a level equivalent to a degree.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Responsibility for people reflects day-to-day management of a team of engineers; physical effort reflects some continued on-site work.

levels.title: Lead end user computing engineer
levels.pcfLevelDescription: A lead end user computing engineer has expert technical understanding and is accountable for vendor and supplier management. At this level, you will work with relevant IT operations and other functions, such as technical architecture, to understand lower level productivity, development and feasibility.
responsibilities: Set the standards for the organisation's devices, builds, and end user software, including shared clinical workstations.
Manage suppliers of devices, repairs, and end user services, and hold them to agreed service levels.
Work with technical architects to choose and test new device types, such as mobile devices for ward and community staff.
Lead the technical response to end user computing incidents, such as a failed update affecting clinical workstations.
Plan the device lifecycle and capacity, and advise on refresh costs.
Lead and develop senior engineers.
qualifications: Extensive experience of end user computing, including managing suppliers.

levels.title: Principal end user computing engineer
levels.pcfLevelDescription: A principal end user computing engineer owns the strategy roadmap and leads on resourcing, learning and development for their team. At this level, you look at the bigger picture and understand trends in the business.
responsibilities: Own the end user computing strategy and roadmap, including how staff will reach clinical systems in hospitals, clinics, patients' homes, and the community.
Make sure the device estate supports safe, fast access to patient information at the point of care.
Advise senior leaders on device investment, risks, and the costs of refreshes and new technologies.
Lead the response to estate-wide device risks, such as operating systems reaching end of support and resilience against ransomware.
Lead resourcing, learning, and development for end user computing teams.
Work with health and care partners on shared device and access standards.
qualifications: Extensive experience of leading end user computing for a large, multi-site organisation.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: The UK GDaD PCF suggests Band 8c for this level (G6). This reference places it at Band 8b, in line with principal roles in other technical families, because its scope is one technical area rather than a directorate.

roles.title: Infrastructure engineer
roles.summary: Infrastructure engineers design, build, run, and support the networks, servers, storage, cloud platforms, and hosting that the organisation's digital services depend on. They keep this infrastructure available, secure, and recoverable, and work with suppliers and architects to change it safely. In health care, one infrastructure failure can stop clinical systems across hospitals and community services at once.
healthContext: Clinical systems need very high availability, so infrastructure is designed for resilience and changes are planned around clinical activity.
Engineers take part in on-call rotas, because infrastructure faults at night or at weekends can stop patient care.
Networks connect medical devices, such as infusion pumps, patient monitors, and imaging equipment, which need network segmentation and careful change following IEC 80001-1.
Health care is a frequent target for ransomware, so backups must be protected, tested, and restorable within agreed recovery times.
Infrastructure often mixes old and new technology, including legacy clinical systems that cannot easily be patched, so engineers put compensating controls in place.

pcfRole.name: Infrastructure engineer
pcfRole.description: An infrastructure engineer designs, builds, manages and supports the infrastructure services that underpin all internal user services and services to the public.

levels.title: Associate infrastructure engineer
levels.pcfLevelDescription: As a trainee, you will work in an established team and support infrastructure engineers in their daily work, under their direction.
responsibilities: Support infrastructure engineers with routine tasks, such as server builds, backup checks, and network changes.
Monitor infrastructure and report alerts and faults to the right team.
Follow change, security, and information governance procedures in all work.
Record configuration and asset details accurately.
Work towards an infrastructure apprenticeship or equivalent qualification.
qualifications: Enrolled on, or working towards, an infrastructure or networking apprenticeship or equivalent.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Knowledge is scored at the level the job needs once training is complete enough to do the work.

levels.title: Infrastructure engineer
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
Working in a team of infrastructure specialists and engineers, an infrastructure engineer supports and maintains infrastructure solutions and services as directed and according to departmental policy.

At this role level, you will:
- ensure services are delivered and used as required
- work with and support third parties to provide infrastructure services
responsibilities: Build, configure, and maintain the servers, storage, networks, and cloud services that host clinical and corporate systems.
Patch infrastructure promptly, balancing security risk against the need to keep clinical systems available.
Run and test backups and restores, including for critical clinical systems.
Support segmented networks for medical devices and other clinical equipment, working with clinical engineering teams.
Investigate and fix infrastructure faults, including as part of the on-call rota.
Automate routine tasks using scripts and infrastructure as code.
qualifications: A degree in computing or a related subject, relevant technical certifications, or equivalent experience.
Experience of supporting production infrastructure.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Mental effort reflects frequent prolonged concentration on unpredictable faults, including on-call work out of hours.

levels.title: Senior infrastructure engineer
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
Working in a team of infrastructure specialists and engineers, a senior infrastructure engineer builds, administers, supports and maintains solutions as directed and according to departmental policy.

At this role level, you will:
- ensure services are integrated, delivered and operated as required
- work with and support third parties in providing infrastructure services
- work with technical architects to translate architectural designs into operations
- provide input into overall management - workforce, budget, technology roadmaps, projects and tasks
- lead and direct infrastructure specialist teams in building, managing, supporting and maintaining solutions according to departmental policy (if taking a managerial path)
responsibilities: Design and build infrastructure solutions from architects' designs, with the resilience that clinical services need.
Plan and lead major infrastructure changes, such as data centre moves, network refreshes, and cloud migrations, around clinical activity.
Design and test disaster recovery and ransomware recovery for critical clinical systems.
Lead the technical response to infrastructure incidents and drive fixes for their causes.
Manage compensating controls for legacy systems and medical devices that cannot be patched.
Lead and coach infrastructure engineers.
qualifications: Substantial experience of designing and running production infrastructure, at a level equivalent to a postgraduate diploma.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Mental effort reflects frequent prolonged concentration during incidents and complex changes, including out of hours.

levels.title: Lead infrastructure engineer
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A lead infrastructure engineer manages third party provision of infrastructure services and the provision of expertise to develop architectural solutions for infrastructure services, throughout the service product life cycle.

At this role level, you will:
- oversee programmes and projects
- work with technical architects to translate the architectural designs into operations and support technical architects in operationalising the designs
- lead and direct infrastructure specialist teams in building, managing, supporting and maintaining solutions according to departmental policy (if taking a managerial path)
responsibilities: Lead the infrastructure for a major platform or group of services, and set its technical direction.
Manage third-party infrastructure suppliers, and hold them to service levels for availability and recovery.
Oversee infrastructure programmes, such as network renewal or moves to cloud hosting.
Make sure infrastructure meets security, information governance, and medical device network standards.
Lead infrastructure teams and develop their skills.
qualifications: Extensive experience of leading infrastructure engineering for complex, high-availability services.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: The UK GDaD PCF suggests Band 8b for both lead and principal infrastructure engineers. This reference places lead at Band 8a, so that the two levels sit in different bands, in line with lead and principal roles in other technical families.

levels.title: Principal infrastructure engineer
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A principal infrastructure engineer is an accomplished technical leader.

At this role level, you will:
- develop strategic and tactical engineering roadmaps for technologies and services in your area of responsibility, ensuring they're future-proofed and that the organisation derives maximum value from investment in technologies
- potentially own the operational relationships with suppliers, ensuring services and products are delivered and aligned to industry best practice and regulatory and contractual requirements
- work with technical architects to translate the architectural designs into operations and support technical architects in operationalising the designs
- lead and direct infrastructure specialist teams in building, managing, supporting and maintaining solutions according to departmental policy (if taking a managerial path)
responsibilities: Develop the infrastructure strategy and roadmaps, so that investment delivers resilient, secure, and sustainable hosting for clinical services.
Own operational relationships with strategic infrastructure and network suppliers.
Advise senior leaders on infrastructure risk, including end-of-life technology, single points of failure, and cyber resilience.
Set recovery time and recovery point objectives for clinical systems with service owners, and make sure infrastructure can meet them.
Lead the infrastructure engineering profession across the organisation and develop its capability.
qualifications: Extensive experience of leading infrastructure engineering across multiple teams or organisations.

roles.title: Application operations engineer
roles.summary: Application operations engineers keep the organisation's applications running in live use, including clinical systems such as the electronic patient record and prescribing, laboratory, and imaging systems. They monitor applications, run scheduled jobs, manage users and access, deploy releases and fixes, and work with suppliers to resolve faults. Their work lets clinical and corporate staff rely on these systems at every hour of the day.
healthContext: Clinical applications run 24 hours a day, so engineers take part in on-call rotas and plan maintenance for the quietest clinical periods.
Failed scheduled jobs and interfaces can delay test results, referrals, or discharge letters, so engineers watch them closely and escalate quickly.
Planned and unplanned downtime needs business continuity arrangements, such as read-only copies and downtime reports, so that clinicians can keep treating patients.
Many clinical applications are supplied and hosted by third parties, so engineers manage suppliers and their changes carefully.
Changes to clinical applications follow the clinical risk management process, and some applications may be regulated as medical devices.

pcfRole.name: Application operations engineer
pcfRole.description: An application operations engineer supports, manages and maintains a single application or a suite of applications.

levels.title: Associate application operations engineer
levels.pcfLevelDescription: As a trainee, you will work in an established team and support application operations engineers in their daily work, under their direction.
responsibilities: Monitor applications, interfaces, and scheduled jobs, and report failures to experienced engineers.
Create and change user accounts and access in applications, following role-based access rules.
Carry out routine checks and maintenance tasks using runbooks.
Record incidents and changes accurately in the service management tool.
Work towards an IT apprenticeship or equivalent qualification.
qualifications: Enrolled on, or working towards, an IT apprenticeship or equivalent.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Knowledge is scored at the level the job needs once training is complete enough to do the work.

levels.title: Application operations engineer
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
An application operations engineer maintains services and is responsible for conducting user and security administration.

At this role level, you will:
- monitor applications and be accountable for batch processes
- in some organisations, carry out the duties of an end user computing engineer, such as fixing technical problems, maintaining hardware and liaising with the problem or incident manager
responsibilities: Monitor clinical and corporate applications and their interfaces, and act on alerts and failed jobs before they affect patient care.
Run and check scheduled jobs, such as overnight data loads and interface queues, and resolve or escalate failures.
Manage application users, roles, and access, including removing access for leavers and supporting access reviews.
Produce and test downtime reports and other business continuity outputs for clinical applications.
Log faults with suppliers and track them to resolution.
Take part in the on-call rota, with guidance, for out-of-hours application faults.
qualifications: A qualification in IT, a completed apprenticeship, or equivalent experience.
Experience of supporting business or clinical applications.

levels.title: Senior application operations engineer
levels.pcfLevelDescription: Dealing with more complex issues, a senior application operations engineer is responsible for code deployment and co-ordinating change-based activities, such as taking services live. Depending on the complexity and size of a project and the likely impact it will have on the business, you might manage and maintain certain aspects of an application.
responsibilities: Deploy releases, patches, and configuration changes to live applications, following change and clinical safety procedures.
Coordinate the technical work to take new applications and major upgrades live, including cutover and rollback plans.
Investigate complex application faults with suppliers, infrastructure teams, and clinical system specialists.
Plan maintenance windows with clinical services, and make sure downtime procedures are ready.
Provide evidence for clinical safety cases, such as test and deployment records.
Act as an escalation point on the on-call rota for out-of-hours faults.
qualifications: Substantial experience of supporting live applications, at a level equivalent to a degree.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Mental effort reflects frequent prolonged concentration during go-lives, deployments, and out-of-hours incidents.

levels.title: Lead application operations engineer
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A lead application operations engineer defines the application strategy and the strategy for security administration.

At this role level, you will:
- liaise with leads within IT operations on how applications are performing and changes that need to be put in place
- potentially manage and maintain certain aspects of an application (depending on the complexity and size of a project, and the likely impact it will have on the business)
responsibilities: Set the operational approach for a group of applications, including monitoring, resilience, and support arrangements.
Set standards for user and security administration across clinical applications, working with the security team.
Report on application performance and availability to IT operations leads, and agree the changes needed.
Lead the technical response to major incidents affecting clinical applications.
Make sure business continuity and disaster recovery arrangements for clinical applications are tested.
Lead and develop application operations engineers.
qualifications: Extensive experience of running live applications, including clinical or other critical systems.

levels.title: Principal application operations engineer
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A principal application operations engineer owns the application strategy and leads on resourcing, learning and development for their team.

At this role level, you will:
- have expert technical understanding
- be accountable for vendor and supplier management
- potentially manage and maintain certain aspects of an application (depending on the complexity and size of a project, and the likely impact it will have on the business)
responsibilities: Own the application operations strategy across the organisation's clinical and corporate applications.
Manage strategic suppliers of clinical applications, including service levels, contract performance, and supplier changes.
Advise senior leaders on application risks, such as unsupported software, single points of failure, and resilience against ransomware.
Make sure the organisation can keep caring for patients safely during prolonged application downtime.
Lead resourcing, learning, and development for application operations teams.
qualifications: Extensive experience of leading application operations for a large organisation.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: The UK GDaD PCF suggests Band 8c for this level (G6). This reference places it at Band 8b, in line with principal roles in other technical families, because its scope is one technical area rather than a directorate.

roles.title: IT service manager
roles.summary: IT service managers make sure the organisation's digital services are delivered to agreed levels and keep improving. They define service levels, manage the service catalogue, report on performance, and coordinate the teams and suppliers that run each service. In health care, they turn what clinical services need, such as round-the-clock availability, into service targets and support arrangements.
healthContext: Service levels for clinical systems reflect clinical risk, so targets for the electronic patient record or prescribing differ from those for a corporate system.
Services are often provided by a mix of in-house teams, suppliers, and services shared with partner organisations, so service managers coordinate across organisational boundaries.
Clinical business continuity depends on IT, so service managers work with clinical and emergency planning leads on downtime and continuity plans.
Clinical staff have little time to report problems, so service managers use monitoring, service desk data, and clinical feedback to find issues early.

pcfRole.name: IT service manager
pcfRole.description: IT service managers are responsible for managing the service delivery of information and communications technology (ICT) services, and working with teams from IT service operations.

levels.title: IT service analyst
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
An IT service analyst is responsible for frontline technical support to end users on issues relating to hardware, software and peripherals. This will include responding to, documenting and resolving service desk incident tickets in a timely manner according to a service level agreement (SLA).

At this role level, you will:
- have excellent problem solving skills to diagnose, evaluate and resolve complex problem situations or, when appropriate, escalate or route them to IT resolver groups
- perform root cause analysis
- develop checklists for typical problems
- recommend procedures and controls for problem prevention
- work independently, share information and assist others with requests for service
responsibilities: Respond to, document, and resolve incidents and requests within agreed service levels.
Produce regular service reports, such as ticket volumes, response times, and the availability of clinical systems.
Check that service catalogue entries and knowledge articles are accurate and up to date.
Look for patterns in incidents and suggest improvements.
Follow information governance rules when handling ticket and service data.
qualifications: An IT service management foundation qualification, a level 3 qualification in IT, or equivalent experience.

levels.title: IT service manager
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
An IT service manager is responsible for defining service level agreements (SLAs) and operational level agreements (OLAs) across all relevant business functions.

At this role level, you will:
- manage a fully functioning multi-sourced service support team with a customer-centric support approach across multiple locations, focused on service availability and performance
- ensure that all service and support functions remain responsive to customer needs
- ensure that the service catalogue and wider IT service operations knowledge library are maintained
- ensure that adequate reporting and service standards are met for your specific service
- ensure that all technical change is communicated and managed, with appropriate governance
- ensure that a programme of continual service improvement is put in place across the wider service delivery function
responsibilities: Define and agree service levels for clinical and corporate services, based on clinical risk and business need.
Manage the support arrangements for a portfolio of services, including suppliers and shared services.
Report service performance to service owners and clinical leads, and agree improvement actions.
Make sure each service has tested business continuity and downtime arrangements.
Keep the service catalogue current, and make sure staff are told about changes to their services.
Run a programme of continual service improvement for your services.
qualifications: Experience of managing IT services to agreed service levels.
An intermediate IT service management qualification, or equivalent experience.

levels.title: Senior IT service manager
levels.pcfLevelDescription: A senior IT service manager is responsible for service management across platforms, multiple channels and services to ensure service availability, performance and process maturity.
responsibilities: Lead service management across several platforms and channels, and improve the maturity of service management processes.
Agree service levels and contract terms with major suppliers of clinical systems, and hold them to account.
Present service performance and risks to senior clinical and operational leaders.
Lead service reviews after major incidents, and track improvement actions to completion.
Align IT continuity plans with clinical business continuity plans, working with emergency planning and clinical leads.
Lead and develop IT service managers.
qualifications: Substantial experience of IT service management across several services.
An advanced IT service management qualification, or equivalent experience.

levels.title: Head of IT service management
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A head of IT service management is responsible for setting the vision and strategy for service management, ensuring processes are owned and maturing.

At this role level, you will:
- lead a team, ensuring adequate resources and capacity
- represent the IT service management function at a senior level
- act as an escalation point for business stakeholders
responsibilities: Set the vision, strategy, and operating model for IT service management across the organisation.
Make sure every service management process has an owner and keeps maturing.
Represent IT service management at senior level, including at clinical and operational governance meetings.
Act as the senior escalation point for clinical and corporate service leaders.
Make sure the service management function has the people, tools, and budget it needs.
qualifications: Extensive experience of leading IT service management in a large or complex organisation.

roles.title: Incident manager
roles.summary: Incident managers restore normal service as quickly as possible when something goes wrong, and keep the effect on users as small as possible. They coordinate technical teams and suppliers, keep users and leaders informed, and make sure incidents are recorded and passed to problem management. In health care, incidents can directly affect patient care, so incident managers work closely with clinical and operational leaders.
healthContext: An outage of a clinical system can delay treatment, so incidents are prioritised by clinical impact, and clinical leads may need to start downtime procedures.
Major incidents can happen at any time, so incident managers take part in on-call rotas and may be called out at night or at weekends.
A cyber attack, such as ransomware, can become a major incident that affects the whole organisation and lasts for days or weeks.
Major IT incidents may need to link with the organisation's emergency preparedness and business continuity arrangements.
Incidents that may have harmed patients are also reported through the clinical incident process and reviewed with clinical safety.

pcfRole.name: Incident manager
pcfRole.description: Incident managers aim to restore normal service operation as quickly as possible and minimise any adverse effects on business operations. This ensures that the best possible levels of service quality and availability are returned and maintained.

levels.title: Incident manager
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
An incident manager oversees incidents and restores normal operations as quickly as possible, with the least impact on the business or the user.

At this role level, you will:
- work on-site, maintaining the hardware and fixing technical problems as quickly as possible
- provide first-time resolution by troubleshooting and diagnosing or escalating faults (or both) to the major incident managers and problem managers to investigate and resolve
- coach apprentices and share knowledge with team colleagues
Your responsibilities may, in some departments, mirror those of an end user computing engineer.
responsibilities: Coordinate the response to incidents affecting clinical and corporate services, from first report to restored service.
Assess the clinical and operational impact of each incident and set its priority.
Keep affected users, the service desk, and clinical leads informed with clear, timely updates.
Escalate incidents to the major incident manager when they meet the agreed criteria.
Make sure incidents are recorded accurately and passed to problem management.
Take part in the on-call rota for out-of-hours incidents.
qualifications: Experience of IT support or operations, including handling incidents.
An IT service management foundation qualification, or equivalent experience.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Mental effort reflects frequent prolonged concentration under time pressure, including on call. Emotional effort reflects frequent indirect exposure to the effect of outages on patients and staff.

levels.title: Major incident manager
levels.pcfLevelDescription: A major incident manager manages significant outages and crises and reports issues to problem management. At this level, you will work closely with workplace services, infrastructure, applications operators and communication managers. In some departments, you may also be the head of service.
responsibilities: Lead the response to major incidents, such as outages of the electronic patient record, network failures, and cyber attacks.
Run incident calls that bring together technical teams, suppliers, clinical leads, and communications staff.
Advise clinical and operational leaders on when to start and stop downtime and business continuity procedures.
Brief senior leaders and, where needed, link with the organisation's emergency response arrangements.
Lead post-incident reviews and make sure lessons are learned and acted on.
Develop and test major incident plans with business continuity and emergency planning leads.
qualifications: Substantial experience of managing incidents in complex, high-availability services.
An advanced IT service management qualification, or equivalent experience.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Mental effort reflects frequent prolonged concentration during major incidents, often out of hours. Emotional effort reflects frequent indirect exposure to the effect of major outages on patient care.

roles.title: Problem manager
roles.summary: Problem managers find and fix the root causes of incidents, so that faults stop happening again. They analyse incident data, run root cause investigations, record known errors and workarounds, and track fixes with technical teams and suppliers. In health care, repeated faults in clinical systems waste clinical time, erode trust, and can create patient safety risks, so removing them matters.
healthContext: Repeated small faults, such as slow logins or failed prints on wards, add up to lost clinical time, so problem managers look for patterns as well as major failures.
Some problems create clinical safety hazards, such as results not reaching the right clinician, and are assessed with the clinical safety officer.
Root cause investigations often involve suppliers of clinical systems, and are managed through contracts and service levels.
Workarounds for clinical systems must be safe and clearly explained to clinical staff.

pcfRole.name: Problem manager
pcfRole.description: Problem managers aim to resolve and control the root causes of incidents caused by errors within the IT infrastructure. In this role, you will be expected to work to prevent the recurrence of these incidents.

levels.title: Problem analyst
levels.pcfLevelDescription: At this level, you will be responsible for maintaining software systems once they are up and running and, where necessary, support the problem manager in co-ordinating the resolution of any problems.
responsibilities: Analyse incident data to find repeated faults and trends across clinical and corporate services.
Record problems, known errors, and workarounds in the service management tool.
Support root cause investigations by gathering logs, timelines, and other evidence.
Track actions with technical teams and suppliers until fixes are in place.
Check that workarounds for clinical systems are safe and clearly explained to users.
qualifications: Experience of IT support or operations.
An IT service management foundation qualification, or equivalent experience.

levels.title: Problem manager
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A problem manager picks up feeds from numerous sources, such as the service desk, with the aim of putting in place continual improvements to stop incidents such as regular service outages recurring.

At this role level, you will:
- resolve emerging and recurring problems
- perform root cause analysis to minimise the adverse impact of incidents caused by errors within the IT infrastructure
- work closely with major incident managers
- deal with problems and root cause analysis
responsibilities: Run the problem management process across the organisation's services.
Lead root cause analysis after major incidents and for recurring faults, using structured techniques.
Prioritise problems by their effect on patient care, staff time, and service risk.
Assess problems that may create patient safety hazards with the clinical safety officer.
Hold technical teams and suppliers to account for permanent fixes, and report progress to service leaders.
Work with major incident managers to make sure lessons from incidents lead to change.
qualifications: Substantial experience of problem or incident management, at a level equivalent to a degree.
An intermediate IT service management qualification, or equivalent experience.

roles.title: Change and release manager
roles.summary: Change and release managers make sure changes to IT services are assessed, approved, scheduled, and carried out safely, and that releases are planned and coordinated. They run the change advisory board, own the configuration management database, and coordinate releases across teams and suppliers. In health care, they make sure changes to clinical systems are timed and tested to protect patient care.
healthContext: Changes to clinical systems can harm patients, so change assessment includes clinical safety review and evidence from the clinical risk management process.
Clinical services run every day, so change windows are agreed with clinical services and avoid their busiest periods.
Many changes come from suppliers of clinical systems, and must still be assessed when the supplier controls the release.
Emergency changes, such as urgent security patches, must balance cyber risk against the risk of disrupting care.
An accurate configuration management database shows which clinical services a change could affect.

pcfRole.name: Change and release manager
pcfRole.description: Change and release managers lead the change advisory board, ensuring adequate risk assessment and scheduling of technical changes and releases. They own the configuration management database and the access, security and configuration of change activities and release procedures.

levels.title: Configuration analyst
levels.pcfLevelDescription: A configuration analyst provides administrative support to the change and release manager, helping to maintain the integrity of the configuration management database (CMDB) and independently solving smaller problems.
responsibilities: Maintain records in the configuration management database, including the clinical services each component supports.
Check configuration records against discovery tools, and fix gaps and errors.
Prepare change records and agendas for the change advisory board.
Answer routine queries about configuration items and how they relate.
qualifications: An IT service management foundation qualification, a level 3 qualification in IT, or equivalent experience.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: The UK GDaD PCF suggests Band 6 for this level (HEO/SEO). This reference places it at Band 4 because the level provides administrative support to the change and release manager, with mostly awareness-level skills, and sits below the change and release analyst. Information resources is above the band profile because maintaining the configuration management database is the main duty.

levels.title: Change and release analyst
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A change and release analyst plans and rolls out software, and designs and carries out procedures for the distribution and installation of changes to systems and services.

At this role level, you will:
- undertake analysis after release and set the plan for upcoming changes
- liaise with DevOps and service designers
responsibilities: Assess change requests for risk and impact, including the effect on clinical services and patient safety.
Plan and schedule releases, agreeing change windows with clinical and operational services.
Check that each change has testing, a rollback plan, and clinical safety sign-off where needed.
Coordinate releases with DevOps teams, suppliers, and the service desk.
Review releases afterwards and plan upcoming changes.
qualifications: Experience of IT operations, release, or change work.
An IT service management foundation qualification, or equivalent experience.

levels.title: Change and release manager
levels.pcfLevelDescription:
A change and release manager ensures that technical changes to IT services are adequately assessed for impact, prioritised, scheduled, authorised and implemented. They ensure this is done in line with processes and using appropriate tools. They chair the Change Advisory Board (CAB).

At this role level, you will:
- provide an escalation point
- make decisions for all technical changes
- co-ordinate releases and interdependencies
responsibilities: Chair the change advisory board, including clinical and operational representatives when changes affect patient care.
Decide on technical changes, and authorise emergency changes such as urgent security patches.
Coordinate releases and their dependencies across in-house teams and suppliers.
Own the change, release, and configuration management processes and the configuration management database.
Act as the escalation point for change conflicts and failed changes.
Report on change success, failed changes, and incidents caused by change, and drive improvements.
qualifications: Substantial experience of change and release management, at a level equivalent to a degree.
An intermediate IT service management qualification, or equivalent experience.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Planning is above the band profile because the role schedules releases and their dependencies across many teams and suppliers.

roles.title: Security operations analyst
roles.summary: Security operations analysts watch for, investigate, and respond to cyber security threats to the organisation's systems and data. They triage alerts from security monitoring tools, investigate suspicious activity, contain incidents, and help fix weaknesses. In health care, fast detection and response protects clinical services and confidential patient information from attacks such as ransomware.
healthContext: Health care is a frequent target for ransomware and data theft, and one attack can stop clinical systems across the organisation.
Containment decisions, such as isolating a server or part of the network, must weigh security risk against the effect on patient care, so analysts work with clinical and operational leads.
Networks include medical devices and legacy systems that cannot run security agents or be patched quickly, so analysts rely on network monitoring and compensating controls.
Monitoring covers access to patient records, so analysts help detect inappropriate access by insiders as well as external attacks, working with information governance.
Security monitoring runs around the clock, so analysts may work shifts or on-call rotas.

levels.title: Junior security operations analyst
levels.summary: A junior security operations analyst monitors security alerts, triages them using runbooks, and escalates events, with guidance from experienced analysts.
responsibilities: Monitor alerts from security monitoring and endpoint tools, and triage them using runbooks.
Gather evidence about suspicious activity, such as phishing emails or unusual logins, and escalate it.
Check phishing emails reported by staff, and help remove malicious emails from mailboxes.
Record events and actions accurately in the case management tool.
Run vulnerability scans and remind system owners about fixes that are due.
qualifications: A qualification in computing or cyber security, a cyber security apprenticeship, or equivalent experience.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Mental effort reflects frequent prolonged concentration on monitoring and triaging unpredictable alerts.

levels.title: Security operations analyst
levels.summary: A security operations analyst investigates and contains security incidents, writes detection rules, and improves the organisation's security monitoring.
responsibilities: Investigate security incidents, work out their scope, and contain them, working with system owners and clinical services.
Write and tune detection rules, and run threat hunts based on current threats to health care.
Monitor for inappropriate access to patient records, and pass cases to information governance.
Assess vulnerabilities by risk, including their effect on clinical services and medical devices.
Improve runbooks and tools after incidents.
Take part in the on-call rota for out-of-hours security incidents.
qualifications: A degree in computing or cyber security, relevant security certifications, or equivalent experience.
Experience of security monitoring or incident response.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Mental effort reflects frequent prolonged concentration during investigations, including on call. Emotional effort reflects frequent indirect exposure to distressing material in patient records and to the pressure of live incidents.

levels.title: Senior security operations analyst
levels.summary: A senior security operations analyst leads the response to significant security incidents, leads threat hunting, and guides the work of the security operations team.
responsibilities: Lead the technical response to significant security incidents, including ransomware and data theft, and coordinate with incident management.
Advise clinical and operational leaders on containment decisions that affect patient care.
Lead threat hunting and threat intelligence work, and share information with health care security partners.
Set priorities for detection engineering and monitoring coverage, including for medical device networks.
Lead exercises that test incident response with technical and clinical teams.
Coach and guide security operations analysts.
qualifications: Substantial experience of security operations and incident response, at a level equivalent to a postgraduate diploma.
Relevant advanced security certifications, or equivalent experience.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Mental and emotional effort reflect leading the response to serious incidents under pressure, often out of hours, where clinical services are at risk.

roles.title: Security engineer
roles.summary: Security engineers design, build, and run the technical security controls that protect the organisation's systems, data, and users. They work on identity and access, endpoint and network protection, encryption, logging, and cloud security, and help product and infrastructure teams build security in. In health care, they protect clinical systems and patient data while keeping access fast for clinicians at the point of care.
healthContext: Security controls must not get in the way of urgent care, so engineers design strong authentication that still works quickly on shared clinical workstations.
Medical devices and legacy clinical systems often cannot be patched or run security software, so engineers design network segmentation and compensating controls.
Ransomware is a major threat to health care, so engineers harden systems, protect backups, and limit how far an attack can spread.
Clinical systems are often supplied and supported by third parties, so engineers assess supplier security and control their remote access.
Changes to security controls on clinical systems go through change management and, where needed, clinical safety review.

levels.title: Security engineer
levels.summary: A security engineer builds, configures, and maintains security controls and tools, and helps teams fix security weaknesses.
responsibilities: Build and maintain security controls, such as endpoint protection, firewalls, email security, and security logging.
Configure identity and access controls, including multi-factor authentication and privileged access.
Help infrastructure and product teams fix vulnerabilities and harden systems to agreed standards.
Segment networks to protect medical devices and legacy systems, working with infrastructure and clinical engineering teams.
Review the security of new systems and supplier remote access before they go live.
Take part in the on-call rota to support security incident response.
qualifications: A degree in computing or cyber security, relevant security certifications, or equivalent experience.
Experience of building or running infrastructure or security tools.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Mental effort reflects frequent prolonged concentration on complex technical work and incident support, including on call.

levels.title: Senior security engineer
levels.summary: A senior security engineer designs and leads the delivery of significant security controls, and advises teams on secure design.
responsibilities: Design and lead the delivery of security controls, such as privileged access management, security monitoring, and backup protection.
Advise product and infrastructure teams on secure design for clinical and patient-facing services.
Design compensating controls for medical devices and other systems that cannot be patched.
Assess the security of suppliers and their products, including cloud services.
Support the response to serious security incidents with technical expertise and recovery plans.
Coach security engineers and share good practice across teams.
qualifications: Substantial experience of security engineering, at a level equivalent to a postgraduate diploma.
Relevant advanced security certifications, or equivalent experience.

levels.title: Lead security engineer
levels.summary: A lead security engineer sets the technical direction for security engineering, and makes sure controls work together across the organisation.
responsibilities: Set the technical direction and standards for security controls across the organisation.
Lead the security design for major programmes, such as moves to cloud hosting or a new electronic patient record.
Make sure controls protect against ransomware and support fast, safe recovery of clinical systems.
Balance security with clinical usability, working with clinical leads on access and authentication.
Advise the cyber security manager on technical risk and investment.
Lead and develop security engineers.
qualifications: Extensive experience of leading security engineering for complex services.

roles.title: Cyber security manager
roles.summary: Cyber security managers lead the organisation's approach to protecting its systems, data, and services from cyber threats. They set security policy, manage cyber risk, oversee security operations and engineering, lead the response to major cyber incidents, and build a security-aware culture. In health care, they make sure clinical services can keep running safely, and recover quickly, when an attack happens.
healthContext: A cyber attack on a health care organisation can stop clinical systems and put patients at risk, so cyber security is part of patient safety and business continuity.
Health care organisations often have to meet sector cyber security standards and report serious incidents to the relevant authorities.
Clinical staff need fast access to systems, so security policies are designed with clinicians and tested for usability.
Security depends on many suppliers, including clinical system suppliers and shared services, so supplier assurance is a core part of the role.
Medical devices and legacy systems create long-lasting risks that are managed with clinical engineering and clinical safety teams.

levels.title: Cyber security manager
levels.summary: A cyber security manager runs the cyber security function, or a major part of it, managing cyber risk, security operations, and assurance.
responsibilities: Run security operations, vulnerability management, and assurance work, and report on their performance.
Maintain the cyber risk register, and make sure risks to clinical services are assessed and owned.
Write and maintain security policies and standards, and check that they are followed.
Lead the response to cyber incidents, working with incident management and with clinical and operational leaders.
Run security awareness training and phishing exercises for all staff, including clinical staff.
Line manage security analysts and engineers.
qualifications: Extensive experience of cyber security, including incident response and risk management, at a level equivalent to a master's degree.
A recognised professional security certification, or equivalent experience.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Mental and emotional effort reflect leading the response to cyber incidents under pressure, often out of hours, where patient care may be at risk.

levels.title: Senior cyber security manager
