Prepare bundles, chronologies, and signing packs for contracts and cases.
Carry out defined legal research and summarise the results for lawyers.
Collect documents and evidence for claims and information requests.
Track external legal spending against budgets and report on it.
Train legal administrators in routine tasks.
qualifications: A legal assistant or paralegal qualification at intermediate level, or equivalent experience.

levels.title: Paralegal
levels.summary: Paralegals handle their own caseload of routine legal matters under a lawyer's supervision, such as standard contract reviews, information requests, and claims support.
responsibilities: Review routine agreements, such as software licences, services, and data processing agreements, against the organisation's standards.
Manage a caseload of routine claims or disputes, preparing documents and liaising with external lawyers and indemnity schemes.
Research legal questions and draft advice for a lawyer to review.
Support responses to complex information requests and data subject rights requests.
Keep templates, precedents, and legal guidance up to date.
Coordinate the work of legal assistants and administrators.
qualifications: A law degree or an advanced paralegal qualification, or equivalent experience.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Emotional effort is level 2 because the job regularly reads clinical records and accounts of harm in claims.

roles.title: Legal adviser
roles.summary: Legal advisers are qualified lawyers who give the organisation practical, accurate legal advice and help it manage legal risk. They draft and negotiate contracts, advise on data, procurement, employment, and health and care law, and manage disputes and claims. In a digital health care organisation much of their work is about technology: software licences, cloud and data processing agreements, data sharing, intellectual property in software and data, and the regulation of digital health products.
healthContext: Technology contracts must protect patient data, keep clinical services running, and make sure the organisation can leave a supplier safely.
Using health data for direct care, planning, research, and AI raises questions under data protection law and the duty of confidentiality that need careful advice.
Buying technology with public money must follow public procurement rules, and suppliers can challenge award decisions.
The organisation may build software or data products, which raises questions of intellectual property, open source, and commercial use.
Claims may involve harm to patients, including where digital services played a part, so advisers work with clinical safety, risk, and indemnity colleagues.

levels.title: Legal adviser
levels.summary: Legal advisers are qualified lawyers who give independent advice and handle their own caseload in one or more areas, such as technology contracts, information law, procurement, or employment.
responsibilities: Draft, review, and negotiate agreements, such as software licences, cloud services, and data processing agreements.
Give clear, practical legal advice to managers and teams in your areas of practice.
Advise on data sharing agreements, data protection impact assessments, and information requests.
Advise on procurement processes and contract changes for technology and services.
Manage a caseload of disputes or claims, instructing external lawyers where needed.
Supervise and develop paralegals and legal assistants.
qualifications: A qualified lawyer admitted to practise, or equivalent qualification and experience.
Experience of commercial, technology, information, or public law.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Knowledge is level 7 because the job needs a professional legal qualification and practice experience. Financial resources is level 2 because legal advisers rarely hold budgets. Emotional effort is level 2 because claims and employment cases often involve distressing material.

levels.title: Senior legal adviser
levels.summary: Senior legal advisers are experienced lawyers who lead on complex, high-value, or high-risk matters in a specialist area, such as technology and data, information law, procurement, employment, or claims.
responsibilities: Lead on complex agreements, such as major system implementations, data platforms, and partnerships.
Advise senior managers on novel questions, such as AI, data use for research, and software as a medical device.
Advise on employment law for workforce change, contractors, and employment disputes.
Lead on significant disputes, procurement challenges, and liaison with clinical negligence schemes.
Write templates, playbooks, and guidance for the organisation.
Manage and develop legal advisers and paralegals.
qualifications: A qualified lawyer admitted to practise, with substantial post-qualification experience in a relevant specialism.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Financial resources is level 2 because the job does not hold a budget, though it controls spending on external lawyers for its matters.

levels.title: Principal legal adviser
levels.summary: Principal legal advisers are the organisation's leading experts in one or more areas of law, such as technology and data or information law, and lead its legal work on the most significant matters.
responsibilities: Lead the legal work on the organisation's most significant programmes, contracts, and disputes.
Give definitive advice on novel and high-risk matters, such as large-scale data sharing, AI, and commercial use of the organisation's software and data.
Set the organisation's legal positions and standards in your specialist areas.
Advise directors and board committees on legal risk.
Represent the organisation with regulators, partners, and suppliers on legal matters.
Lead a specialist legal team and develop its capability.
qualifications: A qualified lawyer admitted to practise, with extensive post-qualification experience and recognised expertise in a specialism.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Knowledge is level 8 because the job needs expert legal knowledge across law and technology, built over a long period.

roles.title: Head of legal services
roles.summary: Senior legal leaders make sure the organisation acts lawfully and manages its legal risk well. They lead the in-house legal team, manage external legal advisers, and advise the board and executive on the organisation's most significant legal matters. In a digital health care organisation this includes the legal basis for using health data, major technology and data contracts, intellectual property in software, and the organisation's statutory duties.
healthContext: The organisation is a public body or works with them, so its decisions can be challenged, and it must act within its powers.
The use of health and care data at scale, including for AI and research, carries high legal and reputational risk.
Major technology contracts are long, valuable, and hard to exit, so their legal terms shape the organisation for years.
Legal leaders work closely with the board, the data protection officer, clinical safety, and information governance colleagues.

levels.title: Deputy head of legal services
levels.summary: Deputy heads of legal services lead a major area of the legal function, such as commercial, technology, and data law, and deputise for the head of legal services.
responsibilities: Lead a major area of legal work, such as commercial, technology, and data law, or disputes and employment.
Advise directors on high-risk matters, including major procurements and data programmes.
Manage the panel of external lawyers and the budget for external legal advice.
Set legal standards, templates, and training for the organisation.
Lead and develop several legal teams or specialists.
Deputise for the head of legal services.
qualifications: A qualified lawyer admitted to practise, with extensive post-qualification experience, including leading a legal team.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Knowledge is level 8 for expert knowledge across several areas of law. Information resources is level 5 rather than 6, because the job does not manage organisation-wide information systems.

levels.title: Head of legal services
levels.summary: Heads of legal services lead the organisation's legal function, set its approach to legal risk, and advise the executive and board.
responsibilities: Lead the in-house legal function and the use of external lawyers.
Advise the executive and board on legal risk, statutory duties, and major decisions.
Set the organisation's legal risk appetite and positions on key issues, such as data use and contracting.
Lead legal work on the most significant matters, such as major disputes, public inquiries, and partnerships.
Hold the budget for legal services and show value for money.
Lead and develop the legal team and legal operations.
qualifications: A qualified lawyer admitted to practise, with extensive senior experience of leading legal services.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Financial resources is level 4 because the job holds the legal services budget, not budgets for several services.

levels.title: General counsel
levels.summary: General counsel are the organisation's most senior lawyer, with corporate responsibility for legal services and legal risk, and often also lead corporate governance as board secretary.
responsibilities: Hold corporate responsibility for the organisation's legal affairs and legal risk.
Advise the board and chair on the organisation's powers, duties, and governance.
Make sure major strategies, partnerships, and data programmes are lawful.
Lead the response to the most serious legal threats, such as judicial reviews and regulatory action.
Lead legal services, and often corporate governance and the board secretariat.
Represent the organisation with regulators, partners, and government bodies.
qualifications: A qualified lawyer admitted to practise, with extensive experience at executive or board level.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Financial resources is level 4 because the job holds the budget for legal and governance services, not the organisation's finances.

roles.title: Human resources officer
roles.summary: HR officers and advisers run the organisation's core people services, from contracts, starters, and changes to advice on people policies and support for managers with employee relations cases. They keep employment records accurate and confidential, help managers treat staff fairly and lawfully, and support the people who run digital and clinical services that never close.
healthContext: Many staff work in services that run 24 hours a day, so HR teams advise on shift patterns, on-call and standby arrangements, rest breaks, and working time.
Some cases are linked to patient safety incidents, safeguarding concerns, or professional registration, so HR staff work closely with clinical leads and follow the right processes for each.
Digital, data, and technology staff are in short supply, so fair and quick HR processes, from contracts to flexible working requests, help the organisation keep the people it has.
HR records are highly confidential personal data, and some include health information, so HR staff apply information governance rules every day.
Staff in this reference are paid on a banded pay structure with job evaluation, so HR staff explain how bands, increments, and allowances work.

levels.title: HR assistant
levels.summary: Provides accurate administrative support across the employment life cycle, working to set procedures and service standards with an HR officer or adviser close by.
responsibilities: Prepare contracts, offer letters, and variation letters from standard templates.
Enter starters, changes, and leavers in the HR and payroll system before payroll deadlines.
Answer routine questions from staff and managers by phone, email, and the HR helpdesk.
Take notes at formal meetings, such as attendance and grievance meetings, and keep case files in order.
Keep personal files and records confidential, accurate, and in line with retention rules.
qualifications: A level 2 or 3 qualification, a business administration apprenticeship, or equivalent experience.
Experience of accurate administrative work with confidential information.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: People is level 2 because the job gives basic HR information and advice to staff and managers; emotional effort is level 2 for indirect exposure to distressing case material when taking notes and filing case records.

levels.title: HR officer
levels.summary: Runs HR administration for a group of services and gives first-line advice to managers on people policies, checking the work of HR assistants.
responsibilities: Run starters, changes, and leavers for a group of services, solving unusual or complex cases.
Advise managers on routine policy questions, such as annual leave, flexible working, and attendance triggers.
Check the work of HR assistants and train them on processes and the HR system.
Produce standard workforce reports, such as absence and turnover, for managers.
Support HR advisers with employee relations cases by preparing papers and arranging hearings.
Suggest improvements to HR processes, templates, and self-service guidance.
qualifications: A level 3 HR or business qualification, or equivalent experience.
Experience of HR administration, including HR and payroll systems.

levels.title: HR adviser
levels.summary: Gives professional HR advice to managers in a group of services and manages a caseload of employee relations cases, working to defined policies with a senior HR adviser available for complex cases.
responsibilities: Advise managers on conduct, capability, attendance, grievance, and dignity at work cases, from first concern to outcome.
Support formal hearings, advising the panel on policy, process, and fair outcomes.
Advise on reasonable adjustments, flexible working, and occupational health referrals.
Advise managers on working time, on-call, and rota rules for services that run 24 hours a day.
Support small organisational changes, such as changes to working patterns, including consultation with staff.
Train managers in people policies and how to apply them.
qualifications: A recognised HR professional qualification at intermediate level, or equivalent experience.
Experience of advising managers on employee relations cases.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: People is level 3 because the job gives core HR advice as its main duty; emotional effort is level 3 because the job frequently deals with distressing employee relations cases, such as allegations, ill health, and staff in crisis.

levels.title: Senior HR adviser
levels.summary: Leads HR advice for a directorate, handles the most complex and sensitive cases, and supports HR advisers, working with broad freedom within the organisation's people policies.
responsibilities: Manage complex and high-risk employee relations cases, including those linked to patient safety incidents or safeguarding.
Lead or commission investigations and coach managers who investigate.
Lead organisational change for a service, such as a restructure or a new on-call rota, including formal consultation.
Advise on banding for new and changed roles and take part in job evaluation panels.
Analyse case and workforce data for the directorate and recommend action on trends.
Draft and review people policies, working with staff representatives.
Supervise and develop HR advisers.
qualifications: A recognised HR professional qualification at intermediate or advanced level, or equivalent experience.
Substantial experience of managing complex employee relations cases and organisational change.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Emotional effort is level 3 for frequent exposure to distressing casework; people is level 3 for core HR advice and supervising HR advisers.

roles.title: Recruitment officer
roles.summary: Recruitment officers run the organisation's recruitment service, helping managers attract, assess, and appoint the right people quickly, fairly, and safely. In a digital health care organisation they compete with other sectors for scarce digital, data, and technology skills, so they combine efficient processes with active sourcing, a strong employer brand, and good use of skills frameworks.
healthContext: Digital, data, and technology specialists are in short supply and often paid more elsewhere, so recruiters sell the purpose of the work, flexible working, and career pathways, not only pay.

Roles that access patient records or work with patients need pre-employment checks, such as identity, right to work, references, criminal records checks where the role needs them, occupational health clearance, and professional registration.
Vacancies in services that run 24/7 can affect patient care, so recruiters prioritise critical roles and track time to hire.
Fair, inclusive recruitment helps the workforce reflect the patients and communities it serves.
Recruiters use the role profiles and skills in this reference to write consistent adverts and job descriptions and to design fair assessments.

levels.title: Recruitment assistant
levels.summary: Provides accurate administrative support for recruitment campaigns and pre-employment checks, following set procedures with a recruitment officer close by.
responsibilities: Publish adverts and manage vacancies in the applicant tracking system.
Arrange interviews and assessments and send correspondence to candidates.
Carry out pre-employment checks, such as identity, right to work, and references, and chase outstanding items.
Answer routine questions from candidates and managers by phone and email.
Keep recruitment records accurate, confidential, and in line with retention rules.
qualifications: A level 2 or 3 qualification, a business administration apprenticeship, or equivalent experience.
Experience of accurate administrative work and dealing with the public.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: People is level 2 because the job gives basic HR information and services to managers and candidates.

levels.title: Recruitment officer
levels.summary: Runs recruitment campaigns from start to finish for a group of services, advising managers on the process and checking the work of recruitment assistants.
responsibilities: Run recruitment campaigns from vacancy approval to start date, keeping managers and candidates informed.
Advise managers on adverts, shortlisting, interviews, and fair selection.
Make conditional offers, agree start dates, and resolve problems with pre-employment checks.
Plan recruitment events and bulk campaigns, such as for apprentices or new services.
Report on time to hire and campaign progress, and suggest improvements.
Check the work of recruitment assistants and train them on the system.
qualifications: A level 3 HR or business qualification, or equivalent experience.
Experience of running recruitment campaigns and applicant tracking systems.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Planning is level 3 because the job plans several campaigns and events at once and adjusts them as vacancies and candidate availability change.

levels.title: Digital talent partner
levels.summary: Works with digital, data, and technology leaders to attract and appoint scarce specialists, using active sourcing, talent pools, and fair, skills-based assessment. Also known as senior recruitment officer.
responsibilities: Partner with hiring managers in digital, data, and technology teams to plan hiring and agree what good looks like for each role.
Source candidates directly through professional networks, communities, and talent pools.
Write adverts and job descriptions using the role profiles and skills in this reference and the UK GDaD PCF.
Design skills-based assessments, such as technical exercises and portfolio reviews, with hiring managers.
Use pay and market data to advise on hard-to-fill roles and starting salaries within the pay rules.
Grow early careers routes, such as digital apprenticeships and graduate schemes.
Manage the agency and recruitment advertising budget for the campaigns you run.
qualifications: A recognised HR or recruitment qualification, or equivalent experience.
Experience of recruiting specialist roles, ideally digital, data, or technology roles.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Information resources is level 4 because the job adapts reports and talent pool records in the applicant tracking system as a significant duty.

levels.title: Recruitment manager
levels.summary: Manages the recruitment service and team, sets its standards, and leads improvements to speed, quality, candidate experience, and inclusion.
responsibilities: Manage the recruitment team and service, setting priorities and service standards.
Lead improvements to the recruitment process and applicant tracking system, including automation and self-service.
Analyse recruitment data, such as time to hire, offer acceptance, and diversity at each stage, and act on it.
Shape the employer brand and recruitment marketing with the communications team.
Manage recruitment agency use and the recruitment budget.
Make sure recruitment follows employment law, safe recruitment rules, and the organisation's policies.
qualifications: A recognised HR or recruitment professional qualification, or equivalent experience.
Experience of managing a recruitment team or service.

roles.title: Human resources business partner
roles.summary: HR business partners work alongside directorate leaders to make sure the organisation has the people, skills, structures, and culture it needs to deliver its services. They turn the people strategy into plans for each directorate, lead organisational change, and give senior advice on the most complex people issues. In a digital health care organisation much of this is about building and keeping digital, data, and technology capability.
healthContext: Digital, data, and technology skills are scarce, so business partners lead workforce plans that combine recruitment, apprenticeships, reskilling, and retention, and use skills frameworks such as this reference for gap analysis.
Many services run 24/7, so changes to rotas, on-call, and service models need careful consultation and attention to staff wellbeing and safe staffing.
Digital roles are often new or fast-changing, so business partners make sure job descriptions are evaluated consistently and banded fairly against similar roles.
Organisational change often involves clinical and care staff as well as digital teams, so business partners work with clinical leaders and staff representatives.
People risks, such as reliance on contractors or a small number of experts, can become risks to patient-facing services.

levels.title: HR business partner
levels.summary: Is the senior HR adviser to the leadership team of a directorate, leading its people plan, organisational change, and complex employee relations, within the organisation's people strategy.
responsibilities: Advise the directorate leadership team on people risks, priorities, and plans.
Lead the directorate's workforce plan, using skills gap analysis against this reference to plan recruitment, development, and new roles.
Lead organisational change, such as restructures and new service models, from business case through formal consultation to implementation.
Oversee complex and high-risk employee relations cases and advise senior managers and panels.
Use workforce data, such as turnover, vacancies, agency spend, and staff survey results, to challenge and support leaders.
Advise on banding and reward for new and changing roles, including recruitment and retention premiums.
Lead and develop HR advisers who support the directorate.
qualifications: A recognised HR professional qualification at advanced level, or equivalent experience.
Substantial experience of advising senior leaders and leading organisational change.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: People is level 4 because the job delivers the full range of HR services to a directorate; policy is level 4 because it develops people practices for several services; emotional effort is level 3 for frequent exposure to distressing casework and change.

levels.title: Senior HR business partner
levels.summary: Business partners several directorates, or the largest and most complex ones, such as digital and technology, and leads people programmes that reach across the organisation.
responsibilities: Advise executive and senior leaders of several directorates on people strategy, risk, and organisational design.
Lead large or sensitive organisational changes, including service transfers and changes to 24/7 working patterns.
Lead an organisation-wide people programme, such as a digital careers framework or a retention plan for scarce skills.
Handle the most sensitive cases, such as those involving senior staff or a risk of legal claims, with legal advisers.
Shape people policies and consult on them with staff representatives.
Lead, coach, and develop HR business partners and advisers.
qualifications: A recognised HR professional qualification at advanced level, or a master's degree in HR or a related subject, or equivalent experience.
Extensive experience of HR business partnering at senior level.

levels.title: Head of HR business partnering
levels.summary: Leads the HR business partnering service across the organisation and makes sure every directorate has a people plan that delivers the people strategy.
responsibilities: Lead and manage the HR business partner and HR adviser teams.
Make sure every directorate has a workforce and people plan linked to its service and financial plans.
Lead the organisation's approach to organisational change, consultation, and partnership working with staff representatives.
Report people risks and workforce performance to executive committees.
Hold the budget for the business partnering service.
Work with leaders of recruitment, learning, and organisational development to deliver joined-up people services.
qualifications: A recognised HR professional qualification at advanced level, or a master's degree in HR or a related subject, or equivalent experience.
Extensive experience of leading HR teams and organisational change.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: People is level 5 because the job manages a large part of HR across the organisation.

roles.title: Learning and development specialist
roles.summary: Learning and development specialists help staff gain the skills they need to deliver safe, modern, digitally enabled care. They analyse learning needs, design and deliver learning in person and online, run the learning management system, and build career pathways. In a digital health care organisation a large part of their work is growing digital, data, and technology skills, both for specialists and for the whole workforce.
healthContext: Clinical and care staff need training on new clinical systems before go-live, often across shifts and sites, so learning is planned around services that run 24/7.
Some training is mandatory, such as information governance, cyber security awareness, and safeguarding, and compliance is reported to the board.
Growing scarce digital skills from within, through apprenticeships, reskilling, and career pathways, is often faster and cheaper than recruiting them.
Skills frameworks such as this reference, the UK GDaD PCF, and ESCO give a shared language for skills gap analysis and development plans.
Learning must be accessible to staff with different needs, working patterns, and levels of digital confidence.

levels.title: Learning and development coordinator
levels.summary: Coordinates the organisation's learning offer, running bookings, the learning management system, and training records, and supports the delivery of courses.
responsibilities: Schedule courses, book rooms and trainers, and manage bookings and waiting lists.
Maintain courses, enrolments, and completion records in the learning management system.
Produce reports on mandatory training compliance for managers.
Answer questions from staff and managers about the learning offer.
Support trainers in sessions, including setting up online classrooms and collecting feedback.
Administer apprenticeship enrolments and reviews with training providers.
qualifications: A level 3 qualification, a learning and development apprenticeship, or equivalent experience.
Experience of administration and of using a learning management system or similar.

levels.title: Learning and development officer
levels.summary: Designs and delivers learning for a range of staff groups, including digital skills and system training, and evaluates its effect.
responsibilities: Deliver training in person and online, such as induction, digital skills, and management essentials.
Build e-learning and short guides in the learning management system, making them accessible.
Work with digital teams to plan and deliver training for new clinical and business systems before go-live.
Support managers to identify team learning needs and plan development.
Evaluate courses and improve them using feedback and results.
Coordinate apprenticeships, working with providers, learners, and managers.
qualifications: A recognised learning and development or training qualification, or equivalent experience.
Experience of designing and delivering training to adults, in person and online.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: People is level 3 because the job teaches core training as a main duty; research is level 2 because it regularly evaluates learning.

levels.title: Learning and development specialist
levels.summary: Leads the analysis, design, and evaluation of learning programmes for a major area, such as leadership, digital skills, or system training, working with broad freedom within the learning strategy.
responsibilities: Analyse learning needs for a staff group or profession, using skills gap analysis against this reference.
Design blended learning programmes with clear outcomes, from e-learning to coaching and practice in the workplace.
Design training strategies for large clinical system changes, including super-user networks.
Evaluate the effect of learning on skills, performance, and services, and report it.
Commission and quality-assure external training providers.
Coach and develop learning and development officers.
qualifications: A recognised learning and development qualification at intermediate or advanced level, or equivalent experience.
Substantial experience of designing and evaluating learning programmes.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: People is level 4 because designing training programmes is the main duty.

levels.title: Digital skills lead
levels.summary: Leads the organisation's programme to grow digital, data, and technology skills, for specialist professions and for the whole workforce, using skills frameworks to plan careers and close gaps.
responsibilities: Lead the digital skills programme, including digital literacy for all staff and development for digital, data, and technology professions.
Run skills gap analysis across digital teams using the role profiles and skills in this reference, and report the results.
Design career pathways from apprenticeships to senior roles, linked to bands and job evaluation.
Build partnerships with universities, colleges, and training providers, and make full use of apprenticeship funding.
Manage the digital skills budget and evaluate return on investment.
Lead a small team of learning and development staff.
qualifications: A recognised learning and development qualification at advanced level, or equivalent experience.
Substantial experience of building skills programmes, ideally in digital, data, or technology.

levels.title: Head of learning
levels.summary: Leads learning and development across the organisation, setting the learning strategy and managing the learning team, budget, and systems.
responsibilities: Set the organisation's learning strategy, linked to the people strategy and workforce plan.
Lead and manage the learning and development team and its services, including mandatory training and the learning management system.
Hold the learning budget, including apprenticeship funds and external training spend.
Report learning activity, compliance, and impact to executive committees.
Lead leadership and management development programmes with organisational development colleagues.
Make sure learning is accessible, inclusive, and available to staff on every shift.
qualifications: A recognised learning and development or HR professional qualification at advanced level, or a master's degree in a related subject, or equivalent experience.
Extensive experience of leading learning services.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: People is level 5 because the job manages training across the organisation.

roles.title: Head of people
roles.summary: The head of people and the people leadership team set the organisation's people strategy and lead its HR, recruitment, learning, organisational development, and workforce functions. They advise the board on culture, workforce, and employment risk, and make sure the organisation can attract, grow, and keep the people it needs to deliver safe digital health services.
healthContext: The organisation competes with other sectors for scarce digital, data, and technology talent, so people leaders balance pay rules and job evaluation with flexible working, career pathways, and a strong purpose.
Services that run 24/7 depend on safe staffing, sustainable rotas, and staff wellbeing, which the board expects people leaders to monitor and improve.
Culture affects patient safety, so people leaders link staff experience, speaking up, and inclusion to the quality of care.
Workforce plans are made with partners across the health and care system, and staff may move between organisations when services change.
Banded pay with job evaluation means new and changing digital roles must be evaluated consistently, and pay decisions must stand up to equal pay scrutiny.

levels.title: Head of HR
levels.summary: Leads a large part of the people function, such as HR operations, employee relations, and business partnering, and sets its standards. Also known as assistant director of people.
responsibilities: Lead HR operations, business partnering, and employee relations, managing several team leaders.
Set people policies and the organisation's approach to employment law and risk.
Lead partnership working and negotiations with staff representatives.
Oversee the most serious cases, including those involving senior staff or legal claims.
Lead workforce reporting to committees, including equality and pay gap reporting.
Hold the budget for the HR services you lead and improve their value for money.
qualifications: A recognised HR professional qualification at advanced level, or a master's degree in HR or a related subject, or equivalent experience.
Extensive experience of leading HR services at senior level.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Communication is level 6 for negotiating highly contentious matters with staff representatives; emotional effort is level 3 for frequent exposure to serious employee relations cases.

levels.title: Deputy director of people
levels.summary: Deputises for the director of people and leads several people functions, such as workforce planning, learning, organisational development, and reward, across the organisation.
responsibilities: Deputise for the director of people, including at board committees.
Lead workforce planning, learning, organisational development, and reward across the organisation.
Lead the digital, data, and technology workforce plan, using skills gap analysis to set priorities for recruitment, development, and retention.
Lead the organisation's reward strategy, job evaluation, and equal pay assurance within the agreed pay framework.
Lead culture, engagement, and inclusion programmes and measure their effect.
Hold budgets for several people services and lead their improvement.
qualifications: A recognised HR professional qualification at advanced level, or a master's degree in HR or a related subject, or equivalent experience.
Extensive experience of leading several people functions.

levels.title: Director of people
levels.summary: Is the executive lead for people, culture, and workforce, accountable to the chief executive and the board for the people strategy and the whole people function.
responsibilities: Set the organisation's people strategy and culture, and lead the people function.
Advise the board on workforce, culture, employment risk, and the people impact of strategy.
Lead the organisation's response to scarce digital and data skills, with the chief digital officer.
Make sure the organisation meets its legal duties as an employer, including equality and health and safety at work.
Represent the organisation on people matters with health and care partners, regulators, and staff representatives.
Hold the people directorate budget and set workforce cost controls with the director of finance.
qualifications: A recognised HR professional qualification at the highest level, or a master's degree in HR or a related subject, or equivalent experience.
Extensive experience of leading a people function at executive level.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: People is level 6 for corporate responsibility for the organisation's people and HR function.

roles.title: Procurement officer
roles.summary: Procurement officers help the organisation buy the goods and services it needs, lawfully and at good value, from routine purchases to formal tenders. In a digital health care organisation much of this spending is on software, cloud services, licences, devices, and technology services, so they work closely with digital, information governance, and clinical safety colleagues as well as with budget holders.
healthContext: Public procurement rules apply to the organisation's spending, so every purchase must follow the right route, keep a clear audit trail, and treat suppliers fairly.
Many purchases are digital, such as software licences, cloud subscriptions, and devices, and need security, data protection, and clinical safety checks before contract.
Suppliers of clinical systems can hold patient data, so contracts need clear terms on data protection, data ownership, and data return.
Buying through frameworks and dynamic purchasing systems built for the public sector can save time, but call-offs must still follow each framework's rules.
Public spending must show value for money and social value, such as local jobs, skills, and lower carbon.

levels.title: Procurement assistant
levels.summary: Provides purchasing and administrative support, following set procedures, with a procurement officer close by.
responsibilities: Raise and amend purchase orders in the purchasing system, checking them against contracts and approvals.
Resolve routine invoice and receipting queries with suppliers, budget holders, and finance.
Get quotes for low-value purchases following the organisation's rules.
Keep supplier records, catalogues, and the contract register up to date.
Answer routine questions from staff about how to buy.
qualifications: A level 2 or 3 qualification, a procurement apprenticeship, or equivalent experience.
Experience of accurate administrative or finance work.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Financial resources is level 2 because the job raises and amends orders that commit spending approved by others.

levels.title: Buyer
levels.summary: Buys goods and services through quotations and framework call-offs, including standard software, devices, and licences, within set procedures.
responsibilities: Run quotations and further competitions under frameworks, using standard templates and the e-tendering system.
Buy standard software, devices, and licences, tracking renewals and licence numbers.
Check that standard security, data protection, and accessibility requirements are included before purchase.
Negotiate prices and terms for routine purchases.
Keep a clear audit trail and publish contract award notices where the rules need them.
Analyse spend data to find off-contract spending and suggest better routes.
qualifications: A procurement qualification at certificate level, a procurement apprenticeship, or equivalent experience.
Experience of buying through quotations or frameworks.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Financial resources is level 3 because the job buys supplies and services on behalf of budget holders.

levels.title: Procurement officer
levels.summary: Runs procurements of moderate value and complexity, including formal tenders, from planning to contract award, with a senior procurement officer available for advice.
responsibilities: Run formal tenders and framework competitions from planning to award, managing timetables and clarification questions.
Help budget holders write clear, outcome-based specifications, including technical and data protection requirements.
Set up evaluation, check bids for compliance, support evaluators, and record moderation.
Write award reports and feedback to bidders, and manage the standstill period.
Include social value and sustainability questions that fit the contract.
Hand over contracts to contract managers with clear mobilisation and exit plans.
Train budget holders in how to buy and supervise procurement assistants.
qualifications: A recognised procurement professional qualification at intermediate level, or equivalent experience.
Experience of running formal tenders under public procurement rules.

levels.title: Senior procurement officer
levels.summary: Leads complex procurements, such as clinical systems, cloud services, and technology services, and advises on the right route to market, working with broad freedom within procurement policy.
responsibilities: Lead complex and high-value procurements, choosing the right route to market and procedure.
Lead early market engagement and requests for information, keeping competition fair.
Design evaluation criteria and weightings with technical, clinical, and information governance leads, and lead moderation.
Make sure contracts for technology include interoperability, security, data ownership, exit, and data return terms.
Negotiate with bidders where the procedure allows it, and agree final terms.
Advise on contract changes, extensions, and direct awards, and the risk of challenge.
Coach and check the work of procurement officers and buyers.
qualifications: A recognised procurement professional qualification at advanced level, or equivalent experience.
Substantial experience of leading complex tenders, ideally for technology or clinical systems.

roles.title: Category manager
roles.summary: Category managers plan and manage a category of the organisation's spending, such as software and cloud, technology services, devices, or clinical systems, over several years. They pool demand, understand the supply market, shape requirements with digital and clinical leaders, and plan procurements and renewals so that the organisation gets value for money, avoids lock-in, and keeps its services safe and running.
healthContext: Technology is one of the organisation's largest and fastest-growing areas of spend, and much of it is subscriptions that renew every year.
Clinical systems are hard to replace, so category plans start early, test the market, and plan for interoperability and data portability to keep future competition possible.
Cloud and software contracts must meet security, data protection, and data residency requirements for health data.
Public procurement rules apply, and many categories are bought through public sector frameworks, so category managers choose the right route for each need.
Category strategies include social value and carbon reduction, such as device reuse and greener data centres.

levels.title: Category manager (digital and technology)
levels.summary: Manages a category of digital and technology spend, such as software, cloud, devices, or technology services, with a category strategy agreed with digital leaders.
responsibilities: Write and deliver the category strategy for digital and technology spend, with budget holders and technical leads.
Analyse spend, contracts, licences, and renewals across the category, and plan the pipeline of procurements.
Lead the most complex procurements in the category, such as cloud platforms and clinical systems.
Analyse supply markets and lead early market engagement.
Negotiate commercial models, such as enterprise licences and consumption-based pricing, and track savings and value.
Make sure contracts include interoperability, data ownership, exit, and data return terms that avoid lock-in.
Report category performance, risks, and savings to the head of procurement and digital leaders.
qualifications: A recognised procurement professional qualification at advanced level, or equivalent experience.
Substantial experience of buying digital and technology services.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Financial resources is level 4 because the job sets how a major category of the organisation's spending is bought; research is level 2 for regular market analysis.

levels.title: Senior category manager
levels.summary: Manages several categories, or the organisation's largest and riskiest category, and leads collaborative buying with other organisations.
responsibilities: Lead category strategies for several categories, or for strategic technology and clinical systems.
Lead high-value, high-risk procurements and negotiations, including strategic platforms and enterprise agreements.
Lead collaborative procurements with other health and care organisations.
Advise digital and clinical leaders on the commercial risks and costs of technology choices.
Set social value and sustainability goals for the categories you lead.
Line manage and develop category managers and procurement officers.
qualifications: A recognised procurement professional qualification at advanced level, or equivalent experience.
Extensive experience of category management and complex technology procurement.

levels.title: Head of category
levels.summary: Leads category management across the organisation's spending, setting the category approach and managing the category team.
responsibilities: Set the category management approach and the pipeline of procurements across the organisation.
Lead and manage category managers and their teams.
Make sure category strategies support the organisation's digital, clinical, and financial plans.
Report savings, value for money, social value, and commercial risks to executive committees.
Lead relationships with public sector buying organisations and framework providers.
Hold the budget for the category team.
qualifications: A recognised procurement professional qualification at advanced level, or a master's degree in a related subject, or equivalent experience.
Extensive experience of leading category teams.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Financial resources is level 5 because the job sets how spending is bought across several services.

roles.title: Contract manager
roles.summary: Contract managers make sure the organisation gets what it pays for after a contract is signed. They manage supplier performance, payments, changes, disputes, renewals, and exit, and build relationships with key suppliers. In a digital health care organisation many of the most important contracts are for clinical systems, cloud hosting, and technology services that patients and staff rely on every day.
healthContext: Clinical system outages or failures can affect patient care, so contract managers monitor availability, incident response, and support levels closely and use contract remedies when needed.
Suppliers often process patient data, so contracts are managed with information governance and security colleagues, including data protection terms, audits, and breach handling.
Exit and data return must be planned from the start, so that patient records can move to a new system in a usable format and old copies are securely deleted.
Contract changes must follow public procurement rules, so contract managers check whether a change needs a new procurement.
Supplier releases can change how a clinical system behaves, so contract managers make sure suppliers meet clinical safety obligations.

levels.title: Contract manager
levels.summary: Manages a portfolio of contracts, including technology and clinical system contracts, from mobilisation to renewal, working within the contract management framework. Also known as contract officer.
responsibilities: Manage a portfolio of contracts, keeping the contract register, documents, and key dates current.
Run regular performance reviews with suppliers, using service levels and key performance indicators.
Check invoices against contract terms and resolve billing disputes.
Process contract changes and variations within the procurement rules.
Track licence use, renewals, and notice periods, and start renewal planning early.
Keep exit plans and data registers up to date for each contract.
Work with information governance and security colleagues on supplier data protection and security checks.
qualifications: A recognised procurement or contract management qualification, or equivalent experience.
Experience of managing service contracts, ideally for technology.

levels.title: Senior contract manager
levels.summary: Manages the organisation's strategic and high-risk contracts, such as the electronic patient record and cloud hosting, and leads relationships with key suppliers.
responsibilities: Manage strategic contracts for clinical systems and technology services, including mobilisation of new contracts.
Lead strategic reviews with key suppliers, covering performance, roadmap, risks, and improvement plans.
Use contract remedies, such as service credits and remediation plans, when performance falls short.
Negotiate contract variations, renewals, and settlement of disputes.
Write and test exit and transition plans, including data return in standard formats and secure deletion.
Assess supplier risks, such as financial health, cyber security, and supply chain, and plan for supplier failure.
Coach and supervise contract managers.
qualifications: A recognised procurement or contract management qualification at advanced level, or equivalent experience.
Substantial experience of managing strategic technology or outsourced service contracts.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Financial resources is level 4 because the job manages the spend and assets of high-value service contracts.

levels.title: Lead contract manager
levels.summary: Leads contract and supplier management across the organisation, setting the contract management framework and managing the contract team.
responsibilities: Set the organisation's contract management framework, standards, and tools.
Lead the contract management team and its portfolio of contracts.
Lead the management of the most critical supplier relationships and resolve major disputes.
Set standards for exit planning and data return, and lead exits from strategic contracts.
Report contract performance, supplier risk, and savings to executive committees.
Advise on termination, re-procurement, and supplier failure.
qualifications: A recognised procurement or contract management qualification at advanced level, or equivalent experience.
Extensive experience of leading contract management for complex services.

roles.title: Head of procurement
roles.summary: The head of procurement and the commercial leadership team lead how the organisation buys goods and services and manages its suppliers. They set procurement policy and commercial strategy, make sure spending is lawful and gives value for money, and advise the board on commercial risk. In a digital health care organisation they give particular attention to technology and clinical system contracts, supplier resilience, and exit.
healthContext: Large technology and clinical system contracts can shape services for a decade, so commercial leaders plan for interoperability, portability, and future competition from the start.
Critical suppliers support services that run 24/7, so supplier failure and cyber incidents in the supply chain are board-level risks.
Public procurement rules apply, and the organisation must be able to defend its procurement decisions if challenged.
The organisation is expected to deliver social value and carbon reduction through its spending.
Commercial leaders often work with other health and care organisations on collaborative buying and shared contracts.

levels.title: Head of procurement
levels.summary: Leads the procurement function, setting procurement procedures and standards and managing the procurement and purchasing teams.
responsibilities: Lead and manage the procurement and purchasing teams.
Set the organisation's procurement procedures, templates, and thresholds, in line with public procurement rules and financial rules.
Assure the most complex and high-value procurements and their award decisions.
Manage the procurement pipeline and make sure procurements start in time.
Report procurement compliance, savings, and social value to the audit committee.
Hold the procurement team budget and develop the team's skills.
qualifications: A recognised procurement professional qualification at the highest level, or equivalent experience.
Extensive experience of leading procurement under public procurement rules.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Policy is level 5 because the job sets procurement procedures for the whole organisation; financial resources is level 5 because it controls how spending is bought across many services.

levels.title: Head of commercial
levels.summary: Leads procurement, category management, and contract management together as one commercial function, and sets the commercial strategy.
responsibilities: Lead the commercial function, including procurement, category management, and contract management.
Set the commercial strategy, including the approach to technology and cloud contracts and lock-in.
Lead negotiations with strategic suppliers, such as clinical system and cloud providers.
Lead the response to supplier failure and serious contract disputes.
Advise executive directors on commercial risk, value for money, and the commercial case for major investments.
Lead collaborative commercial work with other health and care organisations.
qualifications: A recognised procurement professional qualification at the highest level, or a master's degree in a related subject, or equivalent experience.
Extensive experience of leading commercial functions.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Communication is level 6 for negotiating highly contentious commercial matters with strategic suppliers.

levels.title: Director of procurement and commercial
levels.summary: Is the organisation's senior commercial leader, accountable for procurement and commercial policy, and advises the board on commercial strategy and risk.
responsibilities: Set the organisation's procurement and commercial policy and strategy, approved by the board.
Advise the board and executive team on commercial strategy, risk, and the largest contracts and investments.
Assure the organisation's compliance with public procurement rules and its readiness to defend challenges.
Lead executive relationships with strategic suppliers and public sector buying organisations.
Set social value and sustainable procurement goals and report outcomes to the board.
Lead and develop the commercial leadership team and the organisation's commercial skills.
qualifications: A recognised procurement professional qualification at the highest level, or a master's degree in a related subject, or equivalent experience.
Extensive experience of leading commercial functions at executive level.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Policy is level 6 for corporate responsibility for procurement and commercial policy; emotional effort is level 2 for occasional exposure to stressful disputes, supplier failures, and challenges.

roles.title: Administrator
roles.summary: Administrators keep teams and services running by handling the organisation's day-to-day administration: correspondence, diaries, meetings, records, data entry, ordering, and enquiries. In a digital health care organisation they support digital, clinical, and corporate teams, and often handle confidential information about patients and staff.
healthContext: Administrators often see confidential patient and staff information, so they follow information governance rules closely.
Enquiries may come from patients, care staff, and the public, and some callers may be anxious or distressed.
Accurate records and data entry matter, because errors can flow into clinical systems, reports, and payments.
Many administrative processes are moving to digital tools, so administrators help test and adopt new ways of working.

levels.title: Administrative assistant
levels.summary: Carries out routine administrative tasks for a team, following set procedures with supervision close by.
responsibilities: Answer calls and emails, take accurate messages, and pass enquiries to the right person.
Enter and update data accurately in the team's systems.
File and scan documents and keep shared folders in order.
Book meetings and rooms, and send out papers.
Order stationery and supplies within set procedures.
qualifications: Good literacy, numeracy, and keyboard skills.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Physical skills are scored at level 3 for advanced keyboard skills, with speed and accuracy in typing and data entry.

levels.title: Administrator
levels.summary: Provides a full administrative service to a team or service, handling a range of tasks, some non-routine, and organising own workload.
responsibilities: Manage diaries and arrange meetings, events, and travel for a team.
Take minutes and action notes for team meetings and follow up actions.
Handle routine correspondence and enquiries, drafting replies where needed.
Maintain records, trackers, and databases, and produce simple reports.
Process orders, invoices, and expenses within set limits.
Show new staff the team's administrative procedures.
qualifications: A level 3 qualification in business administration, or equivalent experience.

levels.title: Senior administrator
levels.summary: Leads the administration for a service or directorate, supervising other administrators and improving administrative processes.
responsibilities: Coordinate the administrative service for a directorate, allocating work to administrators.
Take formal minutes for management and programme meetings.
Write and improve administrative procedures and templates.
Produce reports from trackers and systems for managers.
Monitor spending on administrative budgets and raise variances.
Train and supervise administrators and apprentices.
qualifications: Substantial administrative experience, at a level equivalent to a foundation degree.

roles.title: Executive assistant
roles.summary: Executive assistants give senior leaders high-level administrative and business support. They manage diaries, correspondence, meetings, and papers, act as a point of contact for the leader's office, and use judgement to deal with matters on the leader's behalf. They often handle highly confidential and sensitive information.
healthContext: Senior leaders in health care deal with patient safety incidents, complaints, and staff cases, so executive assistants regularly handle sensitive and confidential material.
Executive offices work closely with boards and committees, so accurate papers, minutes, and governance records matter.
Diaries must make room for urgent matters, such as serious incidents and service outages, at short notice.

levels.title: Executive assistant
levels.summary: Provides executive support to a director or senior leader, managing their diary, correspondence, and meetings.
responsibilities: Manage a senior leader's diary, setting priorities and resolving clashes.
Handle correspondence, drafting replies and dealing with routine matters on the leader's behalf.
Prepare papers, presentations, and briefings for meetings.
Take minutes and track actions for the leader's meetings.
Act as the first point of contact for the leader's office, using tact and discretion.
Arrange travel, events, and visits.
qualifications: Substantial experience of administrative support to senior staff, at a level equivalent to a foundation degree.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Communication is scored at level 4 because the job regularly handles sensitive matters that need tact and persuasion with senior internal and external contacts.

levels.title: Senior executive assistant
levels.summary: Provides executive support to the chief executive, chair, or an executive director, and coordinates the business of their office.
responsibilities: Manage the diary and priorities of the chief executive or an executive director.
Handle sensitive correspondence, including complaints and enquiries from partners and regulators.
Coordinate executive team meetings, papers, and action logs.
Take formal minutes for executive and committee meetings.
Track commitments and deadlines across the executive office and chase progress.
Supervise other assistants and cover across the executive office.
qualifications: Extensive experience of executive support, at a level equivalent to a degree.

levels.title: Executive office manager
levels.summary: Manages the executive office, its staff, and its business cycle, and makes sure the executive team and board are well supported.
responsibilities: Manage the executive office team, setting priorities and supporting their development.
Plan the business cycle for the executive team, including forward plans and papers.
Make sure briefings, papers, and correspondence are accurate, timely, and well judged.
Coordinate the executive response to urgent matters, such as serious incidents and enquiries.
Manage the executive office budget and its systems.
Improve executive office processes and tools.
qualifications: Extensive experience of executive support and office management, at a level equivalent to a degree.

roles.title: Project support officer
roles.summary: Project support officers help projects and programmes run smoothly by maintaining plans, registers, and documents, organising meetings, and producing reports. At senior levels they run the project management office (PMO), giving leaders a clear view of progress, risks, and benefits across the organisation's portfolio of digital change.
healthContext: Digital health projects need clinical safety, information governance, and security approvals at set points, so project support tracks these as key milestones.
Projects often depend on clinicians and care staff whose time is limited, so planning around clinical rotas and service pressures matters.
Portfolio reporting helps leaders decide which changes go ahead when clinical services are under pressure.

levels.title: Project support officer
levels.summary: Gives administrative support to one or more projects, maintaining records and organising meetings under the guidance of a project manager.
responsibilities: Maintain project documents, with version control, in the project repository.
Update action, risk, issue, and decision logs.
Organise project meetings, send papers, and take action notes.
Collect updates from the team for status reports.
Handle routine project correspondence and enquiries.
qualifications: A level 3 qualification in business administration or project support, or equivalent experience.

levels.title: Project coordinator
levels.summary: Coordinates project controls for several projects or a programme, maintaining plans and registers and producing regular reports.
responsibilities: Maintain project plans, registers, and trackers for several projects.
Produce regular status and highlight reports.
Track project budgets and spending, and raise variances.
Check that projects follow the agreed method, including clinical safety and information governance steps.
Coordinate project boards, papers, and actions.
Support project managers with stakeholder communications.
qualifications: A foundation project management qualification, or equivalent experience.

levels.title: PMO analyst
levels.summary: Analyses progress, risk, and benefits across a programme or portfolio, and runs project management office processes.
responsibilities: Analyse progress, risks, issues, dependencies, and benefits across projects.
Produce portfolio dashboards and reports for programme and portfolio boards.
Run planning, change control, and assurance processes.
Help project managers set up projects with the right controls and documents.
Maintain the PMO's tools, templates, and guidance.
Coach project support officers.
qualifications: A project, programme, or portfolio management qualification, or equivalent experience.

levels.title: PMO manager
levels.summary: Manages the project management office for a programme or portfolio, setting standards and giving leaders reliable insight into delivery.
responsibilities: Lead the project management office and its staff.
Set project and portfolio standards, methods, and tools.
Give senior leaders clear insight into portfolio progress, risks, and benefits.
Run portfolio governance, including prioritisation, gateway reviews, and change control.
Monitor programme budgets and resources, and report on them.
Coach project managers on method and controls.
qualifications: A recognised project, programme, or portfolio management qualification, or equivalent experience.
Experience of running a project management office.

roles.title: Governance and risk manager
roles.summary: Governance and risk staff make sure the organisation is well run and in control of its risks. They support the board and its committees, run the risk management framework and registers, keep policies and governance registers in order, and coordinate assurance and audit, so that leaders can make sound decisions and show they meet their legal and regulatory duties.
healthContext: Health care organisations carry clinical, information, cyber, financial, and reputational risks, so the risk framework must bring these together for the board.
Boards must show they are assured about patient safety and quality, so governance staff link clinical safety and quality reporting into committees.
Regulators and auditors expect clear records of decisions, risks, declarations of interest, and policies.
Serious incidents and service failures need fast, well-documented escalation through the governance structure.

levels.title: Governance officer
levels.summary: Supports the governance cycle for committees and keeps risk, policy, and governance registers up to date.
responsibilities: Coordinate committee meetings, forward plans, papers, and minutes.
Maintain the risk register, prompting risk owners to review their risks.
Keep governance registers up to date, such as declarations of interest, gifts, and hospitality.
Maintain the policy register and track policy reviews.
Coordinate evidence for audits and track audit recommendations.
Answer routine governance questions from staff.
qualifications: A degree or a governance qualification, or equivalent experience.

levels.title: Senior governance and risk officer
levels.summary: Runs parts of the governance and risk framework, advising directorates on risk and supporting senior committees.
responsibilities: Run the risk management process for directorates, challenging risk scores and controls.
Prepare risk and assurance reports for senior committees.
Support senior committees, including the audit and risk committee, with papers and formal minutes.
Review policies for compliance with the policy framework, law, and equality duties.
Train managers in risk management and governance processes.
Coordinate the organisation's response to regulator and audit requests.
qualifications: A degree or professional qualification in governance or risk management, or equivalent experience.

levels.title: Governance and risk manager
levels.summary: Manages the governance and risk service, including the board and committee cycle, the risk framework, and assurance mapping.
responsibilities: Manage the board and committee cycle and the governance team.
Run the organisation's risk management framework and the board assurance framework.
Advise directors on risks, risk appetite, and escalation.
Map assurance across the organisation's main risks and work with internal and external auditors.
Keep standing orders, schemes of delegation, and the policy framework up to date.
Coordinate the governance response to serious incidents and regulator enquiries.
qualifications: A professional qualification in governance or risk management, or equivalent experience.
Substantial experience of corporate governance or risk management.

levels.title: Head of corporate governance
levels.summary: Leads corporate governance and risk for the organisation, often acting as board secretary, and advises the chair and board on governance.
responsibilities: Design and lead the organisation's governance framework, including the board and its committees.
Act as board secretary, advising the chair and board on governance, conduct, and compliance.
Own the risk management framework and risk appetite, and advise the board on strategic risks.
Lead the annual governance statement and governance reporting.
Lead the governance, risk, and assurance team.
Represent the organisation with regulators and auditors on governance matters.
qualifications: A professional qualification in corporate governance, or equivalent experience.
Extensive experience of leading governance and risk at board level.

roles.title: Communications officer
roles.summary: Communications staff help the organisation explain what it does to staff, patients, the public, partners, and the media. They write and publish content, run internal communications and campaigns, manage digital and social media channels, handle media enquiries, and protect the organisation's reputation, especially during incidents and outages.
healthContext: Communications about health services must be accurate, clear, and accessible, because patients may act on them.
Campaigns often aim to change behaviour, such as encouraging patients and care staff to use a new digital service.
Service outages, cyber incidents, and data breaches need fast, careful communications with patients, staff, partners, and the media.
Stories about patients need consent and must protect confidentiality.

levels.title: Communications officer
levels.summary: Writes and publishes content for internal and external channels and supports the communications team with routine media and campaign work.
responsibilities: Write and edit news, intranet content, newsletters, and social media posts.
Publish approved content on the website, intranet, and social media.
Log media enquiries and monitor coverage.
Support campaigns and events with content and logistics.
Check content for accuracy, accessibility, and plain English.
qualifications: Experience of writing for different audiences, or a qualification in communications or a related subject, or equivalent experience.

levels.title: Senior communications officer
levels.summary: Plans and delivers communications for projects and services, handles routine media enquiries, and manages channels.
responsibilities: Plan and deliver communications for projects and service changes.
Respond to routine media enquiries and draft press releases and statements.
Manage content plans for digital and social media channels, and report on performance.
Write case studies, including patient stories, with consent.
Advise colleagues on writing clearly for patients and the public.
Coach communications officers.
qualifications: A degree or qualification in communications or a related subject, or equivalent experience.

levels.title: Communications lead
levels.summary: Leads communications for a major programme or area, such as internal communications or digital channels, and handles sensitive media work.
responsibilities: Lead communications and engagement for a major programme, such as a new clinical system.
Plan and evaluate campaigns that encourage patients and staff to adopt digital services.
Handle sensitive media enquiries and prepare spokespeople.
Plan communications for incidents and service outages with operational teams.
Advise leaders on how to communicate change and difficult messages.
Supervise communications officers.
qualifications: A degree or professional qualification in communications, or equivalent experience.
Experience of planning and evaluating campaigns.

levels.title: Communications manager
levels.summary: Manages the communications team's work and channels, and leads media handling and communications for incidents.
responsibilities: Manage the communications team, its work plan, and its budget.
Lead reactive and proactive media work, including during incidents and data breaches.
Manage the organisation's channels, brand, and content standards.
Advise directors on communications and reputational risks.
Evaluate communications and report on their effect.
Work with partner organisations on joint communications.
qualifications: A professional qualification in communications, or equivalent experience.
Substantial experience of media relations and managing communications.
levels.jobEvaluationNotes: Emotional effort reflects occasional handling of distressing material during incidents and in patient stories.

levels.title: Head of communications
levels.summary: Leads communications and engagement for the organisation, sets its strategy, and advises the board on reputation.
responsibilities: Set the communications and engagement strategy for the organisation.
Lead and develop the communications function and manage its budget.
Advise the chief executive and board on reputation, stakeholder engagement, and communications risk.
Lead crisis communications during major incidents.
Build relationships with senior partners, journalists, and patient groups.
Shape how the organisation explains its digital services and its use of data to the public.
qualifications: A professional qualification in communications, or equivalent experience.
Extensive experience of leading communications for a complex organisation.
